ihe Subeeription List will open on Wedemsday. the 25th day of June. and close on or before Thursday. the 26th of June. THE FUSTIAN CUTTING MACHINE COMPANY UNITED.
INCORPORATED UNDER THE COMPANIES ACTS, 1862 to 1886. CAPITAL, £lOO,OOO.
Divided into 8,000 Preferred Shares and 2.000 Deferred Shares of .810 each.

Issue of 7,000 preferred shares, payable as follows ;—£l on Application; RI on Allotment; £2 on the Ist November, 1890; and the balance as and when required. It is not expected that more than £5 per Share will be called up during the next 12 months.

The profits of the Company divisible as Dividend will be applied, first, in payment of a preferential Dividend at the rate of 6 per. cent, per annum on the Capital paid up on the Pre- ferred Shares; secondly, in paYment of a Dividend at the like rate on the amount paid up on the Deferred Shares; and of the surplus, one moiety will be divisible amongst the holders of the Preferred Shares, and the other moiety will be divisible amongst the holders of the Deferred Shares. The above-men- tioned Dividends of 6 percent. per annum will not be cumu- lative.

The whole of the Deferred Shares will be allotted under the Agreement of the 20th of June. 1890, hereinafter referred to as fully paid, and the remaining 1,000 Preferred Shares will be subscribed tw as hereinafter mentioned. PROVISIONAL BOARD OF DIRECTORS.

The Company is formed for the purpose of acquiringthrough the Velvet Cutting Machine Syndicate Limited (hereinafter called " The Syndicate") certain Letters Patent, both English and Foreign, taken out in the names of James Hoyle Smith, Andrew Goddard, Lloyd Ifigginbottam, Thomas Mannock, Abraham Sutcliffe, Dugald Scott, George Roger, and Others, for improvements in apparatus for cutting weft pile fabrics, together with the machinery and plant belonging to the Syndicate... . .

11 'The Syndicate comprises the following members :—Wm. Lockett Agnew, Exchange-street, Manchester. Thomas Clemson, Wm. Clemson & Co., Velvet Dyers, Red Bank, Manchester. Wm. Henry Crabtree, Henry Crabtree & Sons, Velvet Dyers, Ardwick. Edward Deakin, jour., H. & B. Deakin' Belmont, Bolton. Thomas Emmott, Thomas Emmott & Sons, Velvet Manufacturers, Oldham. Joseph Hallworth, Broome, Hallworth. and Foster, Velvet Manufac- tnrers, St. Peter's Square, Manchester. Frank Hollins, Horrockses, Crewdson, & Co., Limited, Preston, Manchester, and London. F. Haworth, Richard Haworth & Co., Velvet Manufacturers, High-street, Manchester. William C. Jones. Jones Brothers and Co.. 12, York-street, Manchester. Joseph Leigh, Stockport. J. W. hlakant William Makant, Gilnew, Bolton. J. j. Mann. Fustian Cutter, Ordsal-lane Mills, Salford. Robert Middleton,Middleton Jones, & Co., Ld., Velvet Manu- facturers, Chorlton-street, Manchester. Joseph Moseley, David Moseley & Sons, Ardwick. Dugald Scott, Jones Bros. & Co., 12, York-street, Manchester. William Slater. G. and J. Slater Dunscar, Bolton. Henry Whitehead, John Whitehead, Elton. Bury. James Worrell, jun., and Henry Worrell, J. and J. M. Worrell Id., Velvet Dyers. Ordsal. Salford, most of Whom are conversant with and are largely interested in the velvet trade and can introduce business to a considerable extent.

The Syndicate was formed in the month of September last. for the purpose of testing the patents above referred to. and ascertaining whether machines constructed In accordance with those patents could out weft pile fabrics better and cheaper than could be done by cutting by hand. Until these patents were introduced it has been always .found impracticable to cut weft pile fabrics otherwise than by the old slow process of hand cutting. Since the Syndicate was formed it has at considerable expense conducted under its own supervision a series of practical tests with machines constructed according to these patents, and the result has been to demonstrate to the entire satisfaction of the Directors that an operative can by means of a machine cut, hi a week of 60 working hours, 4 pieces of 24-inch velvet. 110 yards in length, which is practically 4 times as much as an expert operative Can accomplish in the same time by short hand frame cutting, and that the cutting done by the machine is not only much less expensive than, but is also superior to, the cutting done by hand. Some hundreds of pieces have beSni ent by the machines and dyed, and an opinion has been expressed not only by several Dyers, but also by Manufacturers and Merchants engaged is the velvet trade to whom samples have been submitted. that the cutting done by the machines is superior in quality to that done by hand. ' The Directors believe that a handsome profit can be made by machine cutting at less than the lowest price paid for hand cutting, after taking into consideration the cost of acquiring the patents, erecting or renting suitable premises, cost of machinery. depreciation, wages, and all other outgoings. The Syndicate, shortly after its formation, entered into an Agreement with the then owners pf the patents which gave the Syndicate a right to test and sell the patents. This I Agreement was dated the 16th September. 1889. and made 1 between Lloyd Higginbottom, Thomas Mannock, James I Hoyle Smith, and Andrew Goddard of the first part, Dugald Scott of the second part, and the Syndicate of the third part. Acting under the.powers conferred by the last-mentioned Agreement, the Syndicate has by an Agreement dated the 20th of June, 1890, and made between the Syndicate of the one part and the Company of the other part, agreed to sell the patents to the Company for £30,000, payable as to £lO,OOO part thereof in cash and as to £20,000 the residue in fully paid Deferred Shares of the Company. Thq Agreement pro- vides that of this £30,000, £25,000 shall be treated as the price ot the English Patents, and £5,000 AS the price of the Foreign Patents.

The contideration for the sale of the patents will be divided between the Syndicate end the owners of the patents in cer- tain shares mentioned in the said Agreement of the 16th September. 1889, and the terms of the present sale have been Axed by the Syndicate. • The members of the Syndicate are so satisfied of the Com- pany's success that they have agreed to subscribe for Preferred Shares to the extent of £lO,OOO, so that the amount of the Preferred Shares subscribed for by the members of the Syn- dicate-will be equivalent to the full amount payable for the patents in cash. By the terms of the said Agreement of the 20th of June, 1890, the Company is also to take over all the machinery and plant of the Syndicate at the sum of £2,000 ayable on com- pletion of the purchase in cash.. The Directors believe that with increased experienced the rapidity of the machine work will be increased, and that it will be possible at an early date to cut morie that four pieces of velvet per week of the length and width before mentioned. The Company intend to work the English Patents them- selves, and, upon the assumption that each machine will be 'able to cut only three pieces per week, the Directors are con- vinced that the net profits derived by working the English Patents alone will be suffici.-nt to ensure very remunerative dividends for the Shareholders.

It is the intention of the Company to dispose of the Foreign Patents (for which there are several applicants) as early as possible, and the Articles of Association provide that all profits made by the Company by the resale of such patents at an in- creased price shall be (feared as income, and carried to the credit of profit and loss account.
It is iniended to apply for a quotation on the Manchester Stock Exchange.

The Capital—of the Company has not been underwritten, and (except the amount payable to the Syndicate) no promotion money has been or will be paid. The Company will, however, pay the usual brokers' charges, The Reports mentioned below have been made. The above-menticned Agreements of the 16th of September, 1889, and the 20th of June, 1890. are believed to be the only contracts the dates of which and names of the parties to which are required by the 38th Section of the Companies Act. 1867, to be set out herein, but Applicants for Shares must be deemed to waive the Specification a the dates and names of the parties to any other contracts (If there be any) and shall waive all further compliance with that section. Applicatiox for Shares should be made on the accompany ing form and sent with the deposit to the Bankers of the Company, or to the Secretary of the Company at the Com- pany's Offices. If the whole ardount applied for by any applicant is not allotted the surplus paid on deposit will be credited to the sum due on allotment, and where no allot- ment is made the deposit will be returned in full. Prospectuses and forms of application may be obtained at the Offices of the Company. or from the Bankers' Brokers or Solicitors of the Company. Prints of the Memorandum and Articles of Association and copies of the two before-mentioned Agreements and of the re- ports mentioned below may be inspected at the Offices of the Company's Solicitor*. REPORTS. • Mr. Hallworth (Broome, Hallworth, & Foster., Velvet Manu- facturers, Manchester),—.• I have had some hundreds of pieces of velvets and twill velt•ets cut by the cotting machine. I find that they are More satisfactory than hand- cut goods. In the dyed and finished tate they are more satisfactory and are in my opinion of greater value." Mr. Middleton (Midlleton. Jones, & Co. Limited, Velvet Manufacturers, Manchester).—"l have seen the cutting machine at work and have had many pieces cut by it. I consider it has many advantage* over either short or long hand frame cutting. The face of the cloth when dyed is perfectly level and free from the racy and shady appearance of hand cutting. Mr. Henry Worrell (J. A J. M. Worrell Limited, Velvet 13 -ers, Ordsall, Salford).—" I have stood by the cutting machine, timed and carefully measured the quantity of work it was doing. The result of my calculations shows that the machine was cutling at the rate of 4 pieces of 24-inch velvet, 110 yards long, per week. My firm has dyed and finished a large number of machine-cut pieces, and 1 Con- sider the quality of the cutting superior to the average quality of hand cutting." Messrs. Geo. Davies & Son (Patent Agents, Manchester).— For many years we have taken out Patents, and had to do with attempts at making velvet cutting machines. None of these attempts have succeeded, so far as we are aware, until the present ones. We have examlned the Patents, and have made a thorough search through the Records of the Patent Office, and, in our opinion. the Patents are perfectly sound and valid, and the inventions original.

This Company has been formed to acquire and further de- velop the well-known business now carried on by a private registere(l Syndicate under the title of " Sequah (Limited)." The operations of the Syndicate have extended over a period of fifteen months, the business having previously been con- ducted by Mr. W. H. Hartley, who, being desirous of trans- ferring it to a public Company for the purpose of further de- velopment, assigned his rights to the- present Vendor Syndi- cate, which was formed with a view to practically test the commercial value of the remedies before inviting subscriptions from the general public. The remarkable results of the Syndi- cate's trading are seen in the highly satisfactory certificate of the Accountants, given below. Under the management of the Syndicate the business has been rapidly extended with the result that at the present time it is found necessary, in order to cope withthe exigencies of an enormous and growing trade, as also to establish the business in countries to which the Syndicate has, as yet, not been able to ;devote any attention, to largely increase the working capital, and to provide a more exensive personnel than the Syndicate is able tocpmmand. It is well known that a patent medicine, when fully esta- blished and recognised as an efficacious remerly, is a most valuable property. This Is a fact which has been demon- strated by Holloway, Warner, and many others, with whose names the world 12 familiar.

.... The Directors feel confident that there is not at present time a patent remedy which, judged by the steadily increas- ing sale and results, offers an equally substantial investment or equally assured prospects as are offered by the Sequah Prairie Flower and Seqnah Oil. When it is borne in mind that the Vendor Syndicate, con- trary to the general practice of proprietors of patent medi- cines has, by means of the particular system it employs, been enabled to reach the masses of the people without the enor- mous expense of universal journalistic advertisement, the present extensive proportions of the business may be taken as a fair criterion of the effieacy and popularity of the remedies, which, moreover, are voucked for by very numerous testi- monials, not only from patients, but also from clergynen of all denominations. _ _

; Before the Syndicate acquired the property " Sequah "was represented by one person only, but it afterwards became necessary to increase the working staff, and a number of capable men were selected and specially trained for the pur- pose of ixtroducing the medicines. These representatives have for some time past been working with great success, and have largely increased the sales. The increase in said from May, 1889, to May, 1890, has been remarkable, toe number of bottles sold, as shown by the books, being as follows

Cooper Bros. and Co.. the well-known chartered accountants, who have examined the books of the Syndicate :- 14, George-street, Mansion House, London, E.G., 11th June, 1890. We have examined the books of the buslne.'s cart+ d on under the name of Sequah (Limited) for the twelve months ending 31st May, 1890, and we find that the net profit has been £44,584 12s. 9d. We have also ascertained, by examin- ing each quarter separately, that the sales and the net profit have steadily and largely increased in each quarter. The pro- fits of the quarters, taken separately, have been approximately as follows :
Profit for the At the rate per Quarter. Annum of Quarter ending 31st Aug., 1889—£8,951 4 9—£35,804 19 0 30th Nov., 1889...10,844 9 9... 43.377 19 0 „ 2.Bth Feb., 1890...11,822 15 6... 47.91 .2 0

It appears from the ahoy; -Certificate that during the last three months the net profits have been at the rate of over £50,000 per annum.
Having regard to the Company's increased resources, the above profits actually certified, may be taken as a minimum ()inmate, and would yield a dividend as follows _ _ _
Preference Shares of cent £lO.OOO £200,01.0 Ordinary Shares of 20 per cent... 40,000

£50,000 Investors must lake into consideration that even the esti- mated dividend of 20 per cent, does not exhaust the full pro- fits now actually being earned by the Snclicate, aria as these have been steadily on the increase since th commencement, it is fair to assume that much larger dividends will accrpe. Whereas, up to the present the Syndicate has confined Its operations to the sale in the United Kingdom of the two remedies, Prairie Flower and Sequah Oil only, the Company will also acquire several other proprietary articles, which may be profitably put on the market and energetically pushed through the Syndicate Agencies already established, and as these do not in any way clash wills the goods now being sold, they,may be easily introduced to the Syndicate's present con- nection, and should therefore provide an important addition to the Company's business without appreciably increased ex- penditure. 7lltle Company will, moreover, have the means of extending its operatious to the Continent of Europe, and other parts of the world, where, in view of the populations which may be approached, it may reasonably be expected that the profits shouldlat least equal those already obtained in this country. The population of the United Kingdom is only about 38,000,000. whereas that of the European Continent alone reaches the enormous aggregate of over 300,000,000. Negotiations, with a view to commence business in Austria and Russia, have already been started by cue of the members of the present management. Taking the course of business in this country as a precedent, the Directors confidently antici- pate that, under the same management, within reasonable time from the establishment of the Company, the results ob- tained from the Continental bugloss will add very consider- ably to the Company's profits. filte Company will commence with ample working capital, and retain the present staff and management, which have worked with such unqualified success for the Vendor Syndi- cate.

The business will be taken over as from the Ist of June, 1890, up to which date the Vendor Syndicate will pay all out- goings and liabilities. The price to be paid for the same as a going cohcern, including the valuable trade marks, goodwill, extensive stock in trade, and the lease of premises, No. 44, Parringdon-street, E.C., has been fixed by the Vendors, who are the promoters, at £250,000, payable as follows :—£150,001 in cash, £33,333 in fully-paid Cumulative Preference Shares, and the balance. £66,666, in fully-paid Ordinary Shares in the Company, the Vendors thus taking the largest number of Shares permitted by the rules of the Stock Exchange. Thns 50,000 Shares are available for issue as working capital, being the difference between the purchase price and the capital of the Company. No promotion money has been or will be paid, the Vendor agreeing to defray all expenses up to the first allotment of Shares, including brokerage. The following Contracts, relating to the sale of the business. have been entered into : A Contract dated June 19th, 1890, between Sequel (Limited) and William Loomis Sheldon, of the one part, and Sequah (Limited)(being this Company), of the other part and another Contract, dated June 19th, 1890, between William Henry Hartley, cf the one part, and Sequah (Limited) (being this Company), of the other part. A copy of the above Contracts and of the Memorandum and Articles of Association can be seen at the office of the Com- pany's Solicitor. Contracts have been entered into for bringing out the Com- pany, to none of which the Company is a party, and there are also other Contracts which have been made in the ordinary course of business in relation to the carrying on of the same, Including agreements with employes and others. As these may technically be contracts within the meaning of Section 38 of "The Companies Act. 1867," applicants for Shares shall accept the above as notice thereof, and waive any further com- pliance with such section. A Stock Exchange settlement and quotation will be applied for in due course. Applications for Shares should be made on the Form accom- panying the Prospectus, and forwarded to the Company's Bankers, together with a remittance for the amount of the deposit. Where no allotment is made the dep,osit will be re- turned in full. If the whole amount applied for by any appli- cant be not allotted, the surplus paid on deposit will be ap- propriated towards the sum due on allotment. . . .
Prospectuses and Forms of Application can be obtained at the Offices of the Company, and from the Bankers, Brokers, or Solicitor. _ _ _ _

D TUMMY. Th, owd fella's deod an' gone, His heart wur true as gowd, A kindlier or fairer mon Ne'er laid i' graveyard mowd. No tongue speyks ill ov.him, He scorned wocle'er wur bad, Fond memory meks eawr eyeseet dim, An' pony a heart feels sad. Aye, he's laid low at last,
We'at meet on earth no mooar,

His happy soul deoth's river's passed, An' stans on't gowden shore. Just peep i' th' churchyard's nook, Thad heop o' sodden clay Shows his last shop,—we nobbut took Him to id t' other day. Tho' he's gone quately hooam, Fond Fancy likes to leod Eawr thowts on th' track he used to rooam, An' we kornd think him deod ! For when we wander reawnd Each owd familiar place, We bear his voice's welcome seawnd,

An' see his smilin' face. Hey, mony a woodland wawk, An' mony a meal we've shared;' 'Twur grand to hear th' owd tawk While t' bride aboon us paired. He'd lived for mony a year I' th' bonny country side Height fain to greet Fair Natur' theer As Summer's sunny bride. His words wur true an' wise,

His ways wur allus kind, His goodness showed wod deep Faith lies At rest i' monhood's mind. His knowledge free wur gi'en ; An' th' gossips used to say, I' heigh position he'd ha' bin, But trubble blocked his way. He bed bin browt up weel, His gentleness towd thad: Beawt pride, his presence med us feel Respect for th' good owd lad. Wod little he'd to spare Wur doled i' charity; Poor sufferers mingle sigh an' prayer

When benefactors dee. He'd hobbled wi' his stick, Deawn broo a tidy while; But tho' worn eawt, an' pale an' sick, His thin face wooar a smile. An' when at th' last ov o' Faith led him wi' id leet, He quately turned his face toft wo, An' bade this world " good fleet." Aye, good owd Tumray's gone Aboon to t' gowden shore; & simple, plain, God fearin' mon; We'st see his like no mooar. Content he lived an' deed As payshunt Christians shuct An' th' epitaph o'er him shud read— "His aim wur—doin' good."

Not a legal point—Punctuation. Pen—The stiletto of civilisation. Man is only miserable so far as he thinks himself so. A stag party would be twice as enjoyable if a few dears were invited.

Ink—A melancholy euid in which the modern stiletto is too recklessly dipped. If others did not sometimes annoy us we should not realise how much we annoy others. In true marriage the wife must give as well as take— give love and forbearance, and help and comfort. On sir Oozes- Garrnoenn.—" Great Scott, what a lot of food that man eats! Be must be what they call a stowaway." Frugality, diligence, punctuality, veracity—these are the grand fountains from which money, and all real values and velours, spring for men. Woman: "You're the first tramp I've seen about here this spring." Tramp: "Yes, ma'am; I always was noted for my enterprise and push." Wife: "I must have thirteen shillings." Husband: "Thirteen, my dear, is an unlucky number. I'll make it twelve." Byer alter she asked fourteen. A woman has suggested that when men break their hearts it is the same when a lobster breaks one of his claws—another sprouts immediately and grows in its place. Cabby (to bicyclist) : "That horse o! yours 'II no need muckle feedin' or whuppin'." Bicyclist: "No, jist a wee bit taste o' ile noos and therm, an' a touch o! a screw driver!"

II" I have at last consented to my daughter's marriage with George. You know he saved her from drowning whilst bathing." Little Tommy (speaking up) : "Sister told me it was a put-up job." A.: "I have been very fortunate in my love affairs." B.: "And vet you have never married." A.: "Precisely; that is what I mean. According to my notion, the men who are most unlucky in love are those who get mar- ried."

Jones last Saturday received the following note from a friend :—" Come and dine with me to-morrow at six o'clock, with two or three friends." (Jones, who is a very liberal person, arrives promptly at the appointed hour with three of his friends). Mrs. Watts: "Mr. Watts and I make it a rule never to quarrel before the children. If we have any argu- ment with each other, we always send them out of the room." Mrs. Potts; "I have often wondered why your children were out in the street so much."

John K. Adams died in New Jersey the other day, at the age of 78, and when on his dying bed he figured up tbat all the good he had ever been to earth was to kill a mad dog, break three colts, and marry a cross-eyed woman who couldn't find any other husband. "My hands are awfully cold," said the pretty girl, suggestively, during the last quarter of a starlit sleigh ride. "Why didn't you briar a muff with you?" asked the practical young man, Prosaically. "I did !" she snapped; but she wouldn't explain where the muff had gone to, and he has been wondering ever since just what she meant.

"Hear on't man ? " was the reply. " Wcy, aa hear on't ivvory day : watch wor wife for that. She elwis fetches her ower when thor's owf wrang ?" No applause.) Missionary: "Yes, my friends, 10,000 suits of clothes!" (Waits for applause, but none comes.) Missionary (desperately) : "Or 1,190,500 glasses of whisky.' (Audience, to a man, rises to its feet and shrieks with excitement).

Young Winkle: "Dick, my boy, will your sister Polly be home this evening ?" Little Dick: " Guesso." Winkle: "It is only a night or two since I called, but I'd like to call again this evening if P.hought she'd be home. Here's some candy for you, Dick." Little Dick: "Thanks, awfully." Winkle: "Now, Dick, I want you to be a good little friend of mine." Little Dick: I'll be careful not to let her know you're coming."

Docroa AND Flamm—lt is two o'clock in the morn- ing; Doctor P—, who has been hurriedly summoned, is at the bedside of a patient. After examining her gravely, he says in a solemn voice: "Madame, if you have any matters to arrange, send for your lawyer; furthermore, if you have any religious faith, give, orders that a priest be called." "Mercy!" cries the terrified patient; "then lam lost?" For at least five minutes the doctor makes no answer; the lady is on the point of fainting. "No," he says at last, "but I should be sorry to be the only one awakened for nothing."

THE UNATTAINABLE. On occult sciences she dwelt—this learn-ed Boston Miss; Bile talked of Nowness of the Then, and Thatness of the This. "And do you not," she asked, " in times of fervour long to grasp 'The distant Unattainable—the Just Beyond your grasp?"

'The rude Chicago mind to which the question was addressed Looked in her far-off, soulful eyes, and candidly confessed: "Indeed I do, just lots of times?" Oh, Concord, calm thy shades! "It's when I'd reach an itching just between my shoulder blades."

LiSZT—AND THE PIANO FlEND.—Wrapped in his dress- ing-gown and with feet encased in slippers, Franz Liszt was sitting comfortably one evening in his armchair, ready for work and inviting inspiration. On the floor above, in the apartments of a banker, a noisy musical fioir4e was in progress. The keys of the piano, brutally treated, seemed to be flying to pieces and suffering as much as the master himself. Polonaises had succeeded waltzes, and nocturnes had followed polonaises, when suddenly the doors of the salon opened—and who entered? Liszt in person, still wrapped in his dressing- gown. Imagine the astonishment with which the bril- liant assembly was filled by this apparition as strange as unexpected! But to the revered master everything was pardoned, even eccentric behaviour; and all watched his movements with the keenest curiosity. With slow steps Liszt walked toward the piano, and the young key. pounder who was sitting at it quickly left his place. Liszt sat down at the instrument, carelessly swept his fingers over the keys as if to prelude, and then, suddenly, he shut down the cover and put the key in his pocket. And immediately, with the same tranquil air with which he had entered, he went out and returned to his room, where he could work at his ease. I hear that Sir George Trevelyan's youngest son, following in the steps of his father and elder brothers, has won the highest classical prize atllar- row for which he was of an age to compete. The heredity of scholarships among those great-nephews of Lord Macaulay is very curious.

It is almost settled that Lord 'Ripon will be the candidate of the 'Progressives for the chairmanship of the London County Council. His name is most favourably received, and he is willing to stand, pro- vided the party unite in his favour. There is, there- fore, very little doubt of his election.

Dr. Edward Aveling was born in Ireland in 1851, of a family wonderfully old, with a genealogical tree that reaches back to the Crusades. "I can boast," he says, "of having grandsires that richly deserved banging." lie is, says M. Lafargue, "of feverish activity, explicable, perhaps, by the mixture in his veins ot French and Irish blood.:"

The proprietors of the 'Times" have bought the original drawing of le grand Blowitz, who formed the subject of a cartoon in Vanity Fair in December • last. The " Times " should also acquire the original -drawing of another distin- guished member of its staff—now deceased— Pigott.

Mr. Dillon has been chaffed over a pretty little piece of enthusiasmwhich occurred at Mr. O'Brien's weddink. A warm-hearted lady admirer, to whom Mr. Dillon has always been an heroic figure, took him round the neck and kissed him. Mr. Dillon was a trifle embarrassed by this token of esteem, but he bore the ordeal with great good humour.

The Hon. John Collier, who painted the portrait of Mr. John Barns in the Grosvenor Gallery, is a son- in-law of Professor Huxley. Mr. Collier married his deceased wife's sister, and would thus be honored with the -censure of the House of Lords.

" All that time," writes Mrs. Fenwick Miller, "Mr. Collier lived with his father-in-law, and the confid- ence that he inspired in his adopted family has been strongly proved'by their giving him another daugh- ter for his second wife. Sach marriage are not legal in England; but that they are illegal is solely owing to clerical bigotry. Again and again the House of Commons has passed the Act of Parlia- ment to make such unions again lawful, as they were in Great'Britain up to 1834; and again and again the 'bishops' votes alone in the House of Lords have caused the rejection of the Bill. Accord- ingly, except among people as clerical as the bishops themselves, there is no social stigma on such marri- ages. Professor and Mrs. Huxley accompanied their daughter to Sweden last year, and there gave her formally to their son-in-law. In English law it is not a marriage, but English society ascepts it, and public opinion sanctions it.

The German Emperor is giving practical effect to his views on the great social question of the day. He has written to the authorities at Konigsberg, expressing 'his approval of the inhabitants of the town decorating their houses with flowers and branches of trees during his recent visit, instead of indulging in costly fites and erecting expensive triumphal arches. He added that in his opinion nothing gave a demonstration so much real value as the spontaneous participation of the poor.

The eighteenth annual report of the Amalgamated Society of Railway Servants states that the society has addedl7,soo members to its ranks and increased its funds by £B,OOO during the year. For some years this society had done but little recruiting. The events of the annua mirabilis of labour have,however, made themselves felt, and the new Union of Rail- way Workers. which Mr. John Burns floated in the autumn, has been a most stimulating auxiliary to the elder society.

Sit Morell Mackenzie is to give fifteen lectures in America at the rate of £l3O a lecture—making a nice little sum of £2,000. Sir Morell will lecture at New York, Philadelphia, Boston, Washington, Baltimore, Chicago, St. Louis, and several other cities in the States. He has declined to go west of Omaha or South of Richmond, but will lecture in Canada, both' at Montreal and Toronto. .He will leave England at the end of September, and will be back at the beginning of November.

Ascot, to say the plain truth, is a great place for gambling. "Bad Ascots" and "Black Ascots" are known to all writers of sporting fiction. Nowadays, too, ladies have taken to betting with that earnest resolve toequal men which has produced a female senior wrangler and a fenole senior classic. " What sort of day have you bri having?" I heard one grandly dressed dame ask another. "I've won this last race," was the answer; "but I've lost on the day." It was difficult to persuade myself that I was not listening to the after-mess talk of two cavalry subalterns.

While the Rev. H. D. Rawnsley, of Keswick, was lunching last week with Lord Tennyson, at Fresh- water, news was brought that a buzzard, a kite, and a hoopoe had been shot in that neighbourhood. The poet, who, in the name of Queen Boadicea, bade the "raven, the kite, and the kestrel blacken round the Roman carrion;" expressed, we are told, "strong indignation" at this reckless destruction of crea- tures that are constantly growing rarer in these isles. The Hampshire folk, though they dwell in Gilbert White's county, are apparently not much impressed with the gentle curare of Selborne's re- gard for natural objects.

Writing in her journal "Washington," Miss Kate Field tells the following story of Miss Dorothy Ten- nant. One day, when seeking a model, Miss Ten- nant discovered a likely substitute in the shape Of a crossing-sweeper, and while conducting him to Richmond-terrace, she met her family's old friend, Mr. Gladstone. Greatly amused at her companion, the Grand Old Man exclaimed, "Who's your friend?" Then and there the crossing-sweeper, much to his dismay, was presented to the "People's William." On entering the Tennant mansion, this urchin was tremendously impressed by the liveried servant who had opened the door, and, after looking back at him several times, whispered mysteriously to his kind hostess, "I say, miss, why does your big brother wear brass buttons?"

Always thoughtful, Miss Tennant first led her charge to the servants' hall, where she sat beside him as he played havoc with the well-filled dishes placed before him. At the conclusion of his repast, Miss Tennant asked the boy how he liked it. " Proper ! "replied the crossing-sweeper. " Yer mother do cook prime !" Many were the passages traversed before reaching the servants' hall—a fact which made a deep im- pression on the model that was to be, who at last said : "How many rooms yer got ?" On being told, the unbelieving gamix retorted : " Gar'n, yer kiddin'!" "How many rooms have you e inquired Miss Tennant. "Two." "And how many are there in your family ?" " There's eight o' us. There's father an' mother an' the two girls in one room, an' me an' brother Bill an' granny an' the pup in t'other. '

That Prince Bismarck is a man of many parts every one is aware, but how many people know that he has in his time played the part of a law court reporter/ Yet such is, indeed, the case, for after passing his State examination in law at the University of Berlin, the embryo Chancellor was made official law reporter at one of the courts of that city. But Bismarck the young law reporter lacked the discretion and diplomacy ot Bismarck the Chancellor. He one day engaged in a wordy war with a certain pig-headed witness, and at last threatened the object of his wrath that he 'would have him kicked out. The judge, however, re- proved the young reporter by saying that he attended to the kicking out. "Well," said Bismarck to the objectionable witness, "be careful what you say, or I will get the judge to kick you out."

THE SIGNALMAN ON THE MIDLAND.

There sre probably aboait a million men employed in varions capacities on the Railways of Great , Britlan—a number large enough, if they were soldiers, to overrun Europe. Upon the intelligence, fidelity, and physical condition of this vast army depend the lives of the multitudes who are constantly travelling by rail. Any sudden and serious disability happening to one of them may result in a disaster which would put hundreds of tamilies in mourning. Accustomed as it is to safe and swift conveyance frcm point to point, the public scarcely realises this fact. The following brief narra- tive, which is strictly true, will therefore be read with interest 1—

On the Midland Railway, twenty-three miles south of Carlisle, there is a little station called Culgaith. Here there is.a 81gna14box in which Signalman Andrew Agge is to be found on duty daily. As is the cafe with all other signal boxes, this one contains the levers and the usual complicated electric and mechanical contrivances for making and receiving signals. Mr. Agge is on duty nearly every day, and takes his luncheons without leaving his post. He is a sturdy man of thirty-five, in good health, and no complaint has ever been made against him by the Company or by the public ; yet an incident occurred a few years ago that came near depriv- ing laina of his position and his life. For some time he had not felt well, the worst and most dangerous phase of his indisposition being a kind of giddiness that would seize him unexpectedly and, as he described it, " Set everything to .moving and twisting round and round." The doctor told him frankly that it was a symptom of a still more radioal complaint brought on by two much confinement, and by his irregular habits of eating and sleeping, and that he had better abandon his work for a while, and try a change of scene.

But this was easier said than done. He had a family to support, and couldn't afford the luxury of a vacation. He knew no other business, and could not risk the loss of his place. His work was always done, however, no matter how he felt. But it is only fair to say he had many anxious hours over it. His ailment, which he had discovered to be indigestion and dyspepsia, now set up more alarming symptoms. A physician at Appleby assured Agge that there was serious trouble with his kidneys and bladder. "It is," said the doctor to the Signalman, -44 the result of the condition of you diges- tion. Your blood is poisoned by your stomach, and every organ of the body is crippled by it." This was a miserable outlook for Agge, who went back to Culgaith with small courage for his work. He took howl, though, as well as he could, and kept it up until one morning several weeks afterwards. He was in his box as usual when of a sudden a sharp pain shot thr-u, g I him as though he had been stabbed with a . gAt tumbled down on the locker in the ignaL nil lay there all the forenoon in acute distress ,aici . . For the time his work was a seconc ary consici ration. I Unable to remain in that position any longer, I,e laid down and rolled on the floor. The pain in his hips and back was so intense that he compared it to being cut with dull knives, and pierced with hot irons. Agge was alone when the attack came, and as nobody except rail- way officials are allowed in the signal boxes, it was some time before his plight was discovered. Finally, I however, the station-master came in, the neighbours were summoned, and the suffering man was put into a trap -and taken to his house, half a mile away. There he was ill for weeks, part of the time unconscious. When the physicians had avowedly got to the end of their resources it was agreed that the Signalman's end was only a matter of a very little time. This was the situation when a singular thing happened. Two or three years before, while Agge was feeling the earlier symptoms of his disorder, he had taken a medicine that held him; getting better, he put the bottle aside, still half full, and forgot it altogether. Now, as he was almost in a dying condition, his memory flashed up one day, and he distinctly recalled where he had put it. A search was made and then it was found. The prostrate signalman began using it and, to the astonishment of neighbours and doctors, in a few days was able to get out of doors. We may mention that the medicine was the well-known preparation, Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup, although to advertise the article is not the chief motive for this little narrative. As a matter of fact, Signalman Agge kept on doctoring himself with it, and it cured him be its nature what it may. He went back to his box long ago, and this inci- dent is printed in order that the reader may know more of the character and experience of a large and faithful body of public servants.

div.p: THE DESIGNS FOR THE WATKIN
TOWER.

It was announced, on Wednesday, that the committee of jurors who had to award prizes in respect of the com- petitive design for the Watkin Tower have presented their report. They.say that the designs were of. varying merit, and although there were good points about many of them, they must confess to a feeling of dissapoint- ment on the whole as to the result of the competition, there being no single design which they could recom- mend as it stands for execution. They award the first prize of 500 guineas to the joint designs of Messrs. A. D. Stewart, J. M. Maclaren, and W. Dunn, 21, King William- at., Strand, London, and the second prize of 250 guineas to that of Messrs. J. J. Webster and T. W. Haigh, 67, Lord-st., Liverpool.

The Duchess of Fife (Princess Louise of Wales) was delivered of a stillborn male child on ,Monday evening, at East Sheen Lodge, Richmond; Surrey. The medical men in attendance were Dr. Marshall, of Barnes, and Dr. Matthews Duncan, of London. Dr. Laking called on Tuesday for the purpose, it is under- stood, of making a report to the Princess of Wales. .The Duchess, last Wednesday, was quite well, and attended the meet of the Four-in-Hand Club in Hyde Park, where, however, she got a severe wetting. Up to a few days., ago it was intended that her Royal Highness should be at Ascot this week. Constant inquiries as to her Royal Highness's condition have been received from the Queen and other members of the Royal family. The Princess of Wales arrived at East Sheen Lodge on Wednesday morning from Sunninngdale, to visit her daughter, the Duchess of Fife.

div.head: FUTURE OF CRICKET. LIVIN'G LEGAG%
div.p: THE FUTURE OF CRICKET. LIVIN'G LEGAG%
BY W. G. GRACE.
In concluding his article on cricket, to which we referred recently as appearing in the current issue ot the "English Illustrated Magazine," Mr. W. G. Grace says:— ... _

And so it may be safely said • that the batting all round is better to-day than in the past. Ido not mean to say that the giants of the past would not be giants to-day; but I do say that were those players with us now they too woula play in improved form, and that for one good batsman then we have a dozen now. The public have a clear knowledge of that fact. We have only to take a stroll round the ground while a great match is being• played to learn what they consider good play. I have an immense respect for the barn-door or stone- wall style, but must confess to siding with the crowd when they praise the player who times the straight good-length ball,and splays, it hard and clean away from the wicket. With my brother, E.M., at his best at point, g )od old Jupp, in his later days, bad a lively time of it when.playing at Clifton or his county. Ball after ball I bowled to him which he kept. playing beck quietly-; 'then the particular ball came, and E. M. rushetl in and caught him almost off the bat. The disgust that crept over Jupp's face as point, slip, and short-leg crowded round him, and his helplessness under the circum- stances come up before me now. -And yet Jupp was considered a good back-player. Playing forward is also more general, and that, too, owing to improved wickets. Good players know that in playing forward they are now less likely to meet with a kioking ball which would bit them on the fingers, and so play forward with the greatest confidence to 'balls which they used to watch carefully and in many cases play back to. And short-pitched balls which were blocked then are now pulled across the wicket owing to the same cause.

But bowling more than batting has been affected by the improvement of the grounds. How rarely do we see a real good fast bowler now? The time has gone past when pace alone could obtain a wicket. It was not an uncommon plan for a fast bowler to send in a fast short one, knowing that the half- prepared wicket would cause it' to bound very high and make it dangerous for the batsman to hit. When that is done now, the bowler is not surprised to see it hit to the boundary. And so we have more head-work in the bowling, a better length, more break, but less pace. .The important point the bowler must bear in mind-is not to exceed his strength, or he will very soon go to pieces, and get hit all over the field. No ball can be punished so easily as the short fast one on a good wicket. All good bowlers indulge in an occasional fast one; but that is a different thing to the express pace some bowlers used to keep up for an over or two. Messrs. Soofforth, SteeL and Turner, among the gentlemen, Alfred Shaw, Lohmann, and Briggs among the pro- fessionals, have been the most prominent bowlers for years past. Spafforth's wonderful power lies in his variety. Whether he breaks six inches or twelve he takes good care that the ball will hit the wicket, should it beat the batsman: and he keeps varying his pace till begets the batsman in two minds, and then treats him to a fast yorker. He has been more effective with fast yorkers than any bowler I know. A. G. Steel is another of the tantalizing bowlers. Rarely do you get two balls in succession the same pace from him; and if there is a weak spot in your defence he keeps hammering at that until you make a mistake. The same may be said of Turner. He is always well within his strength, and ever varying his pace. Lohmann and Briggs work on the same lines. Alfred Shaw had the least break of the lot, except on sticky wickets, but his wonderful com- mand of length more than compensated for it. All of them bowled with their heads. They saw that the improved wickets were adding to the bats- man's chances, and that simple fast bowling would nc f meet the case: so they cultivated variety of pace-breaking from both sides, and only departing from a good length when the oaman had mastered them. Southerton was one of that school, and a proficient at it too-: but the' wickets were not so good in his days and helped him considerably. He used to tell with great glee how, after trying me with dodgy breaks 'for an hour or two, he in despair sent up a simple, harmless one,with no'break at all, and beat Me. There was nothing in the ball, but it was unexpected, and it came off. I have seen Lohmann bowl batsman after batsman with a simi- lar. ball. The batsmen admitted it was as simple a ball as any bowler could bowl, but they expected something differentfrom him.

I am beginning to hope that very shortly we shall have an increase of very fast bowlers. The success of Mr. S. M. J. Woods and Mold last year warrants me in saying that good fast bowlers would baffle a great many batsmen who are now at home witk medium-paced breaks. The day of terrific pace and careless length is at an end, but a fast bowler who could bowl a good length for a dozen overs would be invaluable to any of our county elevens

Out-fielding has also benefitted by the improve- ment in the grounds. Years ago, the pitch was rolled carefully by some clubs, but very rarely any- thing outside it. As long a's the grass was kept short most clubs were content ; and cover-point, long-leg, and thern out-fieldsmen generally, had tp be very quick of eye and hand to stop the ball with certainty even when it was travelling straight to them. To-day the roller is in use all overthe ground, and he would not be considered a first-class fielder who failed to pick up the ball corcectly and smartly on the run.

The wicket-keeper is another who has benefited. He dispenses with a long-stop to bowlers who are not a bit slower than some to whom it was thought necessary to have a long-stop placed years ago, and this, in a great degree, may be ascribed to the im- provement of the ground. There is no need to compare the wicket-keepers of the present with those of the past, but I cannot help saying that the doings of Messrs. Philipson, McGregor, Pilling, and Sherwin in 1889, without long-stops, are worthy of the highest praise. I have no need to mention Blackham ; he was not here in 1889, but he is still at the top of the tee in that part of the game. I should be less than human were I to abstain from saying something about the future of the game. Ido not lay claim to the gift of prophecy, and have too much respect for the bare and simple truth to think that my opinion will be, considered of exceptional value there. What I desire to say is based on my past experience, and may be said in very few words.

There is more cricket played to-day than at any time previously, and good cricket, too. We have only to look at the growth of county cricket and observe the crowds that turn out to look at the play, whether the match be between first or second-class counties, to realize that the game is played more than ever. There are counties enough to form three classes, and the classification of them is a question for the immediate future, Eight is the number of the first-class cotinties at present, and I do not see how that can be increased. Playing home and home matches with each other means forty-two days, or seven weeks of actual play, and that is as much as cricketers can manage to play, as they have so many other first-class matches to take part in out of a season which,from beginning to end, lasts about sixteen weeks. Second-class counties might be limited to six in number, third-class to four; and these might fulfil engagements with each other without interfering much with other important fixtures.

The hardest nut to crack will be the promotion of the second-class to the first, and the third to the second ; not an easy matter, I admit; still, in the interests of the game, it will have to be cracked. The point has been under consideration, and a sub- committee of the Cricket Council was appointed in December last ; and I save no doubt it will be thoroughly and impartially weighed, and some deci- sion arrived at before the end of this season. I cannot predict that, outside of the Australian matches, there will be more exciting contests in 1890 than there were in 1889. The weather cannot be worse, for one thing, and it is not unlikely that individual and club scores may be larger. It will be a very exceptional display that will outshine the Gentlemen a. Players' match at the Oval, last year. There will be plenty of good batsmen this season, but I do not know of any rising phenomenon who will surpass the achievements of the best players of the last six years in any part of the game. Thereis a fine opening for good fast bowlers. I could count on the fingers of one hand the batsmen who can play a fast first-class bowler with confidence. Mr. S. M. J. Woods, Mold, Beaumont, and Bowley are sure to do good work in the coming season, but after you have named these there are not many fast bowlers left. _ _

The last word to my friend and comrade of many years, Lord Harris, who is giving up the ganae for the sterner duties of life. He will be a great loss to his county, a greater loss to the cricket world gene- rally. lie is one of the few who has contributed with both hands and head to the history of the game, and carries the heartiest wishes of every cricketer to his new sphere of work.

CHAPTER XXXII. LIGIIT IN GROSS DARKNESS.

Mmut Woo',row) fully expected that he would have 'suffered terribly during the first days of his imprison- ment. He wondered then to find how calmly they glided by and how he settled to the routine of work and exercise. He forgot that the one great element that would have depressed him was wanting. He wau troubled, certainly by a desire to know what Martin tad done, and how Ruth fared. but he was not prostrated by remorse. One day while, cheerfully enough, he was busy over that contemptible waste of time, picking oakum, and wondering when he would be drafted off to 130171 e convict station, thinking, too, how delightful it would be to see the light of day once more, instead of the subdued gloom in which he lived, when he was startled by the sudden rattling of a key in his door, and it was thrown open, and a warder ordered him to come out. He followed the man with.ut a word, and, to his surprise, found that he was led to the visitor's room, a place where the prisoner wait separated by a double row of bars from his visitor, a warder occupying the passage between the double bars. By this arrangement prisoner and visitor could not get within five feet of each other, and the warder tut at one end and looked on. _ _

Mark's calmness left him as he saw a slight figure in deep mourning throw up her veil, and as bhe uttered his name stretch out her arms between the bars, against which she pressed her haggard face. "Ruth! my darling child!" he groaned, as he, too, pressed against the bars, and gazed in the piteous, yearning eyes. A slight cough made them both aware of what they had forgotten—the presence of the warder—and in his agony Mark turned fiercely towards the man, who now left his seat, recolnising in him the elderly official with whom he had shaken hands on the day of his

"Can't help it, sir," he said with strange compassion. "Now, look here, no attempts at escape." " Absurd!" exclaimed Mark. r.vs "Honour bright? There, I believe You, sir. Look here, say what you like to each other; I shall be as deaf as a beetle, sir. I've got (rime feeling left in me if lam a warder. But don't lose time."

He went bank- to his seat, took a paper from his breast, and bent down his head and began to read; while, as Mars returned to his station opposite his visitor, she uttered a wad of misery. "Oh, Mark, Mark!" she cried; "haa it come to this " _ _ _
"My poor chili!" he groaned; " but God bless you for coming. How did you contrive it?" "Dear Mr. Klopetock has been trying for per- mission ever since, and it was through one of the theriffs."

"And I thought myself forsaken by all," he cried. "Forsaken ! " she sobbed; "oh, Mark, dear, how could you think it, when my every thought has been of you?' "But tell me quickly," he sai4—the warder's presence now forgotten—" Ruth, my child, you do not believe me guilty of this crime?" She drew herself up, gazing placidly in his face, and, as he returned her look, never had be seemed to sweet and beautiful before.
",You!" ahe cried. " Guilty! Oh, Mark, can you ask?"

"Thank God!" he said, reverently; and he stood /or a few 'laments with banded head. "Ruth, my ehild, I can bear it now. You have taken a load from my mind. You are here to say good-bye. You are young yet. Heaven helping us, Ruth, ten years will not kern so great a time- w3r€, may live to meet "Oh, hush, hush!" she claa:. piteously. "It must be found out long before that. Ten years. Oh, Mark, Mark, if it is not, I shall die!" "Oh, no, no, my child," he said. "There is such a thing as hope. Come, come, you must be calm—calm as I am," he continued, piteously. "Let us talk of other things. You will live with Miss Klop,stock ?" "I suppose so," she said, wearily. "But tell me, Ruth," he said eicitedly, 'nave you seen Martin?" "Yes." "Tell me when. What he said."
"Said ?" she cried, with a show of indignation that made his heart beat heavily; and the presence of the old warder wasquite. forgotten. "He insulted me."
"What •E[Ow
"Shall I tell you ?" she whispered, as she held the bars, and closing her eyes, laid her forehead against the cold, black iron.
" kes—quiekly—alt he said f' "He said that he was going away on a long journey to another land."
" Yes—yes. Quick: " For he could not bear the disgrace you bad brought n 111:121/Iheitslailliiithat ?" said Mark, bitterly. "Well, go on."

She pulsed for a few moments, and there was a strange contraction in her face as she went on. "Ho asked me to go with him—to be his wife." "The villain:" whispered Mark to himself, as a aerrible feeling of hatred sprang up against this man. "And you?" he said aloud, in a voice he hardly knew. "What did you say?" "What did I lay, Mark?" she answered, as she unclosed her eyes, and turned upon him a look so full of pity, pride, and yearning that' he fell a-trembling an& olutethed at the iron bars. "Can you, Mark, ask me that? Mark, Mark," she whispered, "why will you be yes,elinlrbl h yes. inde?P " I it panted. d. " is unmaidenly and strange in me that I speak as I do, Mark, remember you are to be dead to me these ten long years—ten long years— or for ever. Heaven help 'me, I cannot bear it—my heart will break—my heart will break!" She sank upon her knees, clinging wildly to the bars, while she shook in her agony; and the warder rose, but Mark made a fierce gesture to him to keep back..

"Oh Ruth, my darling!" her groaned. "Mark," she cried, making an effort to master her emotion, and rising once more, "ball I tell you what I said? I told him he was a coward and cruel to forsake his brother in distress; that I had tried, heaven knows how herd, to make him lend a better life—tried as a sister should try to win back an erring brother; but that now, in this sore time of distress, he had raised in me feelings of hatred and diegust, and that I loved you as I always had loved you, with all my heart," "Oh, Mark," she continued, gazing on his pale, drawn face, "you have always been my patient, log- suffering hero, but I have tried to hide my love, for you always seemed so distant and so cold, I thought you despised me." "Distant !—cold! Oh, my darling, my darling, I would not show the agony I felt, for I thought your love was all for him."

" For him:" the cried, flashing up—" for Martin? Mark, he struck me—be was brutal to me when I refused to go, and I had to run to Miss Klopstock for help. But I ought not to tell you this. Mark, dear Mark, I never thought of him but aa a sister should think of a brother. But tell me, before I go—tell ma you are not angry with me ft. r what I have said. TM me that you do not despise me." "Ruth! Despise you l" . .

"1 o6uld not hide it longer, now that they have torn you from me. But, remember this, dear Mark, you take my heart with you, go where you will, and that my only thought is of the time when we meet again, here or in a better world,"

"Here, my darling, my love," he cried, passionately; "here, my own! For you have given me life and strength of will. You have sent hope thrilling through every vein—light into my dark heart, which is suffering for your dear take. Ruth, I have always loved you, but never till now did I think it could be returned. But ten years—what are ten years now? I can wait, and— Oh: so soon—so soon!" _ _ . _

" Yes, sir; the time is up," said the warder, quietly. "Poor girl! She has fainted." It was so; for, as the warder approached, Ruth stretched out her hands to Mark, pressing her face to the bars, as she gazed piteously in his eyes, and then, uttering a weary sigh, she sank heavily upon the floor. "Oh, warder, this is maddening!" groaned Mark. "Open this place—let me go to her." "Come, come, sir, be a man," said the old warder, with rough commiseration. "I'll do my best. She shall be well attended to." _ _

_ It was useless to appeal; Mark knew that, and he was led back to his cell, where he threw himself upon the seat, asking himself which predominated, joy or despair. His mind now was in a very chaos. For what hxd be done ? Sacrificed himself for a worthless villain, believing that he was serving the woman he loved, when it-had all been self-deception. There were moments when he asked himself whether ke was awake, or whether this was some dream born of his over-excited brain. But no, it was true; Ruth loved him. He had the confession from her own lip, and what he had thought love for his brother, was bat the sisterly affection and gratitude of her pure young heart.

now he was to be separated from her for tea years—the oup of joy had been held to his lips, and then snatched away. How was he to bear now this terrible punishment for another's crime? "But it is worth ten or twenty years of such suffer- ing to win a love like hers," he cried, joyously. "For she does not believe it, and she never will believe my guilt." Ten years of waiting, full of hope, tempered by patients, and she would still be young and beautiful, ready to welcome him back as a martyr for her love, and to his filial duty, for some thy he would tell all. Yes: she would still be young; but he—in ten years' time—what would he be then?

Yes: after ten years of such punishment as his? It would be cruel to her to make her wait, poor child, for the love of an elderly, broken man. His was to be a martyr's life, he told himself with a sad smile; and when she had recovered somewhat —gay at the and of six months, when his turn w4ult.l come to write, be would tell her that she was free. There was a rattle of the lock once more; the door opened, and as he sat staring blankly before him in IBS despair, a hoarse-voiced warder said: "The governor wants to see number forty-nine.'

div.p: CHAPTER X.XXITI.
THE END OF A LOVE AFFAIR.

THE sergeant of police who arrested Mark and got up the case against him had an idea that a detective force was an unnatural growth, and quite unneessary. 'You have your plain conAtables, and your sarg,n-Its, inspectors, and superintendents, so what mor., dl, you want," he would say; and with such feelings in hi, breast he had really felt an intenso rivalry against the favoured detective force.

He had succeeded in unravelling the Humphreys' mystery, as he called it, but he was pot satisfied ; and as the affair went on he could scarcely sleep for fear that some detective should disarter where the large sum of money stolen had been bidden; and it wee the culmination of his hopes that he might be the finder of that money, and reap friim it honour as well as reward. _ _

Toere was more than one is it, he thought; and after a good deal of consideratson, he made up his mind what to do. One night, as Samson Hall 'Awl coming away from the office, he was met quite promiscuously by the ser- geant, who shook hands in the most triendly way. "Glad to see you so much bett, r ; very glad to see you so much better, Mr. Hall. Just leaving business? Ah, so am I. What's more, before I go home, I'm just going to have one—one only—glass of Scotch, hot, with a bit of lemon in it, and one pipe. What do you say?" Samson Hall said if it was to be only one glaQs, and one pipe, he did not mind, and the reqiilt was an adjournment to a little old-fash.oned puhe house in a back street, where, as they sat and smoked, the con- versation naturally turned upon the robbery. "Looks to me," said the sergeant, "as if there was more than one in it." Samson nodded. "I shouldn't be at all surprised if that good-looking brother was in it, eh ?" Samson looked at the door, then at the window, and ended by touching the sergeant on the breast with the waxy end of his pipe. "If I had the hunting up of the money that was stolen, Mr. Sergeant," he said, "I should keep my eye on the handsome brother." _
"That's what I've been a-doing some time," said the sergeant to himself. Then aloud: " Loose fish, eh ? " .

" Awful ; and nice ones used to be after him. Bet- ting chaps; Fleet-stresters, with horse-shoe pins in their breasties, and always got a good thing on, with tips for their friends." "Ah, yes. Let's see; Dick Worrall used to come after him, didn't he? Handicap Dick, as they call him."

"That's the man," said Samson. "I've seen 'em planning together." "Likely chap," said the sergeant to himself; "but I've turned Dick inside out, and he won't do. Let's see," he said aloud; " that young spark was courting the pretty girl up at home, wasn't he?" " Deesay he was," said Samson; "but he had a lady up Hackney way. I've followed him there twice; 19, Ladyship.terrace. Nice little widow party, with a pretty servant." "I say that was artful," said the sergeant, laughing, as he finieht d his glass and rang. "I must have one more. Wonderful entail glasses they give you here." " Ah, they do," said Samson, who made no oppo- sition to his glass being refilled, especially as he was not to be called upon to pay. Half an hour after, sergeant and porter parted in the most friendly manner, the former seeing the latter to a Bow omnibus, and promising to call some evening for a quiet pipe in Songbird-lane. "Goal-bye; take care of yourself," said the sergeant. "You're not very strong yet ;" and as soon as be was alone, he started to walk to Hackney, saying thought. fully to himself: " I've got the wrong man, and now I'm going to have the rigbt one—and the (ash." Two or three evenings later, little Mrs. Appleby was seated by her open window, for it was very warm, and she had not lit the lamp, preferring to sit and think, for she was in very low somas. As long as it had been light, she had watched for the coming of Mr. Alfred Denville; and if she had lit the lamp now, she could not have watched any longer, so she preferred the dark, and watched on as he had watched for many nights now, but still he did not come.

The poor little woman's heart was very sore, and. her appetite was falling off; but the never for a moment mistrusted her lover. He WM ill the was sure, or he would have been thero before now; but it certainly was most unaccountable that he should net have answered either of the three letters she had sent.

"He must be ill, I'm sure," she thought; and when an unpleasant fancy intruded itself, to the effect that Alfred had hardly been to see her since that night when he had the money, the crushed out the idea, and grew quite excited. ." Stith a shame I "she exclaimed. "Why, he came that evening, and bi ought the heavy box containing his mother's papers, that day Lizzybetla Ann had gone for her holiday; and then he came on the Monday following. He'll be here soon, rm sure." She brightened up at the thought, and still sat in the dark. _ _

But then it occurred to her that Liszybeth Ann had been a very long tinse gone ,for her supper beer; and then it eisq occurred toner that Linybeth Ann had been a taus tune gene on the twe previous nights; and as she theilight this, she heard the murmur of voices, and her maid exclaimed; ; • "Well, I must go now. She'll wonder where I'm gone." " Sweethearting," thought little Mrs. Appleby; and then, thihtting of her own condition, she smiled, and felt very lenient towards her maid. "Not she," a tall, dimly seen figure whispered; " she's busy courting with her own flame—Mr.—what did you say?" " Alfred Denville. There : what do you want to know for ?" " I don't want to know, my dear. I only want to see you." "He hasn't been for days now, and she's in no end of a-taking about it." " Hasn't he, though?" "No. You men are all alike, and it's my belief that he'll never come again. Hush! Here he is." Liztybeth Ann drew aside into the next doorway, as a step she recognised came along the street, passed close to where she and her companion stood, and, running up the steps, he had hardly touched the knocker before little Mrs. Appleby had openel the door. "At lasts" she cried, flinging herself in the young man's arms.

"Yes," he said; "at last, but now I cannot stay long." "But where have you been?" in Yorkshire with my lawyer," he said. "We have had to search the registers at three out-of- the-wt.y places in tumble-down old churches for certain entries; but at last we have got it all in trim. On. more entr, which I go down by tho fast train to- morrow to get, and then all is done; and then I'm going to ask you to grant me something very near and dear to my heart. Will you be generous, and give it?" "I don't know," she said, softly. "Ask me, and see." _ _ _

"I will," he said, smiling; and the little widow felt as happy as could be. "Oh, by the way—" said her visitor. "What'. that ?" he cried, starting. "Only Lizzy beth Ann come in from fetching the supper beer," said the lady. "Why, how nervous you are: '

"Over anxiety about my affairs," he said; and, the blind having been drawn down, he ate heartily of the supper spread upon the table in the hope that he would come; and then, after it was cleared away, the spirit stand was placed upon the table, with a jug of hot water, the sugar, and lemons, and Lizzybeth Ann was told that she could go to bed when she liked. Lizzybeth Ann was di?gusted with Mr. Alfred Denville's coldness, and she had found a new lover, so felt independent, and the consequence was that she went off to bed, leaving the visitor there talking to the little widow. "I put your box in this cupboard," she said; "b!, cause I think it is the safest; and when you want here's the key." She showed him one of a very bright bunch, and then she prattled on about how old Mr. Appleby used

DIVISION. Consideration of the Local Taxation Bill in Committee being resumed, a division was at once taken on the question that clause 1 (appropriating funds for the pur- chase of public-house licenses) should stand part of the Bill, with the following result :—For the clause, 228; against, 224. The announcement of the num- bers was received with loud cheering from the Opposition. Mr. T. P. O'CoNNos moved to report progress, in order, as he put it, to afford the Government an opportunity of considering their posi- tion. Mr. SMITH said it had been generally ex- pected that Mr. Storey, whose speech was interrupted by the adjournment of the debate on Tuesday night, would resume his speech, and the division had been taken by surprise. The motion to report progress was withdrawn, and clause 2, appropriating money for the purchase of licenses in Scotland, was then taken. Mr. S. Williamson moved an amendment to apply the money to the improve- ment of fishery harbours and the remission of school fees. After some discussion the amendment was with- drawn.

div.head: TERRIBLE DUEL.
div.p: A TERRIBLE DUEL.

Two pistol shots, fired in rapid succession, were heard by persons passing a cellar, in Maple-st., New York, the other evening, and a policeman was called to the place. He entered, and two men were found lying dead, both shot through the heart. Each man clasped a revolver, and there was every evidence to show that they had fought a duel at short range, or else had agreed to mutual murder by way of suicide, The bodies were subsequently recognized by an old woman, who said they were her lodgers, William Culin and Charles Des- mond.

div.head: DOWN ON THE "SHADOWS."
div.p: DOWN ON THE "SHADOWS."

An action arising out of the system of " shadowing " by the police in Ireland has resulted in a verdict for £lOO being obtained against three members of the constabu- lary for assault and trespass. The plaintiff in the case, which was tried in Dublin before Mr. Justice Gibson and a jury and lasted three days, was the Rev. Father Kennedy, of Meelin, who complained that one Sunday after Mass he, having called a meeting of his people in connection with the Tenants' Defence Fund,was followed to his residence by the defendants, who insisted on being present at the meeting, and who nothwithstanding his remonstrance and resistance, pushed their way into his house. The defendants asserted that the meeting was a gathering of the suppressed Meelin branch of the National League, but this plaintiff denied, and informed one of the defendants that the use to which he was about to put his house was a perfectly lawful one.
MR. GLADSTONE ON THRIFT.

Mr. Gladstone, speaking on Wednesday night at the annual meeting of the South-Eastern Railway Provident Savings Bank, held at the Cannon-st. Hotel, London, claimed immense superiority for the English railway system over those of continental countries. As contrasted with their predecessors in the old coaching days the life of railway servants favoured regularity and thrift, the latter being a virtue which was not a distinguishing characteristic of our countrymen, though it was on the increase. This was shown by a large augmentation of the annual deposits in the Post Office Savings Bank, indicating that the great masses of the people were mov- ing upwards in character and responsibility. He earnestly trusted the people would more and more see how deep was their interest in the extension of provi- dent habits, which were directly connected with sobriety, a virtue of the highest importance in a country where temptations to insobriety were among the greatest dangers.

div.head: PENNSYLVANIA MIRING • DISASTER THIRTY-ONE LIVES LOST.
div.p: THE PENNSYLVANIA MIRING • DISASTER THIRTY-ONE LIVES LOST.

NEW YORK, TUESDAY Moimma.—Authentic details ve at last arrived concerning the dreadful explosion and loss of life at the Hill Farm Mine, which is situate on the outskirts of Dunbar, a small town in Pennsylvania. The early account of the disaster exaggerated to some extent the loss of life. At the time of the disaster fifty- seven men were at work in the mine, twenty-six being in one chamber and thirty-one in another. The explo- sion occurred in the chamber containing the larger num- ber of men, and was caused by a miner's pick penetrating an air hole and causing a sudden and suffocating outrush of gas. In the confusion which prevailed on the men discovering their danger, a lamp was overturned, and a deafening explosion ensued. One miner who survived the explosion endeavoured to run through the flames, which now raged with great fury in a part ot the cham- ber, but he was speedily overpowered by the intense heat, and his fearfully burnt and almost unrecognisable body was the first one found by the exploring party. Warned by the noise of the explosion the twenty-six miners in the other part escaped before the fire had reached them, and none were injured. Up to the present only two corpses have been recovered, and these are in such a charred and unrecognisable condition as to preclude the faintest hopes of there being any survivors. At midnight last night the rescue party returned to bank, and reported that they %vele unable, owing to the fire, which was spreading all over the mine, to reach the remaining twenty-nine corpses. The scenes around the pit's mouth are most distressing, hundreds of women and children being gathered in groups eagerly awaiting the return of the next rescue party. NEW YORK, TIIESDAY.—Latest despatches from Dunbar state that tht Hill Farm Colliery has now caught fire, and dense volumes of smoke and flame are ascending the shaft. All hope of saving any below has been abandoned, and the work of rescue is stopped. A priest has read the burial service for the dead at the mouth of the pit.

THE WIEDEMANN-WALPOLE CASE. -- • The hearing of Miss Wiedemann's action against Mr. Robert Walpole for breach of promise was resumed on Monday, in the Queen's Bench, plaintiff continuing her evidence. She said that her child was born near Char- lottenburg, where her mother lived. She afterwards came to England, and fulfilled several engagements as governess. She tried to find Walpole, but failed, and his mother told her he was married.

Cross-examined : She swore at the previous trial that her child was alive, believing it was, although the nurse said it died at birth. She went to Constantinople in June, 1882, travelling thither with the Countess Winski. She did not visit M. de Crenneville at Constantinople,and never, had a child by him. The Solicitor-General read a letter from M. de Crenne- ville, an official in the Austrian Consular service, saying that he met the plaintiff in Cyprus, and she extorted money from him, by saying he was the father of her child. The plaintiff denied these statements. The Solicitor-General here put in a certificate of the the birth of a child of Valerie Wiedemann.

Plaintiff denied it was her child. The plaintiff recounted the history of her relations with the defendant in Constantinople, and her cross- examination on this point was postponed.—Uriah Cook, a detective, related - how he acted for the defendant in getting the plaintiff away from Cannes.—The Court afterwards adjourned. In the Queen's Bench Division, on Tuesday, the case of Weidemann v. Walpole was continued. The plaintiff, in further cross-examination, said she lived at Oxford in 18'TO. She then made a further statement, describing her career as a governess and teacher, from the death of her father, a clergyman, in 1888. Mr. Robert Horace Walpole deposed that it was agreed between them beforehand that he should go to her room, and that when there she made no resistance. She obtained his ring from his room. He did not give It her, and although he frequently asked her for it she refused to return it. Mrs. Laura Sophia Frances Walpole, mother of the defendant, denied that she told plaintiff at Cannes that her son was to marry a rich girl, ner had she made faces at Miss Wiedemann from her carriage. The Solicitor-General then.. addressed the jury for the defendant, and at the conclusion of the learned gentle- man's address the court adjourned. MiSs yfiedemann's action against Mr. Walpole was re- sumed In the Queen's Bench, on Wednerday, when Miss Wiedemann replied to the Attorney-General. She con- tended that Detective Cook's evidence corroborated her case, and commented on the absence of M. de Crenne- vile from the box% Mr.lustice Matthews, in summing up, characterised thirease as deeply interesting. Plain- tiff had told her story in a simple, artless way, and it was difficult to listen to her and not believe there was some substantial foundation for the charge against the 'defendant. For the defence, however, it was submitted that the defendant had fallen' into the toils of a clever designing womani The only evidence of corroboration of the plaintiff's statement was that of Detective Cook, who was employed by therdefendant. If the jury were not satisfied with. this corroborative testimony they must finda verdict for the defendant.—The jury retired at ZO minutes to two. After deliberating nearly two hours, the jury returned, when the foreman said they had dis- cussed the matter thoroughlv, and there was no chance of their agreeing.—His lordship then discharged the fury.
