div.head: TEI i, .EXAMINER, SATURDIY, JUNE 21,:1:890
div.p: TEI i, .EXAMINER, SATURDIY, JUNE 21,:1:890
MAR,RIAUE OF MISS MARY ANDERSON

On Tuesday, Miss Mary Anderson, the well-known actress, was married to Mr. Navarro, in the little Catho- lic church of St. Mary's, Holly-place, Hampstead, in which the artiste has frequentlybeen a worshipper. The officiating clergyman was the Rev. Canon Purcell. The proceedings were strictly private, no one except the wedding party being allowed into the church. The bride, who was accompanied by her sister, was given away by her stepfather. Miss Anderson wore a dress of white satin, embroidered with lace. Immediately after the ceremony the bride and bridegroom and their friends proceeded to 16, Frognal.road, where the wedding break- last was laid. The reason for the extreme privacy with which the marriage was celebrated is the death lately of a near relative of Mr. Navarro, in consequence of which he is in the deepest mourning, and also on account of the serious illness of Mrs. Griffin, Miss Anderson's mother. It is intended that the happy pair shall spend their honey- moon in Venice.
TIIE ATTACK ON JUDGE BRISTOWE.

The German dentist Hermann Arnemann, who was sentenced recently to twenty years' penal servitude for shooting Judge Bristowe at Nottingham, was found dead in &cell at Leicester Gaol, on Tuesday, having hanged himself to the ventilator by means of his braces. He had served nearly nine months of his sentence, and had ap peared cheerful.
MR. T. P. O'CONNOR AND THE "STAR."

The "Freeman's Journal" London correspondent says :—The arrangement for Mr. T,P. O'Connor's retire- ment from the editorship of the " Star " wad signed and settled yesterday. Mr. O'Connor gets £17.000. He held £2,000 worth of shares, which are taken by the com- pany, in addition to the £15,000 he gets under the agree- ment. It is said that Professor Stuart is to be the new editor, and Mr. H. W.,Massingham will probably assume the position of acting editor. The change takes effect immediately.

div.head: BABY FAMENG.
div.p: BABY FAMENG.

A coroner's jury at Mortlake Wive found a verdict of manslaughter against a woman named Muncey for hav- ing caused the death of one of the children whom she "farmed." An inspector under the Baby Fanning Act said that Muncey had registered the deaths. of twelve children since the year 1882. Two men, who were referred to as Dr. Davis and the" so-called Dr." Thomas, were declared by the jury to be deserving of the grayest censure.

div.head: EAST AFRICAN SETTLEMENT.
div.p: THE EAST AFRICAN SETTLEMENT.
CESSION OF HELIGOIAND TO GERMANY.
A BRITISH PROTECTORATE OF _ZANZIBAR.

:de-S-Weir from Lord Salisbury to Sir E. Malet re- specting the East African question was issuhd on Tues- day night as a Parliamentary paper.' It detailed the outlines of an agreement with Germhny on points in dispute, alike in East and Central Africa and in Ngaml- land,Damaraland,and Togoland. It concedes to Germany all territory between one degree south of the Equator from the Victoria Nyanza to the Congo Free State in the north to the Stevenson Road in the south. The German Government has agreed to surrender all the territory it occupies or claims north of the British sphere of influ- ence. This wil! place under British control the Sultan- ate of Witu, with the islands of Manda and Patta, and the territory up to the Juba, of which the German Gov- ernment have recently assumed the protectorate, com- prising a coast-line of more than 200 miles. It is added that England will further assume, with the consent of the Sultan of Zanzibar (which has been given), and with the full concurrence of Germany, the exclusive protec- torate over that sultanate, including the islands-of Zan- zibar and rem la. This completes the concessions with regard to Africa, but the Premier then proceeds to state that her Majesty's Government are prepared to propose a bill to Parliament which shall transfer the island of Heligoland to Germany, adding that her Majesty's Government are of opinion that the island, having no defences, would constitute a heavy addition to the responsibilities of the Empire in time of war, without contributing to its security. Her Majesty's Government therefore think that the extension of British influence and dominion upon the East Coast of Africa, which will be the result of the pre- sent arrangements, is a sufficient inducement to the Government of this country to allow the island in ques- tion to be joined to the empire of Germany. Conditions will, however, be made securing all the inhabitants of the island now living from compulsory naval or military service, and also providing for the continuance of the present Customs tariff for the term pf 20 years.

div.head: OUR CONNECTION WITH THE ISLAND.
div.p: OUR CONNECTION WITH THE ISLAND.

The " Times," in its leading columns, says :—ln itself the connection between the little Frisian island and Great Britain is extremely slight, and it is not even sacred by long prescription. It came to us as a part of the possessions of the Hanoverian Kings, and remained British in 1814, says Lord Salisbury, because of its proximity to Hanover. Probably there was also an idea that it might be fortified and used as a means of blockad- ing the Effie and Weser in case of war. But the fortifi- cation of the iSlap4ha fllways rein4l2l4 ft fliers project, And it has wet, risa to gieater Miiitfiff; d?gnfty tnati is given by the possession of a battery and a coastguard station. Heligoland consists of a rock islandi a mile long, and of a sand island, which can accommodate in I summer some 2,000 holiday-makers from Hamburg and Bremen. The fixed population of the place may also reach that number ; and it is said that only one inhabit- ant, the Governor, is at all certain to be English. Even his subordinate officials are natives or Germans; and if any English visitors find themselves themselves there in thebathing season, it is not as they would visit Jersey or Guernsey, but as they might visit some out-of-the-way foreign region. STRATEGICAL VALVE OP HELIGOLAND.

The following remarks appeared a few days ago in a Unionist weekly journal :—" The extraordinary Sugges- tion that Heligoland should be given over to Gerniany can only be based upon ignorance, for the Germans have no more claim to the island than they have to Gibraltar. If any Continental Power has a right to grumble at our possession of Heligoland it is Denmark. The great stra- tegical value of Heligoland is, of course, unknown to the "irresponsible chatterers" in the House of Commons. The island fully commands the mouths of thP Elbe and the Weser, and if it were converted into a naval station, the whole trade of Hamburg and Bremen could be en- tirely stopped in case of war, for both 'ports could be easily blockaded. If Heligoland belonged to Germany, it would speedily become the Gibraltar of the North Sea, and the great German ports would then be safe from all attack.

div.head: GERMAN PRESS ON THE SETTtEMENT.
div.p: THE GERMAN PRESS ON THE SETTtEMENT.

BERLIN, WEDNESDAY.— This morning's neivspapers generally express satisfaction with the Anglo-German agreement concerning Africa. Attention is, however, directed to the concessions with which the arrangement has been purchased. On the other hand the cession of Heligoland is most joyfully welcomed from a national point of view. Above all satisfaction is expressed at the fact that the arrangement settles all the contested points between Germany and Er,gland, and establishes the best relations between both Governments for the near future. The circumstance is looked upon as a guarantee for the maintenance of peace, and at the same time as a success for the British Government. The Norddeutsche Allge- meine Zeitung, describes the arrangement as the result of a fortunate battle, in which there were only victors and no vanquished. A perlin correspondent says the African Agreement has tollen received with general and warm approval. The extreme Colonial party are disappointed, but their com- plaints find no echo in the nation at large. The Vienna journals lay 'stresi on the fact that good relations between Germany and Great Britain are now thoroughly assured. Special gratification is felt at the cession of Heligoland. The Paris." Temps," commenting on the Agreement, says that when it considers how Lang and glorious has been England's connection with Equatorial Africa and how recent are Germany's claims in that region it is driven to the belief that Lord Salisbury must have bad some powerful reason for his surrender. MR. STANLEY AND THE ARRANGEMENT. _

----- - Speaking on Thursday, at Newcastle, Mr. H. M. Stanley referred to the Anglo-German agreement with regard to Africa, expressed his gratification at Lord Salisbury's action, said that with a stroke ef the pen the Premier had acquired for England a valuable territory, maintained that the chiefs who were now under the tegis of the British Empire would look upon the day the agree- ment was made as a red-letter day, and said he was hopeful now of the progress of civilisation and commerce in the land he had traversed. One advantage gained was that Germany and England would be interested in securing the freedom qf the Zambesi and Shire rivers, and so the Portuguese difficulty would disappear,

div.head: COMPENSATION QUESTION. By A CONSERVATIVE IN "THE TRADE."
div.p: THE COMPENSATION QUESTION. By A CONSERVATIVE IN "THE TRADE."

The Government, apparently learning no lesson from past experience, has once more gone out of its way to rouse the indignation of,the whole country against the Licensing Clauses. Who called upon theaa to interfere in this delicate matter? Certainly not the trade they were quite content with • the existing state of things, and, fearing interference, only desired to be let alone. Certainly not the temperance party.; to give the publican—or, to be more accurate in these days, that huge monopolist the brewer—a clear right to the re- newal of all his licenses from year to year was certainly not called for by the temperance party. Who then ? No- body knows! It has been proved up to the hilt that the paltry amount of money which it has been propesed shall be set aside out of the ed. a gallon advane.e in the spirit duties to buy up licenses can do so very little that it is really not worth naming. It never was meant to be worth anything, but is a simple blind, unworthy of our great Unionist party, to sugar over, and make palatable a "Brewers' Sale Shop Title Bill." One hears a great deal about the publican, about his vested interest and the hardship it would be to take away his living by taking away his license. Nearly all who argue upon this compensation question, whether for or against, speak of the publican. The truth is that such an individual as the publican, as we used to understand him, is difficult to find. The present vendor of drink is no longer a•publican owning his house, probably handed down from father to son, from generation to generation, and therefore equitably entitled to fair compensation for disturbance if for the public good it should be decided that his calling is no longer needed Nor is he a rent- paying tenant to an ordinary landlord, free to buy in the open market as he thinks fit. The drink vendor to-day is neither of these ; he is either a paid servant put in to manage what is but a branch sale shop of some brewery, or he is a rent-paying tenant of the said branch sale shop, bound absolutely to purchase (in many cases) every drop of excisable liquor, ale, stout, wine, spirit, also mineral waters and cigars, consumed either on or off the pre- mises, from the brewery, and so tied up that if he were caught selling a drop of liquor which did not come fiom. the brewery he could be turned out without a days' notice. To call such a slave a publican, is to elevate him to a position he does not hold. The publican proper began to die out when the brewers' scramble for public- houses began, and now that they have succeeded in get- ting almost every public-house into their fingers, in many cases at fabulous prices, the old publican is dead and buried. What utter folly it is, therefore, to speak of publicans' right to compensation, when at the most there is but an odd one here and there, and with him no one would wish to interfere. As, being free, he buys where he likes and is in a position to give the public a good article, he, at any rate, is the last it would be policy to touch ,unless we wish to still further fall into the hands of the brewer. "The Brewers' Further Monopoly and Sale Shop Title Bill" would be a suitable name for the wretched sugar-coated measure now before the House. The only people who will benefit by it are the brewers. Compensation may be right or wrong, but let there be no mistake about it ; let us know clearly that the people who will get the compensation, if any is given, will be the brewers not the gentlemen usually known as publi- cans; and let us further clearly understand that the basis of purchase will be the bloated values the said brewers have rushed these houses to in their mad scramble to get hold of them. If with these things clearly linderstood the nation decides kr compensation, well and good, but it ought to fully understand them.— From the Manchester Guardian.

The Home Office authorities have in their posses- sion the means of setting forth this information, and there is some reason to believe that Mr. Matthews will not decline to furnish it. It will probably show with startling effect the completeness and wide extension of the system under which EtleilQW4 VQ really co,WIWci by brewers, •

_ At the quarterly conference of the Manchester and Salford Congregational Ministers' and Deacons' Associa- tion, the following petition was unanimously adopted, and ordered to be signed and forwarded by the Chairman to Sir Henry Roscoe :—" That your petitioners regard svith alarm and grave disapproval the proposals in the Local Taxation Bill to create a fund for the purchase and extension of licenses which, having proved obnoxious to the commonwealth, should be suppressed without compensation by the licensing authorities. By so pur- chasing a single license with direct Parliamentary sanction, your petitioners consider that the monopoly will be converted into a freehold, and that your hon- ourable House will have recegniSed aii 040:dished by the precedent a vested interest in a traffic that t4.tatOO long cursed and degraded Christendom. Inasmuch as these licenses to seU intoxicants were not purchased fram the State, and only granted for twelve months,and as the subjects of the realm were not consulted as to whether they wished these temptations to intemperance thrust upon them, your petititioners nray your honour- able Hausa to reject the clauses which provide for the purchase of licenses." At a meeting held org Wednesday evening at the Public Hall, Patricroft, Under the presidency of Mr. E. Davey, a resolution, moved by Mr. F. H. Smith, seconded by Mr. T. S. Brighouse, was unanimously adopted, con- demning in strong terms the licensing proposals of the Government. _ _ _ -

A public meeting was held at Failsworth on Wednes- day night to protest against the compensation proposals ,of the Government. Mr. Robert Jackson presided, and 'on the motion of Mr. J. Middleton, seconded by Mr. J. Wild, and supported by Mr. Councillor Trevor, a resolu- tion delaring against the principle of compensation was passed unanimously. At a meeting of members of the Church of England Temperance Society, held on Thursday, at the West- minster Palace Rotel, London, the determination of the Executive of the Society to support the Government compensation scheme was denounced. Various speakers, some of them avowing themselves to be Conservatives, declared their unyielding hostility to the proposals of the Government, and resolutions were carried, practically with unanimous voting, asserting that the meeting dis- associated itself in the most emphatic manner from the action already taken in the name but without the authority of the Society, claiming a more thoroughly representative basis of election to the Central Council of the Society, and appointing a deputatiou to ask the Executive to change their attitude, and in case of failure in this to make representations to the Government.

div.head: CHILD MARRIAGE IN INDIA.
div.p: CHILD MARRIAGE IN INDIA.

A newly-married Hindoo girl is interdicted by custom when living under her husband's roof, from talking to any but her younger sister-in-law or brothers-in-law. To a vivacious, talkative girl in her teens this custom is equivalent to solitary_ confinement when the husband happens not to possess younger brothers or sisters. A suicide (says the Bombay Gazette") has been com- mitted by a little Hindoo wife in a village in Burdwan because she could find "no one to talk to or play with."

THE POLICE SUPERAN NUATION BILL.

The Police Superannuation Bill was issued to members of Parliament on Monday. It bears the names of Mr. Matthews, Mr. ginith, Mr. Goschen, and Mr. Stuart Wortley. It is divided into three parts, dealing respec- tively with the superannuation of constables, general amendment of preceding Acts, and temporary and supplemental provisions. The rights of every constable to a life pension, who has served twenty-five years of approval service, or been incapacitated by injury, is established, and a gratuity to constables who have served less than 15 years is provided for, as *tell as pensions and gratuities for widows and children. The fund will consist mainly of deductions from pay and fines upon constables, fines under the Licensing Act, and sums pro- vided for by the Local Taxation Bill.

div.head: HOW COLLIERY EXPLOSIONS ARE CAUSED. A RECKLESS COLLIER.
div.p: HOW COLLIERY EXPLOSIONS ARE CAUSED. A RECKLESS COLLIER.

At the Newton Petty Sessions, on • Saturday, be- fore Colonel George McCorquodaleand Messrs. T. 11. Pearson and T. D. Grimkd, James Meadowcroft, employed as a collier at the Collins Green Colliery, was summoned for an offence under the Coal Mines Regulation Act, by unramming a shot which had misfired in that mine, on the 12th May. Mr. For- shaw (Messrs. Davies and Forshaw, Warrington), prosecuted on behalf of the firm. He said the de- fendant was charged with a breach of special rule 12, which prohibited the unramming of any shot which had misfired by colliers. On the night of the date named, Benjamin Brook, fireman in the em- ploy of the Collins Green Colliery Co., attempted to fire one of the shots in the Higher Florida mine, but afterwards found that it had not gone off, and he accor- dingly wrote in the vicinity " Mis-shot here." He also wrote those words at the entrance to one of the levels where all the colliers would see it. But the defendant went lac the place, and unrammed the shot. While he was unramming it, the shot exploded, and it burnt his face and hand. There was no doubt whatever that if there had been gas in the place at the time there would have been a very considerable loss of life and a very serious catastrophe. If the charge was proved, he asked the magistrates to inflict the full fine of £2 and costs.— Benjamin Crook, the underground fireman, gave evl. dence in support of the statement by Mr. Forshaw.--, John Thomas Mehers, underlooker, also Kaye eiridalice. and said he spoke to the defendant about the mat- ter. The defendant told him he was drilling a fresh hole and was getting the shot out when it ex- ploded.—Herbert Seddon, shot-lighter in the mine, said he met the defendant at the bottom of one of the brows. Defendant said to him—" I'd liked to have been done." He repeated the observation, and witness asked him what he meant by it. He replied that there was a shot which had misfired and he was "stemming" it when it went off, and had burned his hands and face. He also said that his Irdy 7al cA.wcn'clwil)l(.)?(l. were- qik e aiiiiig-Or the fac t-na i that it Wii 4their duty to unram or to " stem" misfired shots.—Mr. JactsoU, manager of Collins Green colliery, said the unramming of shots was a very dangerous act. The occurrence in question might have caused a very serious loss of life. It had been admitted by the defendant that he saw flame from the shot when it was unrammed. If there had been any gas in the colliery at the time it would most likely have blown all the colliery up. The prac- tice had been carried on previously, and he wished to press the case against the defendant so that it would not be done again.—The Chairman: The consequences might have been most disastrous.—Mr. Grimke : What was the explosive? Mr. Jackson: Tonite.—The Chair- man : How many hands have you working there? Mr. Jackson: In that particular pit about 210 that morning. , —The Clerk It is almost impossible to estimate what ' the loss of life would have been.—Mr Jackson : The people of the country would have wondered what . had caused the explosion, and neither the Government Inspector nor anyone else could have found out the cause.—The defendant said he was not unramming the shot, and he did notknow it had misfired. —The Chairman (after a consultation with the Bench) said it was a very serious charge indeed. The defendant ought to be thankful that they had not power to inflict a heavier penalty than the one they could do. There had been colliery disasters in the neighbourhood on former occasions and the 200 min in that pit would in all proba- bility have lost their lives as well as the defendant have lost his. They hoped thitt case would be h warning to all, and that they would take care to comply with the rules so carefully laid down for their safety. The defend- ant would be fined the full penalty of £2 and costs. A Liverpool contemporarycomrnenting upon this case, says :—The culpable recklessness with which some coal miners jeopardise their own lives and those of their fellow-workers by striking and exposing lights in the mines and in other ways has become notorious. It was exemplified in a new way on Saturday by theprosecution at Newton-le-Willows, of a collier for having unrammed a misfired shot within the mine. During the operation the cartridge exploded. If there had happened to have been any gas in the mine a catastrophe involving more than 200 lives would have ensued. As it was, happily, the accident occasioned injury to no one except the offender himself, who was seriodily burned about the face and arms. The act therefore brought its own punishment in this case. The exemplary fine of 40s. and costs—a heavy penalty to a man in the offender's station in life—was, however, imposed, so that altogether the offender has in this instance received something like the full meed of his reckless- ness.

FATAL C 11; ACCIPENT.

--- THE RESPONSIBILI VS OF CAR-DRIVE t. A fatal accident, o ;eurred, on Saturdly night, to a man named Henry Bridge (60), a labourer, who had resided with Mr. James McClew, of Queen-st. At about 10,40, Patrick McCormick was driving a horse and cab along Queen-st. when he noticed the deceased running across the road towards the fair ground. He called to him," Where are you going?' but the deceased appeared to take no notice of the question, and ran in front of the horse's head. He was struck in the chest by the shaft, knocked to the ground, and rendered unconscious. McCormick stopped his horse as soon as possible, and the deceased was driven to the Infirmary. He did not recover consciousness, and died at 11.30 the same night. The inquest on the body was held at the White Hart Hotel, Sankev-st., on Tuesday afternoon, before Mr. W. T. Husband, the deputy coroner. James Bridge, 67 Legh-st. cab driver, said the deceased was his father, and had been employed as a labourer at a flour ware- house John Hayes, 2 Park-place, Kendrick-st., said he was in the Fair Ground on the night in question when he saw the deceased step off the footpath near the Brewery as if he intended to cross the street to go to the shooting gallery on the Fair Ground. Seeing a horse and cab coming towards him, the deceased hesitated while in the middle of the street whether to go on or turn back. While hesitating he was knocked down by the shaft of the cab. McCormick, the driver, was driving at a reasonable rate, and he did not think he was to blame for the accident. Williant Hollingworth another witness deposed that McCormick was not driving furiously. The driver made a short statement, in which he said he saw the deceased in the middle of the road and, know- ing him, he called out "Henry, get out of the way." He was not driving furiously. He stopped the horse as soon as possible, put the deceased in the cab, and drove him to the Infirmary. The Coroner, addressing McCormick, said: The public have the first right to the use of the road. A cabman has only the use of the road subject to the safety of the public. When a man, woman, or child is knocked down by a velnc..e the presumption in law is that there has been negligence on the part of the dr ver. The evidence in this case is that the driver was driving slowly and not furiously. At the same time if McCormick had time to shout to the deceased he had practically time to stop the horse.—The Foreman: There are setts in the road, which is on an incline.—The Coroner: Well, lie could have turned the horse round. However, it is for the jury to decide what the verdict shall be, although I do not think there is sufficient negligence to justify a charge of man- slaughter being preferred against the driver.—The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death," and the Coroner, addressing the two cab-drivers present, said he wished cab-drivers to thoroughly understand their posi- tion. It was their duty to take sufficient precautions to prevent accidents when turning street corners or passing , through crowded thoroughfares. Had the driver in question been the worse for drink, the probability is that a verdict of manslaughter would have been preferred against him.

div.p: WIDNES ATHLETIC CLUB SPORTS.

The 23rd annual festival, in connection with Widnes Athletic Club, which was commenced on Friday night, was continued on Saturday. The weather was all that the most ardent sportsman could desire, the heat of the sun being tempered by a genial breeze, and there were no fewer than 5,000 spectators present in the enclosures, while the grand stand was well fill ed,th e occupants being chiefly ladies. The pleasure of the visitors was enhanced by the musical performance of the Soap Works Brass Band, under the conductorship of Mr. Wm. Jennett. FOr many years the sports have been acknewledged as best in the North of England, and on thti present occasion this reputation was fully sustained. The programme comprised 26 events, for which there were about 200 entries which included the names of many well-known athlete', Greater Interest also attached to the meeting beeaUfie tilt) Chalnplonships of the Northern Collates Aniateir Athletic Association, for the mile -„lint efkee‘ and lle wide jump were set down for clecislgn‘ 13 tlie former event Whittick expressed little diftlCuty in carrying off the gold medal from his two opponents, while E. The bicycle contests were full of exciting incidents, and were noticable for the splendid riding of B. W. Piggott, of Dublin, who was mounted on a pneumatic safety of only 25 lbs. weight. IMPORTANT GIFT TO THE ART GALLEY.
At the last meeting of the Museum Committee- the following letter, which explains itself, was read by the Chairman:—
The Beeches,. Moore, near Warrinirr i June 890. The Chairman of the Museum Committee,

Dear Sir,—Having always taken a warm interest in the Warrington Art Gallery, I am desirous of adding to its , attractions and usefulness by presenting to the Corpora- tion a picture by Clarence Whaite. well known as one of our best living landscape painters. The picture is in his best and most vigorous style, and has been pronounced by competent judges to be one of his most successful pro- ductions. It is in beautiful condition, and I feel assured it will prove an attractive acquisition to your collection. I would like it to be carefully placed in the gallery where it could have a suitable light secured to it, and I would suggest that Mr. Chorley, your borough trea- surer, who has had ccnsiderable experience in this way, should to requested to superintend its disposal.—Youra

truly, W. D. HOUGHTON. The reading of the above was, of course, received with acclamation, and a resolution was duly passed convey- ing to Mr. Houghton the thanks of the Committee for this very valuable donation. The painting was immediately transferred to the Art Gallery by Mr. Houghton. and may now be seen in its place. It will be within the recollec- tion of all that amongst the collection of pictures lent by Mr. Houghton to the gallery at the beginning of last year there was a fine watercolour by Clarence Whaite. The picture now become, by Mr. Houghton's generosity, the permanent property of the Corporation, is a much larger and more important work of the same artist. It was painted in 1867, and since its appearance at the Royal Academy in that year, it has not been exhibited in public. The subject, an upland meadow,backed by the wild crags of the Snowdon range, is taken from the hills above Trefriw in the Conway Valley, and is desclibed in the following verse appended to the frame— "A meadow, gemlike, chased In the brown wild, and mowers mowing in it?

The scheme of colour is rich and deep-toned, and the outline of the subject bold and telling. The gemlike character of the patch of meadowland forming the cen- tral middle-ground of the picture results from a remark- able concurrence of conditions in atmosphere and sky. The air has in it the sultriness and heaviness of a sum- mer day, and the mountains are overhung by thunder- clouds and wisps of gathering mist. A strongcontrasting light fr )in a break in the surrounding gloom is thus secured for the bright green of the cultivated patch in the middle of the picture, the sombre tones dr the hills, and the moorland vegetation greatly enhancing the brilliance of the central effect. The range of hills form- ing the back-ground are striking in thafig-uration, and realistic in colour andtrcatment. A fine effect of distance is got by the suggestion of other, and more remote, de- pressions between the superposed crags than the valley in which the mowers are at work. A pleasing group ot figures from theneighbouring homestead occupies a fore- ground richly diversified with the warm tones of heather and mountain verdure. The picture has had chosen for it a central and con- spicuous position in the Art Gallery to which it is, of course, a most welcome addition.

div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY. JUNE 21, 1890

Mr. BALFOUR has refer- the Bill as supporting the principle of corn- whilst SirMICHAEL HICKS-BEACH went whe whole hog, on the eve of the Bristol election, en he said—" The brewers and publicans may ,41-I.slY not feel dissatisfied with the important ro- of the principle of compensation for lloeei,lllses taken away without any default of the iii view of these admissions on the part 442seinbers of the Government—made before the Was in full cry against the measure—it is deucet, now either of hypocrisy or " dementia " Tli,er°test that the bill is not a Compensation Bill. rnliddle into which the Ministry have got I,:lllitelves is ummampled, and it culminated, on tlaecla), evening, in their majority being re- to four. On Monday evening, Mr. flite2.ll actually proposed to postpone the con- to ,74tion of certain clauses of the bill in order tqLlBll On with others, upon which Sir WILLIAM ''''ol:7lt2 promptly suggested that , the Govern- - clsata4l Would do well to postpone the whole of the beeti4es in view of the announcement that had rnade by Lord HARTINGTON as to a Select tatZtaittee " to consider the whole of the compen- iht„ cltlestion." CHURCHILL. What it all amounts to koiselß, that the Government are willing to pro.- % „3443'thing in the shape of a Select Committee Cotii 111-Pensation, if the House will first pass the te, ntation Bill! But the Opposition bird is said: to be caught by such chaff. Mr. GLAIATONE At o„ ';:aittee-e time the prospect of the suggested Corn- ,„sheet liBstuted a solid form at another a cloudy in danger of vanishing into the thinner air. to b h it a a a right to know t whether there was. have first Passed IvieueßrlBlLte":.et.ie to the or ea. hewreitr as ftroaabiel anodne, would ncloutesbleonthe case if the Bill It s because then the principle would • wen', laid down deciding the whole matter. 311t,,Arttt": n_ i b? contrary to sense, prudence, public "DM every principle involved n the :case

' to proceed with the compensation clauses while the proposal for a Committee was hanging over his head. (Cheers.) After this, poor Mr. SMITH had nothing to say; he drew in his horns, like a snail, and retired into his shell, while the House proceeded to discuss various proposals for amending the bemuddled Bill of a bemuddled Government.

ON Tuesday Mr. W. H. SMITH, as Worse And Worse. leader of the House of Commons, made his long-delayed statement as to the course of public business. But &flay has not brought wisdom, and the House, at the close of his speech, was in utter amazement at the folly of the Government. There is to be no attempt to get through the Irish Land Purchase Bill, which was announced as the principal measure of the Session; but in its place the Government are about to introduce a Standing Order to enable them to carry it over as a suspended bill until next session—to be resumed precisely at the point at which it is left during the present session. This is a revolution in procedure, and it will sur- prise no one that Mr. GLADSTONE who, whatever may be said of his Radical tendencies, is more conservative than the Conservatives in these mat- ters, has given notice to refer the question, in the first place, to a Select Committee. Mr. E. RosEarsoN had also a notice‘to give, which was that "when the proposed standing order was moved, he would move to include similar provi - sions for bills which, having passed in that house, had been rejected by the House of Lords, so that bills could be sent to the House of Lords by a formal repitition of the third reading." This, it is not to be denied, is a useful auggestion ; and we do not doubt that if the new standing order is broadly framed it will facilitate legislation. But it is evidence of "midsummer madness" on the part \ of the Government to introduce a train of this kind when the line is already blocked. It is like trying to clear the way by means of a collision ; for col- lision there certainly will be when the matter comes to be discussed. The Government are thinking solely of helping themselves in an emer- gency ; but the Opposition will have an eye to the use of the Standing Order when their turn comes to apply it. There have, it is stated, been five sittings on the Irish Land Purchase Bill ; and to prevent these five sittings being wasted it is the Ministerial idea of wisdom to waste five or more sittings on a new Standing Order! But the climax of fatuity is reached in Mr. Sman's intimation that the Government have resolved to set aside all their measures until they have got the Compensation Bill through Committee. They have taken their stand on the Beer Barrel, and with it they mean to stand or fall. This was found "a staggerer" to some even of the ,supporters of the Ministry, and one of them—Mr. HANBITAY —asked his leaders " serioaly to consider whether they were taking a wise or constitutional step when they postponed Supply till so late in the session." But it is not Supply alone that is to be postponed. The arrangement means that a number of measures of value to the nation are to be sacrificed to a Bill which has been sprung upon the nation like a hid- den mine. The Irish Land Bill is to be hung on the new peg until next year; while the Tithes Bill, the Police Bill, the Western Australia, the ' Indian Councils, the Census, the Savings Banks, the Housing of the Poor, and other Bills are to be left to the chapter of accidents. This means that some of them will be slaughtered at the last moment; and, let the working-classes duly note, it has already been resolved to sacrifice the most important of them all, namely, the Employers Liability Bill. Thus, as Mr. GLADSTONE put it, "a bill touching the welfare of the mass of the people, is to be sacrificed in order to prosecute a measure which the working-classes,from one end of . the country to the other, absolutely detest." Well, so be it; we must expect Toryism from a Tory Go'vernment ; and the Toryism is breaking out all the stronger from having been in some degree kept under for a time by the pressure of the Dissentient Liberals. These misguided allies will at last perhaps realise that what is bred in the bone must out in the flesh; and they will have an opportunity of repenting at the eleventh hour. Liberals will now take fresh courage at the prospect of the next election; for, seeing the Tories bound hand and foot to the "devilish and destructive" traffic, they cannot but rejoice and say as of old—" The Lord bath delievered them into our hands."
"The Party IT is only three weeks since,that the of Tories w9re indignant at a proposal

Surrender." on the part of Sir GEORGE CAMP- BELL to make a bargain with Germany in the sur- render of Heligoland. The Daily Telegraph " denounced the supporters of such a project as "The Party of Surrender " ; the " Standard" sneered at the "irresponsible loquacity of anti- Imperial faddists" ; while the "Morning Post" fell foul of what it styled " the unpatriotic eager- ness to begin the dismemberment of the British Empire." And yet the "dismemberment" has be- gun, and it is begun—save us "ye gods and little fishes !"—by no less a person than the Tory PRIME MINISTER. At the very moment when Barori DE WORMS, on behalf of the Government, was protest- ing against the proposal, and arguing that, if Heligoland was given up to Germany, there would be equal grounds for surrendering the Channel Islands to France and Gibraltar to Spain, Lord SALISBURY, as head of the Government, was actu- ally negotiating for haniing over Heligoland to Germany. It is comical to think how these thoughtless supporters of the Ministry are being "hoist with their own petard." How ridiculous they make themselves now when they are suddenly called upon to "climb down !" Their vagaries and inconsistencies do not, of course, determine whether it is wise or otherwise to oblige Germany by letting her have the little island which she covets. According to WHITTAKER'S Almanac, Heligoland (Holy Land) was captured from Denmark in 1807. Including sandy island, it is about two and two- thirds of a mile in circumference with a population of over 2,000. It is only about 25 miles from the mouth of the Elbe and tho Weser; and this being so, it will be seen that, in case of war, it could be made to command these rivers. It is natural that Germany should wish to possess the island; indeed it would be a most valuable pos- session to her, particularly as it is inhabited by Germans ; but it is just because it is valu- able that it should not be surrendered except for a full equivalent. Whether Lord SALISBURY has made a good bargain in mixing it up with his arrangements with Germany for the partition of East Africa is the point now at issue. We know. so little as yet as to what is really meant by the "give and take" lines which are being laid down in Africa that we hesitate at present to say anything more than that it would have been more satisfac- tory if the arrangement for the cession of Heligo- land had been made entirely separate from the scramble for Africa. We leave it for the Tories to assert that Lord SALISBURY is the leader of "the party of Surrender," and that, with "unpatriotic eagerness," he has begun "the dismemberment of the British Empire."
"TOUCH AND GO."

"Mr. Chamberlain and Mrs. Chamberlain will leave Liverpool for the United States in the Cunard steamer Etruria which sails from the Mersey on Saturday next." Joseph doesn't go to Egypt this time; but all the same he leaves the Government in the throes of a crisis. How these Unionists love each other, and what sacrifices they make to save the empire

As some of the Tories prefer racing to backing up the Compensation Bill, the Government had "a narrow shave" on Thursday, in the House of Com- mons; they had a majority of four only, in the first division They are explaining that this was due to Mr. Storey not going on with his speech when he was expected to do so; but what was to prevent the Government putting up one of their supporters to speak? They may squirm as much as they like, but their doom is fixed when their majority is brought down to four in a House of 452 members.

At the interesting meeting of the Cheshire Agricultural Society which was held at Crewe, ton Monday afternoon, Dr. Fox combatted the sug- gestion that has been made that the cat is a means of spreading diptheria. He sought to fortify him- self with a quotation from Shakespeare,whO speaks of "the harmless necessary cat." But is it not out of place, not to say a trifle late in the day, to quote the great bard as a scientific authority?

What has Dr. Fox to say to the fact that people have perished of hydrophobia from the bite of a cat " Harmless " indeed Why if the ?doctor will take the trouble to inquire amongst servant girls—who know all about it—he will find that for the breaking of pots, pans,and chimney-ornaments, and the consumption of fish, flesh, fowl, and all manner of spirituous liquors, the cat is the most destructive creature in creation. "Necessary cat," if you will, doctor, but "harmless "—never

At the same meeting, Mr. J. A. Davenport ob- served, in a paper on ‘. Milk and Sanitation," that "As a beverage milk is far cheaper and infinitely more nutritious than beer and other stimulating drinks, and we may welcome the introduction of the glass of milk at our railway stations and other places of refreshment, as a proof of the increased favour in which it is being held, and as an evidence of the increased consumpt:on to which it is attain- ing." The substance of his advice to farmers on milk in its relation to disease may be summed up in the words :—" Be clean, 14c1ean, be evermore clean."

The Warrington Board of Guardians seem to have been in a fog, on Wednesday, as to what to do on the question of providing reading for the Workhouse inmates. Literature is evidently not in their line, but, considering that Mr. Gill had given notice of his motion they ought to have been equal to the A. B. C. of subject. Perhaps when the House and Padgate Schools Committee have wrestled with the question, the Board will be able to take a step forward.

It is just possible that the members may be under an impression which prevails in some quart- ers, namely, that they have no authority to spend money as proposed. But they may ease their minds on that point, for the President of the Local Government Board, replying in the House of Com- mons, on May 17th, to a question put to him by Mr. Summers said :—" Boards of Guardians are empowered to defray out of the rates, the cost of supplying the inmates of Workhouses with news- papers, and periodicals, and books." The way is, therefore open to do something—something not extravagant, but reasonable.

In connection with the inquest at Warrington, on Tuesday, arising out of the fatal cab accident, the Coroner did well to call attention to the fact that "the public have the first right to the use of the road." From the way in which some people drive about, they would appear to be under the impression that it is for pedestrians to rush out of their way, and that there is no obligation on their side to pull up, or turn aside, in case of risk of accident. It needs to be emphasized that tbe public—that is, pedestrians—have "the first right to the use of the road."

Mr. W. D. Houghton is entitled to the warmest thanks of the community for his gift to the War- rington Art Gallery of a splendid specimen, in oil, of the work of Mr. H. Clarence Whaite. The picture is very valuable from a monetary point of view—it is worth considerably over £soo—and, as the painter is of high and still rising repute, the value of the work will increase as years go by. It is to hoped that there will be emulators of Mr. Houghton in thus enriching the Art Gallery. There is plenty of room for good things, and an appreciative public.

Cardinal Manning is always clear and intelli- gible. He is not amongst those who hide their thoughts in a mist of words. On Tuesday a depu- tation of Irish Nationalist members of Parliament presented an address to his Eniinence, congratula- ting him on having completed twenty-five years of his episcopate. In reply, he expressed Ins deep sympathy with th 3 Irish people in their political struggles, and affirmed that the soil belonged to the people who lived upon it, and had to be buried in it. This is not a new doctrine, but it is a true doctrine—of which more will be heard in the good time coming.

What next P Lord Salisbury, Mr. Goschen and Mr. Balfour have been writing to the National Conference of Working Men to express approval of a resolution in favour of bringing forward Con- servative working-men as Parliamentary candidates in "suitable constituencies." It is not many years since this trinity in unity were opposed even to working-men having votes—to •say nothing of their becoming candidates. Bow the cat jumps Has the Ethiopian changed his skin?

An important point was raised, on Tuesday evening, during the discussion of the Compensation Bill in the House of Commons, and that was as to whether a member was entitled to vote who has a pecuniary interest in licenses. Mr. Speaker Abbott ruled, in 1811, that "the interest must be a direct pecuniary interest and separately belonging to the persons whose votes were questioned, and not in common with the rest of his Majesty's subjects, or on a matter of State policy."

The Chairman, on Tuesday evening, ruled that the interest in the present case was remote, and that members having money in "the trade" might vote on the bill. But is the interest re- mote in the case, say, of such a member as Sir Gilbert Greenall ? He is part owner of scores of licensee in Warrington, and if any one of them were to be purchased, under the bill, he would benefit directly and pecuniarily. lie would not as a matter of fact be allowed to sit on the Bench when license were being granted—even, when his firm had no interest in them. Why then should he. be allowed to vote for his own endowment?

The Warrington Sanitary Committee have done no more than their duty in taking proceedings against Messrs. Edward Bolton and Sous with reference to the pit—the-death-trap—near Orford-lane. It is not much, however, to impose a penalty of ss. , and costs for" a nuisance" which has resulted in tho loss of six lives in five years. Wo don't quite understand what was meant by saying "it was an unfortunate position for' Messrs. Bolton to be placed in." It is but in a small degree unfortunate to them t• have to properly fence off or drain this pit compared to the terrible misfortune to parents and relations by theloss of six lives. It would seem that Lord Salisbury has been sparred by Mr. Stanley's jibes, for it is made known that a provisional engagement, has been entered into with Germany for the partition of a large portion of East Africa. It involves, curi- ously enough, the cession of the island of Heligo- land to Germany—a proposal which would have driven the Jingoes to the end of their short wits if it had come from Mr. Gladstone. However, Heligo- land is little more than a German Isle of Man. It is a sea-side resort of no great value to us, and if it can be shown that the Prime Minister has obtained a fair equivalent, there will be no just ground of complaint.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 21, 1890
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, JUNE 21, 1890

It is one of the regulations as to Petitions to Parliament that they shall be "fairly written out." Of late, a number of petitions sent in have been "fairly written out" by the type- writer; but they have been rejected as informal by the Committee of Public Petitions, and the matter is to be brought before Parliament. 'Perhaps the members of the Petitions Committee are as sensitive as to their "scholarship" as the Irish butterman, who, receiving a type-written business letter from a certain firm sent it back with the remark that he was not going to be insulted by their printing letters for him; he could read writingas well as any of them.

It is to be hoped that the colliers of this dis- trict will read, mark, learn and inwardly diOst the details of the case against James Meadow- croft, heard at the Newton Petty Sessions, ion Saturday. He was fined £2 and costs for unram- ming a shot, contrary to well-known regulations. The shot had gone off whilst being drilled, and burnt the defendant's hands and face. If there had been gas in that part of the mine, the flash ' would have resulted in a catastrophe; and, as over 200 people were at work, it is appalling to think What the result would have been. The law cannot be said to press heavily on reckless colliers, or the present penalty for such an offence as Meadowcroft committed would be more than £2 and costs.

" Truth " says :—" It is announced in the " Lon- don Gazette" that upwards of 600 original share- holders in the Manchester Ship Canal have for- feited their holdings, representing nearly 1,500 shares, in consequence of their having failed to pay up the calls. Lnmense pains were taken to make this undertaking popular, by inducing working people and small tradesmen to become proprietors; but the issue has been disastrous as might have been expected." It seems to us that disaster is hardly the word in this case. All' that it comes to is that, amongst the many thousands who put down their names for shares, 600 of the smallest holders have been unable, from one cause or another, to pay up, and have thus forfeited.

div.head: SWINE FEVER AT_HALTON..
div.p: SWINE FEVER AT_HALTON..

Martha Richardson, of Sea-lane, Halton was sum- moned before the Runcorn magistrates on Hatton, to answer a charge of allowing swine fever to exist on her premises without giving notice to the police.—lnspector Bowyer stated that on the 6th inst. he visited the pre- mises of the defendant and is one stye he found four pigs, which appeared to be healthy. A second stye was empty, and he made a search with a result that he dis- covered a pig buried in a midden. This animal had the appearance of having suffered from swine fever, and on the following day Mr. Shallcross, veterinary surgeon of Warrington, made a post-mortem examination, which revealed that the pig had died from that disease.—The defendant who said she did not know or she would have given notice; was ordered to pay the costs, 255. TRIVELLIN3 TRUNKS.—Garland, Ironmonger, 51, Bridge- at., Warrington. FAILURE OF A RUNCORN STATIONER. At a meeting of the creditors of Mr. Peter Hopwood, stationer and news agent, High-st., the following state- ment of his affairs, prepared by Mr. Wm. Handley, accountant, was submitted :—Liabilities, trade creditors, £25 9s. sd. ; cash creditors, £6l is. 4d. ; private credi- tors, £2O 6s. 9d.; total, £306 17s. 6d. The nett assets amounted to £139 3s. 4d. The debtor accounts for his deficiency by had debts, depreciation in the value of the r fixtures and stock, interest on loans, and attributes his failure to pressure by creditors and want of capital. As the debtor was unable to make any secured offer of com- position, it was unanimously resolved, after full discus- sion and in order to protect the estate, that the debtor should execute a deed of assignment of the whole of his estate to Mr. Percy E. Land, Chartered Accountant, Manchester, (who represented trade creditors) and Mr. W. Handley, as trustees for the general benefit of credi- tor. RMIGHATION.—Intending emigrants to New York, Boston Philadelphia, San Francisco, Canada, China, Japan. Aus- tralia, or New Zealand, should take tickets (lowest rates) at the" Examiner" Office, by Cunard. Guion, American, and other lines.— John Walker, agent, "Examiner" Office, Bewsev-st.. Warrington.—Advt. FUNERAL OF MR. JOHN WILLIAMS, OF RUNCORN. The mortal remains of Mr. John Williams, of Green- way Meadows, who died, at the advanced age of 82 years, on Wednesday, were interred at Runcorn Cemetery on Saturday. The chief mourners were: Mr. Hugh , Hughes, Mr. J. J. Speakman (son-in-law), Messrs. John c Hughes, Hugh Hughes, John Speakman, Frank Speak- man, Eric and Albert Speakman (grandsons), James Longshaw, Edward Green, William Green, John Green, Henry White, George White, and Jaartes Kirkham (nephews), and Joseph Williams and Henry Faulkner (cousins). The following townspeople also took part in the procession:: Dr. McDougall, Messrs. John Simpson, W. Handley, T. Handley, Joseph Littler, F. Beck, W. L Chadwick, G. Summerfield, John Timperley, Thomas Taylor, W. Powell, W. Cringliall. J. Egerton, W. Gowanlock, H. W. Handley, and H. Chadwick. The Rev. J. Simpson, pastor of Bethesda Congregational Chapel, conducted the burial service and afterwards delivered an address in which he said a noble and good man had passed away, and although they lamented his loss, let them treasure his memory.

div.head: MARRIAGES AT RUNCORN,
div.p: MARRIAGES AT RUNCORN,

On Wednesday morning at 8 o'clock the marriage of Miss Florence Littler, daughter of Mr. Joseph Littler, of Waterloo-road, to Mr. Alfred Lightburn, second son of Mr. J. W. Lightburn, of Heath House, was sOlemnised at Holy Trinity Church. The officiating minister was the Rev. Dr. Preston MA. Miss Edith Littler, was the bridesmaid and Mr. John H. Lightburn officiated as best man. Immediately after the ceremony the newly married pair departed for the Isle of Wight ,where they will spend the honeymoon.—On the same day at the Parish Church Miss Emily Widders, neice of Mr. I. Speakman, chemist and druggist, Bridge-st., was married to Mr. Edward James Reed, of Preston. The bridesmaids were Miss L. Rowan (Preston), ,Miss S. Speakman and Misses Nellie and Annie Speakman, and Mr. Fred Widders, brother of the brae, officiated as best man. Mr. I. Speakman gave the bride away, and the ceremony was performed by the Rev. J. Holden, senior curate. The wedding party was conveyed to and from the church in carriages supplied by Messrs. Yarwood Brothers. During the day Mr. and Mrs. Reed departed for Windermere where the honeymoon will be spent. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED on the premises at J. & W. ! Dutton's, Sankey-at.—Advt. POCKET PICKING AT WIDNES SPORTS. On Monday, at Widnes Police Court, George William Neil, 70, Bidder-st., Liverpool, was placed in the dock, 1 charged with being a rogue and vagabond, and attempt- ing to pick pockets at the Sports Field,Farnworth.—P.C. Almond deposed that about six o'clock on Saturday even- ing'he was on duty in plain clothes on the grand stand at Widnes sports, when he saw the prisoner go behind two ladies in a very suspicious manner. He watched them fo'r a few minutes, and saw the ,prisoner put his hand into both the ladies' pockets. The prisoner their went behind another lady named Carlisle, and put his hand into her pocket also. Witness then took the prisoner Leto custody, but the other mon who had been acting with him got away.=Edivard Williams, Upton, corrobor- ated.—Saperintendent Noblett said he had received a telegram from the Liverpool police thatmorning, stating that there were fourteen convictions recorded against the prisoner, for shophreakingeancl pocket picking.—The Chairman said it appeared from the information before him that the prisoner was an old offender, having served nine and four months respectivel.e for like offences. He would have to go to goal for two months with hard labour.

THE qIiIP CANAL TRAGEDY. In accordance with the decision of the magis- trates, the man Vaughan, who is charged with hav- ing shot a fellow workman on the Ship Canal at Rixton, was on Saturday liberated on hail, pending his trial at Liverpool Assizes. The articles found in his possession were restored to him. We under- stand that Vaughan has been allowed to return to his work in the Ship Canal cutting at Rixton. IRON BEDSTEADS 4t BEDDING.—Garland, 51, Bridge-et., Warrington. DECREASE OF EMIGRATION FROM THE MERSEY. The tide of emigration from the Mersey this year appears so far to compare very unfavourably with preceding years. The season is now very far advanced, and no signs have been shown of any great rush for the West. Liverpool boarding-house keepers are complaining bitterly of the slackness of trade, which, 'they say, is almost unprecedented. The reason assigned generally for the decrease is the good harvest expected all over Europe, which has kept many of the labouring and agricultural element of the population at home. GARDEN TOOL'.—J. S. Garland, IKunmonger, Warrington Earlestown. ASEITON-IN-MAXERFISLD CHURCHYARD. In the House of Commons on Friday Mr. Caleb Wright azked the Home Secretary whether he had seen the statement in a Wigan paper that the vicar of Ashton-in-Makerfield had given notice that, ow- ing to the very limited space available for new graves in the churchyard of the parish, he would not, except under very special circumstances, grant a new grave to any parishioner who was not or who had not been a member of his congregation; and, if so, whether the vicar, in allowing new graves to be opened, was entitled by law to discriminate between parishioners who attended and those who did not attend the services at the parish church. Mr. Mat- thews: lam informed by the vicar that there is room for only a dozen graves left in the churchyard, and, pending the completion of arrangements for its extension, and with the view of avoiding interfer- ences with graves already allotted to private per- sons, he has given notice that no new graves can be allotted to private individuals other than of the congregation, or persons who have some special claim to the privolege. This is not a matter within the jurisdiction of the Home Secretary, and any parishioner who considers himself aggrieved has a legal remedy, as I am advised, if the vicar acts illegally. This churchyard is not the only burial place in the township.

NEW BISHOPS AND THE DISTRESSED CLERGY. The Birmingham Bishopric Endowment Fund has reached £30,000; but, says the" Record," "the pinch has yet to come," and the promoters must do better than has been done with the Bristol Bishopric fund; which stood at £25,000 in 1888, and, not- withstanding a gift of £IO,OOO, is only £42,000 now. The word" pinch "is very suggestive ; but it does not refer to" The Clergy Distress Fund," the man- agers of which state that the applications for relief are" numerous and pressing "—more pressing, we should say, than the demand for additional bishop- rics.—" The Liberator." UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED on the premises at J• & W. Dutton's, Sankey-st.—Adet. DOG OWNERS' FINED. At the Newton Petty Sessions on Saturday, before Col. McCorquodale. George McLaren, was summoned for allowing his dog to be at large and unmuzzled on the Bth June, at IVinwick, and was fined 2s. 6d. and costs.—Edward Williams, Newton, for a similar offence committed on the 6th inst., was fined Is. and costs.—David Boulton, of Golborne, appeared to answer a summons for allowing his dog to be nn- muzzled at Golborne on the 9th June. The defend- ant said he was mislead by what he read in one of the papers that a collar with the name and address was sufficient. If he had violated the law it was a trlistake, and he hoped the Bench would deal with him SS leniently as they could. The Bench stated that under the circumstances they would let him off on the payment of costs.—ThGmas Arnold (Gol- borne),and William Alker (Haydock), were each fined is. and costs for allowing their dogs to be unmuzzled. *.,,* New Tale! New Tale!! "No Robbery,' a stir- ring story dealing with s incidents in the Indian Mutiny, will be commenced in "The Examiner,' on Saturday, July sth. It is from the vigorous pen of Henry Frith, author of "The Mystery of Moor Farm," "On the, Wings of the Wind, "Through Flood, through Fire," &e., &e. PROPAGATION OF TEE GOSPEL AT RUNCORN.

The annual meeting of the Runcorn branch of the society for the Propagation of the gospel in Foreign parts was held in the National School, on Tuesday evening. The Rev. J. Holden presided and speeches were delivered by the Rev. J. H. Wilcocksen (Weston Point), and the Rev. W. Crompton (travelling clergyman for the society.) INSPECTION BY WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The members of Widnes Local Board,on Thursday,he:d their annual inspection of the Gas and Water Works,and of the Fever Hospital. Everything was found in the most satisfactory condition, and the members expressed their approval of the appearance and working of all the con- cerns. At the conclusion of the inspection, the members drove on to Childwall Abbey, where they had tea.

div.head: ROBBED BY ..A SON AT WIDNES,
div.p: ROBBED BY ..A SON AT WIDNES,

At Widnes Police Court, on Phursday,RiChard Tonkies, a noted character, who has been convicted on fifteen occasions, was charged with havinz stolen a half-a. sovereign, the property of his mother, Mrs. Tonkies, of Wright-st. As the mother did not wish to prosecute, the charge of theft was withdrawn, and the prisoner was accused of assaulting P.C. Davidson. When that officer apprehended the prisoner, the latter struck him on the face, and bit his hand severely. He was sentenced to a month's hard labour.

- OPEN AIR CONCERTS AT Rmrcom•r. Last Tuesday evening the Runcorn Volunteer Band I gave an open-air concert in Devonshire Square and con- ferred great, pleasure upon an audience of sdveral hundred persons. On Monday evening next the band will perform the following selections of music on the market around :—March, "rise Rising of the Lark," air by T. t'Woods ; valse, "Blumen um Wege," Carl V. Keller; Grand contest selection, "La Reine de Saba," Rosini ; song "Alice, Where art:thou " (solo T. Knight), R. de Lacey ; cornet polka, "Charing Cross" (solo Sergt. J. Woods) ;.finale, "Rule Brittania " and " God save the Queen." UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED Oil the premises at J. a. W. Dutton's, Sankey-st.--ildst. MARRIAGE OF MR. H. S. TIMMIS, OF WIDNES. At Christ Church, Sefton Park, Liverpool, on Thurs- day, there was solemnised the marriage of Mr. H. Sutton Timmis, eldest son of Mr. T. Sutton Timmis J.P., of Cleveley, Allerton and Widnes and Miss Annie Hodgson Horsfall, fourth daughter of Mr. G. H. Horsfall J.P., of Larkfield, Aigburth. There was a large and fashionable congregation to witness the ceremony which was con- ductedby the Rev. Canon Eyre, with the assistance of a full choir. The bride who was given away by her father; wore a beautiful dress of brocaded silk with court train, tulle veil and orange wreath. Her train bearer was Master Alan Hughes, and the bridesmaids were Miss Horsfall, Miss Edith Horsfall, Miss Timmis, Miss Kate Timmis, Miss Rome, Miss Forwood, Miss Nash, and Miss Springmann, all of whom wore dresses of cream silk crepe, with head-dresses of green velvet and mignonette. The groomsmen were Sir W. Pearce (Cordell, Renfrew- shire), Messrs. Lawrence Bradbury (London), H. B. Steele, J. Hornby, T. M. Bingham, G. Timmis, S. Timms, H. Stewart Brown, and J. Nicholson. Subse- quently an "at home" took place at Larkfield, at which a large number of guests were present. The wedding presents numbered 250. UMBRELLAS RE-COVERED OR the premises at J. & W. Dutton's, Sankey-st.—Advt.

div.head: STRANGE ROBBERY AT RUNCORN.
div.p: STRANGE ROBBERY AT RUNCORN.

A young boy named Hardley was brought before Mr. Brundrit and Mr. C. Reynolds at Runcorn Police Court, on Monday, charged with stealing a purse containing 18s. and two pawntickets, from the person of Mary Wat- son, of 60, Sewell-st. On Saturday night Mrs. Watson was standing near the Salvation Army in Ellesmere-st., when she missea her purse. A boy named Sam!. Green, whose home is in Lock-st., said "There is your money," and he placed 18s. in her hand. He said the prisoner had given it to him, and the prisoner was sabsequently apprehended. He said a boy named Savage had given him the money, and he did not know where the purse was. Evidence was given tO show that Savage was at home at the time. Eventually the purse was found in Bridge-st., and handed to Mr. Dutton, the Market In- spector, who handed it to the owner. Superintendent Large said this was the third occasion on which the pri- soner had been brought into Court. Mr. Brundrit said I the Bench did not consider the case quite proved, and they should discharge the prisoner, but they thought he had had something to do with it. They advised his father to take better care of him. The magistrates thanked Green for the way in which he gave his evi- dence, and for the way in which he had acted in the matter. Whenever he got into temptation, they hoped he would act in the same manner.

BOWLING MATCH AT RUNCORN. At the Bridge Hotel Bowling Green on Monday after- noon, a bowling match took place between Wm. Rhodes and Thomas Woods for a stake of £2O. The game was 101 up, and Woods eventually won easily by 28 points. Mr. Robert Wright officiated as umpire. RECOGNITION OF BRAVERY AT RUNCORN. • In recognition of services rendered by J. H. Woodcock, who on the 10th ult. jumped into the canal at Delph Bridge, Runcorn, and rescued a boy named McEwen, son of a cooper, employed at Messrs. Wiggs' works, from drowning, the Royal Humane Society have awarded him 15s.

• WESLEYAN CHAPEL, DITTON. The anniversary services ih connection with the Ditton Wesleyan Chapel were held on Sunday, when two ser- mons were preached, afternoon and evening, by the Rev. G Scott, of Didsbury. In the morning an address to scholars, parents, and friends was delivered by Mr. B. Brown, of Hough Green. There were good congrega- tions at each service, and collections were made in aid of the school funds. BRUNSWICK MUTUAL IMPROVEMENT CLASS, RUNCORN.

About 80 members and friends of this class spent a pleasant afternoon at Helsby• on Saturday. The pro- gramme consisted of an inspection of Messrs. Taylor's works for the manufacture of telegraph instruments, &c., tea at Mr. J. Jeffs' refreshment rooms, a ramble over the hills, and then home by train. Mr. B. Crosby had charge of the arrangements, and Mr. Pearson con- ducted the party through the works, and both gentlemen were thanked for their able services. . _
