RUNCORN FREE LIBRARY COMMITTEE.

- The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday, under the presidency of Mr. T. Riley ; present, Dr. MacLennan, Mr. W. Handley and Mr. W. Hankinson. It was de- cided that the Library, which was closed for stock-tak- ing, should be opened on July Ist, and that in the mean- time a Cotgreaves indicator, purchased for the convenience of borrowers, should be fixed. It was decided to provide a supplementary cattlogue of the books added during the past year, and that the catalogue and three supplements be sold at a charge of 6d.

div.head: FUSTIAN CUTTING MACHINE COMPANY.
div.p: THE FUSTIAN CUTTING MACHINE COMPANY.

The prospectus of this new company appears in our advertising columns and shows that the Com- pany has been formed for the purpose of acquiring through tke Velvet Cutting Machine Syndicate, Limited, cgitain letters patent for improvements in apparatus for cutting weft pile fabrics, together with the machinery and plant belonging to the syndicate. The test experiments which have been made are stated to have evidenced the vast superi- ority of machine cutting over hand frame cutting by expert operatives, and the directors believe that a handsome profit will be made on the new under- taking. As a proof of this it is stated that the members of the Syndicate are so satisfied of the Company's success that they have agreed to sub. scribe for preferred shares to the extent of £lO,OOO so that the amount of the preferred shares sub- scribed for by them will be equivalent to the full amount payable for the patents in cash.

div.head: "SEQUAH, LIMITED."
div.p: "SEQUAH, LIMITED."

_ This is the title of a new company, whose pros- pectus appears in our advertising, columns, and whose operations are already well known, and have been highly commencled in many parts of the coun- try. As will be seen from the prospectus, the Syndicate Directorate of Sequah, Limited, have de- cided to effect a complete re-construction of the Company, with a view to its re-establishment on a much wider ba.,is. The large amount of business done during the past year, an amount said to be un- precedented in the history of patent medicines, would seem to be an ample justification for this pro- ceeding. The rapid development of the business rendered a considerable further increase in its work- ing capital necessary, and an excellent feature is the fact that the business is not a speculative one,founded on possible estimates, but a sound going concern, with a record of large actual and increasing sales. The present proprietors will retain as large an inter- est in the new Company as is allowed by the Public Companies Act, namely, one-third, and the manage- ment will remain precisely .the same as that which has worked so successfully in the past. The shares now offered to the general public present an extremely rare opportunity for sound investment, and the fact of the shares being in the hands of a large number of different individuals, scattered over the country, will of itself tend to promote the pros- perity of the company. Thousands of persons who have had personal knowledge of the manner in which Sequah, Limited, have hitherto conducted their business and the thousands who had derived personal benefit therefrom will join in wishing success and prosperity to the new Company.

div.head: FARNWORTH GRAMMAR SCHOOL.
div.p: FARNWORTH GRAMMAR SCHOOL.

The annual meeting for the distribution of prizes and certificates to the pupils of Farnworth Gram- mar School, was held, on Monday evening, in the schoolroom. There was only a moderate company present. Mr. E. Carey presided, and he was sup- perted on the platform by Messrs. R. Lewis (sec.). E. Barlow, S. Owen, Bullough, Dr. Hurter, W. Har- rison (head master) and J. 0. Jones (assistant master).— Mr. Lewis announced that Major Cross finding it diffi- cult to put in an appearance at the meetlngs of governors had resigned the position of chairman, and Mr. Carey had been selected to fill his place.—Mr. Harrison read the annual report of the school. He said 20 boys were submitted for examination, and they had good reason to congratulate themselves upon the result, as 18 out of that number had obtained certificates. The two boys who had not been so successful only required five more marks each to gain the certificate, while they had passed alonk with the others in all the compulsory subjects, Five special certificates had been awarded to the school, in addition to the class subjects by the College of Pre- ceptors, while their percentage of passes was 90 per cent. against 77.5, the general result of the entire ex- amination of schools. He considered that the results pointed to the schc4 being in efficient working order, but was sorry that the number of pupils was not so large as might be expected from a town like Widnes. Mr. E. Carey having distributed the prizes, said they were to be congratulated upon the success of the school, and in having such masters as Mr. Harrison and Mr. Jones to help them in their work. They could not all get valuable prizes, but they could all be industrious ; and he was glad to hear that the boys of the school had at all events been industrious, though they had not all had equal success in obtaining prizes. He felt• very sorry that the school had not more boys in it, for if they had more pupils the more successful it would become. They would then be able to provide a better playground than they had now, for the benefit of the pupils. The following is a list of the certificates and prizes awarded :—Certificates : Class 1, pass division, R. Lewis and Griffiths. Class 2, Ist division, Hague, Hutton, Pritchard, Priestnell, and Walker; Second division, F,atock. Class 3, Ist division, Dwerryhousc, Mercer, C. , Lewis, Riley, T. Lewis. Roberts, and Valentine; Second division, T. Ireland and W. Fl. Griffiths; Third division, Denny. Prize list lower form : Scripture history, Dwerryhouse ; English language, Ireland and Roberts; English history, C. Lewis; geography, C. Lewis; arith- metic, T. F. Lewis and Dwerryhouse ; French, Dwerry- house and C. Lewis; Latin, Mercer. Upper form: English language, Walker; English history, Walker and Griffiths; geography, GriffithS ; arithmetic, Walker; algebra, Hufton ; Euclid, Hague, Hufton, and Pritchard; book keeping, Griffiths ; French, Friestnall ; Latin, J. T. Griffiths ; electricity and magnetism. Pritchard; chemis- try, Pritchard; drawing, Pritchard; music, H. H. Lewis. Head master's prize for arithmetic, Warham. The customary votes of thanks concluded the proceed- ings.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse, on Tuesday. Mr. Mclntyre presided, and there were present Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. Daywooa, Taylor, Aaron, Lewis, G. Hall, P. Hall, Priestner, Bretherton, Weir, Lowe, Hewitt, Brand- reth, W. Whitlow, H. Linaker (clerk), H. G!Lina- ker (assistant clerk). MR. JONES' APPEAL.

A letter was read from the Local Government Board with respect to the appeal against the election of the Guardians by Mr. W. H. Jones. The Local Government Board referred Mr. Linaker for their decision to a letter they had forwarded to Mr. Jones, a copy of which was enclosed. The letter has been published in this journal. —Mr. Haywood asked what was the reason of certain voting papers not being delivered.—The Assistant Clerk held up a large bundle of papers, and enquired : Would you like it all read P—Mr. Brandreth : It was explained at the time ; I don't think it is worth while. Several members called out "Go on with other business," and the subject dropped.

INVIUTION TO NORTON PRIORY. Lady Brooke wrote asking for permission for the child- ren of the Workhouse to spend the afternoon. and have tea at Norton Priory, on Tuesday, July 15th. Permission was unanimously given.

'UNPAID CALLS. The Clerk reported that the Overseers of Frodsham Lordship, Helsby, and Acton Grange had not paid the calls, and on the proposition of Mr. Taylor, seconded by Mr. Aaron, the Clerk was instructed to write and state that unless the money was paid in 14 days, proceedings would be taken. INCREASE OF SALARIES. The next business was the application of the Matron (Mrs. Cunnah) for an increase of salary, and the Matron for the information of the Board stated that when the Master and she were appointed nearly four years ago, the salary was £7O and £3O per annum, and subject to £5 per annum being paid for each child. In consequence, however, of the Local Government Board fixing the rate for each chili over five years at £l3 per annum, and under five at £6 10s: per annum,the salary was increased to £BO and £4O, as it now stood. With the exception of the first two months of their appointrhent, they had had no paid assistants, and the duties had been arduous I but had been cheerfully performed. Considering that all her salary was now repaid to the Union except £7 10s. per annum, she considered that she had some claim for an increase of salary, or for a reduc-

tion in respect to the charge of maintenance of their three children. Thd'present salary was net adequate for the duties she had to perform, nor did she knew of any- other Union in the country where the charge for the Master's family was so exorbitant, as at the present time more than one quarter of their joint salary was repaid t• the Union, and according to the rule laid down by the Local Government Board provision would have to be made outside when the children attained the aze of 14 years. In conclusion, she would respectfully- state that the Master and herself undertook the appointment under the clear impression that the salary wasa minimum one. —The Assistant Clerk read a statement which showed that Mr. and Mrs. Cunnah were receiving £69 per annum less than the previous Master and Matron and were besides saving the Union the rations for two officers.— In answer to Mr. Whitlow, the Assistant Clerk said the sum total the Master and Matron derived after paying for their children was £Bl —Mr. Whitlow: That's a great deal better than some of us get.—Mr. Aaron: Grumb- ling again.—Mr. Bmndreth said in 1889, the Finance Committee recommended that the joint salary of the Master and Matron should be increased £2O, and, as he still thought they were entitled to this increase, he moved a resolution to that effect.—Mr. Lewis seconded the motion.—Mr. Taylor said the House was very well conducted, and the first thought and consideration in the minds of Mr. and Mrs. Cunnah had been the interests of the ratepayers. Any- one who had observed the manner in which the house was controlled and the economy exercised must feel satis- fied that justice had been done to the ratepayers; and he thought the Board ought to pay them a reasonable sum for their services, and he contended they were not now adequately paid. Nearly the whole of Mrs. Cunnah's salary was returned for the maintenance of her children, and he contended that no woman in her position ought .to be expected to keep her family. Mr. Cunnah was a man of great ability, and fulfilled his duties to the satis- faction of every reasonable individual, and it was not fair to put him in such a position that his wife practically supported the family. Mr. Taylor referred to the extra work performed by Mrs. Cunnah, who had saved the ratepayers considerable eXpensee. He supported the in- crease in order to encourage Mr. and Mrs. Cunnah in their excellent work.—Me. Whitbw said as times were now, not only the matron but the whole of the officials of the Board ought to feel the depression equally with those who supported there. The farming community were the principal support of the Union and they were suffering from a depressed state of trade. He considered that Mr. and Mrs. Cunnah wore well paid according to their duties, and he moved an amendment that there be no increase of salary. Without increasing the expenses the ratepayers had now more burdens than they could meet fairly.--Dr. Gastaldi drew attention to the work performed by the master and matron, and said it would be an injustice if the increase were not granted.—Mr. Heywood said Mrs. Cunnah had done extra work that would have cost the Board £2O per year, and he strongly supported theincrease.—The Chair- man declared the voting equal—seven for and seven against—and he gave his casting vote in favour of the increase because bethought it wasdeserved.—The motion was therefore carried.

div.head: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD.

The monthly meeting of this Board was held at the Town Hall, on Tuesday afternoon. Mr. T. Sutton Timmis presided, and there were also present the Rev. J. Clarke, the Very Rey. Dean Finegan, Messrs. R. Wade Deacon, C. E. Barlow, B. Brown, S. Quinn, and G. H. Danby (clerk).

DISTRICT EDTYCATION COMMITTEE. This Committee reported that during May (four weeks) the numbers of cases summoned before the Com- mittee were the following :—Application for payment of fees, 137; for contravention of Education Act, 224. Fees were recommended to be paid in 120 cases ; refused 17; number of prosecutions before the magistrates, 56; number of convictions, 49; sent to truant school, 7. The minutes were adopted.

SCHOOL MANAGEMENT COMMITTEE. This Committee's minutes contained the following : Recommendation, that the resignation of Miss Clara Mather, assistant mistress, infant department of the West Bank schools, be accepted, the engagement to ter- minate September 30th, 1890. Recommendation, that Mr. R. Holden Davis, having expressed his willingness to give prizes to those pupil teachers who had distinguished themselves in the annual Scripture examination, they beg to recommend, that the best thanks of the Board be given to Mr. R. H. Davis, and that the offer be accep- ted. That they had let the West Bank infant and girl's playground to a tennis club, from six to nine o'clock each evening, until September 27th, 1890, for the sum of 2s. 6d. per week, and fixed the remuneration of the care- taker, for attending to the same, at 2s. 6d. per week. • The minutes were agreed to, and it was resolved that the thanks of the Board should be given to Mr. Davis. FINANCE COMMITTEE.-LARGE LEGAL FEES. In the minutes of the Finance Committee there was a recommendation that the sum of £l4 9s. be paid to Mr. C. Spencley for legal expenses. In answer to a question, 1 the Clerk said these legal charges were for sending bays Its the truant school, &c. They were charges fixed by the magistrates. The Clerk remarked that each boy sent to a truant school cost the Board a guinea.—The Chair- man thought these were monstrous charges to make.— Dean Finegan asked if it was necessary that Mr. Spencley should always get this money.—The Chairman said he was the magistrates' clerk and their executive officer. —Dean Finegan: It is a monopoly. He suggested that a letter might be sent to the magistrates dealing with the eases and saying that the Board thought those were such large charges as to considerably hamper them in sending children away.—The Chairman said if they left the matter over he would promise that it should be looked into.—The subject then dropped. .

- THE 0 .rit3EERS AND THE BOARD'S CALL. The Finance Committee's statement showed that £7OO had been paid into the bank by the overseers on account of the precept. During the present month a further sum of £1,200 had been paid. This was all the business.

div.head: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS:
div.p: PRESCOT BOARD OF GUARDIANS:

The fortnightly meeting of di-A--P-r—esc—ot :Board of Guardians was held at the Union Workhouse, Winston, onThursday afternoon. Mr. W. Tyrer (deputy Chairman) presided and there were also present the Rev. Dean Fine- gan Mr. F. Stapleton-BrethertonJ.P. ex-officio ; Messrs. Johnson, W. Lowe, J. Leatherliarrow, W. Middle- hurst, J. Marsh, R. A. Graves, J. Ranson, G. Davies, .1. Peover, J. Whalley, E. Syde.r, W. Daine, J. Burchall, J. Griffiths, G. E. Chadwick, J. Mercer, W. Borrows, P. Longton, J. Kenwright, J. Birchall, and S. H. Hartley, (clerk.) THE GUARDIANS AND THE LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD. —The Clerk read a long letter from the Local Govern- ment Board, referring to a recent visit to the Guardians by Mr. Henley, one of their Inspectors, in reference to two sums of £194 10s. 10d. and £135 17s. Bd., which had been received by the Guardians on behalf of the townships of Eccleston and Windle, respectively. The letter narrated the .details formerly published, to the effect that contrary to an intimation received from the Local Government Board, the Board of Guardians had credited each township with the total -sum due instead of re-investing the amounts for the permanent benefit of the townships. The Local Government Board wrote that the only course which seemed open to them was to• direct the re-investment of the sums in question, and they would issue a special order for that purpose.—The' Chairman suggested that the Guardians had better re- serve any action until they received a new order from the Local Government Board.—The Clerk said the money had been handed over to the townships to whom it be- longed.—The suggestion of the Chairman was agreed to. _ .

AN ADJOURNED Aumr. Mr. G. Haslehurst, the Government district auditor, forwarded a notification intimating that the audit of the accounts of the town- ship of Eccleston had been postposed until the2sth July. —Mr. Daine asked why the adjournment had been made. —The Clerk said the Assistant Overseer's accounts were not sufficiently completed. ASSISTANT OVERSEERS AND THEIR SALARIES.--Letters wert' read from Mr. John Kitchen (assistant overseer for Parr and Sutton), Mr. H. A. Twist (Windle); and Mr. E. Baxter (Wootton, &c.), intimating that in consequence of the contributions to the county rate being no longer paid out of the poor rate, but out of county and borough rates, the rate of poundage by which they were paid had decreased and was not sufficient remuneration for the uties of the office.—The communications were referred to. the Finance Committee. TENDERS FOR Strerms.—The Guardians considered the tenders for the supplies required at the Workhouse from the 25th I'une to 315 t December next and the fol- lowing were accepted : Flour, &c., Mr. C. P. Reichardt, Fluyton ; groceries, Messrs. James Lees and Co., Elliott- st., Liverpool ; butter and cheese, Messrs. James Lees and Co., Elliott-st., Liverpool; eggs, Mr. John Collins, St. Helens; wine and spirits, Messrs. Mackie and Glad- stone, Liverpool; linen drapery, Mr. J. B. Pratt, Prescot; woollen drapery, Mr. J. B. Pratt, Prescot ; leather. Messrs. John Matthews and Co., Liverpool; boots and• shoes, Messrs. Pocock Bros., London; coals, Messrs. Richard Evans and Co., Haydock ; ironmongery, Messrs. Guthrie and Scrymgeour, St. Helens; earthenware, Mr. Webb, St. Helens; brushes, Workshops for the Blind, Liverpool; coffins, Mr. Joseph Craven, St. Helens; hay and straw, Mr. J. Sumner, Whiston ; milk and fresh , butter, Mr. William Ramsden, Bold. This concluded the business.

Eight fresh cases of cholera and six deaths occurred on Monday at Puebla de Rugat, in the province of Valencia, Spain, and one-death occurred at a neighbouring village. The Royal Sanitary Council has resolved to establish a sanitary cordon round the infected places, and troops to form th? cordon were to leave Valencia, SELF-ACCUSED OF MURDER. Frederick Bedford, who confessed to the Birkenhead on 16th may, 1888, of Frances Maria Wright, an police that he was one of two men concerned in the murder, elderly lady, at 19, Canonbury-tensce, islington,London, was on Thursday brought up on remand at Birkenhead Police Court, and discharged, there being no evidence against him beyond his own confession, and the London police having declined to take any proceedings against him.
BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

div.head: FIGH'I'ING FA3llti•
div.p: A FIGH'I'ING FA3llti•

Michael McDonald and Patrick McDonald ware charged at the Warrington Borough Court, on Monday, with having been drunk and disorderly, and with fighting each other in the Crown and Sceptre yard on Saturday night. The Mayor thought the two defendants belonged to a fighting family as they had been before. the Court previously for the same offence. Michael said he only fought when he was drunk, and Patrick concurred; it was "the ale that did it." A fine of 10s. and costs 0r:14 days was imposed.

div.head: UPSETTING A MAIL CART.
div.p: UPSETTING A MAIL CART.

For having been drunk and disorderly in Irlatn-st., and for having assaulted a girl named Fanny Mcunfield, on Saturday, Wm. Geoghan was fined IN. 'and costs, or 14 days' imprisonment, at the Warrington Borough Police Court, oa Monday. It was stated by Mr. John Moun- field, that the girl, his daughter, was being wheeled in a mail cart, when the prisoner deliberately took hold of the handles of the cart, and upset it on the girl. He did not desire to press the case. The Bench inflicted the penalty mentioned above.

div.head: ANOTHER MARKET THEFT.
div.p: ANOTHER MARKET THEFT.

Mary Ann Evers of Lord Nelson-st., was on Monday, charged at the Warrington Borough Court. with having stolen a pair of boots, valued at is. 9d., from the stall of Joseph Frisby in the Market. It was stated that on Saturday night the prisoner was noticed handling boots on Mr. Frisby's stall, and her manner being suspicious she was watched by a lad who noticed herto take the pair in question and walk away with them. She was followed and given into custody. Prisoner admitted the charge, but said she had had some drink she must have walked away under the impression that she had paid for the boots. A fine of 10s. and costs, £l, was imposed, or 14 days' imprisonment.

div.head: MEMORIAL TO THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: A MEMORIAL TO THE MAGISTRATES.

Ellen Clough, of flopwood-st., was summoned at the Police Court, yesterday, for assaulting a girl named Sarah Owen, on Monday night last. The girl alleged that on the night in question the defendant entered her mother's house and after using threatening lamtuage put her fist in her face. Defendaut denied the alleged offence and said she was always being abused and insulted by the complainant and her mother. She handed to the Bench a paper signed by about a dozen persons, which stated that the complainant and her mother were most *wive to everyone in the street and would not let any- one be comfortable.—The Bench ordered the defendant to pay the costs, and, commenting on the " memorial" handed to them said the, complainant did not appear to have "clean hands" in regard to the matter.

div.head: ALLEGED CASE OF MANSLAUGHTER.
div.p: THE ALLEGED CASE OF MANSLAUGHTER.

The man Peter Morris, who was charged the previous week with the manslaughter of the woman, Emily Bailey, with whom he had cohabited, was again brought before the Warrington Police Court; on Monday morning. The magistrates' clerk said the Coroner's jury had not con- nected the violence received by the woman with her death, but there was no reason why the prisoner should escape punishment altogether. The charge had now been reduced to one of assault. The evidence given at the inquest as to the prisoner kicking the woman and lifting her by the ears was repeated, and the Mayor said there was no doubt the prisoner had been guilty of a very brutal assault on the poor woman, and he would have to go to gaol for four months with hard labour.

div.head: ROW AT BANK QUAY STATION.
div.p: A ROW AT BANK QUAY STATION.

A collier from Wigan-road, Ashton, named Peter Wads- worth, was charged at tho Warrington Borough Court, on Thursday, with having been drunk and disorderly at Bank Quay Station on the previous day, and was also charged with having assaulted Wm. John Holland, the ticket collector. It was stated that he went to the book- ing office at Bank Quay and tendered 21c1. for a ticket for Bryn. This was not the full fare, and the clerk also declined to book prisoner on the ground 4 his being in a beastly state of drunkenness. A row ensued, and pri- soner used his clogs so freely that they had to be taken off his feet. As the assaulted ticket-collector was not in attendance, the magistrates fined the prisoner ss. and costs for the drunkenness. WINDOW SMASHERS BEWARE.

At the Borough Court, yesterday, before Alderman J. Harrison, Frances Riley was summoned for damaging four panes of glass and window frames of the house occupied by Emma Ford, who stated that the defendant threw an iron grid through the window, and did dam- age to the amount of ss. The defendant was ordered to pay the damage in addition to a fine of ss. and costs.— Two lads named James Leonardy and William Beckett were charged with damaging windows of the old foundry, Foundry-street., the property of James Smethurst. The damage was stated to amount 53. The defendants were seen running about the place with a number of other lads. Mr. Smethurst said a great deal of damage had recently been committed, and he had complained to the police several times about it. About a month ago there Were "60 panes broken, and lads were, in the habit of getting over a wall eight or ten feet high.—Mr. Garnett J.P., said that sort of work must be put a stop to w h a strong hand. There was certainly too much trespass- ing and damage going on in the town.—A fine of 2s. 6d. and costs was imposed upon each defeudant.

div.head: AN IRISH "DANCING MASTER " AT WARRINGTON.
div.p: AN IRISH "DANCING MASTER " AT WARRINGTON.

At the Borough Police Court, on Friday, before Alder- man J. Harrison, William Birch, a middle-aged man, who described himself as an Irishman was charged with begging in Horsemarket-st., on the previous day. Police-constable Bell gave evidence that he saw the pri- soner begging, and in his possession was found 4d.— The Bench : Where did you get the money from ? Prisoner: I sang for it.—The Chairman : Then you worked for it ?—Prisoner replied that he never sang Irish songs, but confined his vocal ability to English and Scotch songs.—Alderman Harrison : It is somewhat atrisnge that an Irishman should have a predilection for Scotch songs, is it not ?—Prisoner : I don't belong to Belfast, your honour. I have a silver plate in my head, owing to an injury which I received when I was a lad. I belong to a place called Kilkenny, and I have been a dancing master.—Prisoner was asked if he would leave Warrington jibe was discharged.—Prisoner replied with evident glee: I will run. (Laughter.)—The Chairman: Which way will you go P—Prisoner : Any way you will let me go. I wish I could rua out on my head. I thank your honour.—He was then discharged.

div.head: LOCAL ROMEO.
div.p: A LOCAL ROMEO.

A young fellow named Charles Molyneux, wascharged at the Warrington Borough Court, on Monday with hav- ing on Saturday night, been on the back premises of Dr. Geary, in Bold-st., for an unlawful purpose, to wit, to commit a burglary. P.C. Caldwell said ha was on duty at Market-gate, shortly before eleven at night, when he was informed by Dr. Cleary that there was a man on the back of his premises. On proceeding there he found pri- soner standing on the doorway. He had the small file produced in his possession. Elizabeth Lee, a servant at Dr. Geary's, said she saw prisoner look through holes in the door, and she called out three times "who is there?" and the prisoner replied that he had come to do a job for himself. She afterwards,however,saw him on the roof of the scullery,and he had just jumped down when the officer caught him. In defence, prisoner said he had gone to see a young woman ha knew. He thought the last witnq.ss was her but he found he was mistaken. Hp was not there for an unlawful purpose. The case was adjourned till the next day, when Inspector Cox stated that from inquiries he ascertained that the prisoner was a man of previous good character and was employed by Mr. Prince, Horsemarket-st. The file had been given to him on Sat- urday-by Mr. Prince to get sharpened. Molyneux was then discharged by,the Bench with a warning not to try the same thing on again at anybody's house.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT.
MoNDAT.—Before the Mayor (Alderman Francomb),
Alderman Da'ies,r. Gornall.

WINDOW BREARING.—Mary 'O'Reily was charged with 'being drunk and disorderly, in Buttermarket-st., on Saturday night ad with having broken three panes in the shop window of Mr. Gallop. A fine of 55. and costs, was imposed. DRUNEENNESS.—J. Galvin, drunk and disorderly, in Irlam-st., on Saturday night, fined ss. including costs or 14 days; D. O'Loughlin, drunk and disorderly, in Buttermarket-st., on the 9th inst., fined ss. and costs or 14 days; Catherine Cunningham, drunk and disorderly, Buttermarket-st., 9th June, ss. including costs ; Thomas Bate, drunk and disorderly, in Old-rd., Latchford, on the 7th June, ss. and costs. DRUNK IN CHARGE OF HORSE AND CART.—Charlotte Lingard for having been drunk whilst in charge of a horse and trap at Market-gate, on the 11th June was -fined 58. and costs. Basecu OF THE PEACE. —J. R. Wood and J. Brown - were charged with having committed a breach of the peace by fighting in Dallam-lane, on 7th June. Brown was dismissed, and Wood was bound over for six months.
COAL WAGONS ON THE FOOTPATH.—For wheeling a coal wagon on the footpath, in Bewsey-st., on the 7th June, and thereby causing an obstruction to passengers, P. Monootan, a lad was tined Is. 6d. _
CHIMNEY 024 FraE.—For allowing the chnnnies of their dwelling-house to be on fire J. Lester and M. A. Foy, were each fined ls._ _ _
itrEp—net.—Before Mr. R. Garnett an the Mayor (Alder-
man Francomb)

A gRIP CANAL WORKER IN TROUBLE.—Wm. Lawless, who said he was employed on a Ship Canal dredger at Rixton, was charged with having been drunk in Rutter- market-st., on the previous evening. It was stated that he had got into the hands of bad characters and bad been robbed of some money. He was fined is. MILITANT FEMALEs:—Martha McCann and Margaret Preston, two women were charged with having been drunk and fighting in Bank-st., on' the previors night, and were each fined ss. and costs. _ -

..... DRIINEENNESS.—John Olives and James Young were charged with having been drunk and disorderly in Church-st., the previous evening. Oliver was ciismissed, but Young was tined ss. and costs or seven days. Eliza- beth Peers,for having been drunk and soliciting prostitu- tion in Fennel-st., was committed to gaol for 14 days hard labour.

Scoot. Cascs.—Patrick Dolly, labourer, Oliver-street, waa charged with neglecting to send his son regularly to school. Mr. Riley, school attendance Inspector, said that aithuugh the lad was 13 years of age, he had not

WARRINGTON OCCASIONAL COURT. TUESDAY.—Before Mr. Edward Greenall. MISCELLANEOUS. James Williams, a Ship Canal labourer, was charged with damaging growing crops at Grappenlaall, the property of Mr. Thomas Jeffs, farmer. The loss is estimated at 2s. The case was clearly proved, and the defendant was. fined 20s. and costs, or 14 day's imprisonment. He wentto prison in default of payment. —Richard Moss, of no settled abode, was charged with sleeping in an out-building at Croft, on the 17th inst., and ; fined 55.—William Hares,charged with being drunk at Riaton, on the 16th inst., as fined ss. and costs. Not being able to pay the fine, the defendants were commit- ted to gaol.
WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS. WEDNESDAY.—Before _Mr._ S. Rigby (in the chair), and
Mr. J. Manson. A Damn FINED. —John William Fairclough was sum- moned for being asleep whi;st in charge of a horse and cart, at Sankey, on the 13th of Tune, and was fined and costs.

UI4SIIIZZLED Doos.—ThomasLshaw was summoned for allowing his deg to beat large unmuzzled,at Penketh, on the 3rd of June. Fined 2s. andcosts.—John Hunt was snmmoned for a similar offence at Penketh, on the 9th of June, and fined Is. and costs.
BICYCLES WITHOUT Lzerrrs.—William Snash and Edwin Amis, were both fined Is. and costs, for riding bicycles without lights, on the night of the 13th of June, at Penketh

ALLEGED ASSAULT.—WiIIiam Robinson was summoned for assaulting Wm. Williams on the 2nd of June at Bur- tonwood.—Mr. A. Browne appeared for the complainant and said that his client worked with the defendant at Collins Green Colliery. On the day in question they had gone down the pit to their work, where his client said to the defendant" What about that 45." meaning a bill which the defendant owed. The defendant said nothing, but struck his client a blow in the neck.—A witness was called who said that the defendant did not strike the complainant but attempted to do so.—The case was dis- missed.

ASSAULT ON A BAILIFF. —Albert Atherton, teamsman, was summoned for having,. on the 9th of June, at San- key, violently assaulted John Browne (county court bailiff).—Mr. Knowles, of Widnes, appeared for the de- fendant, whilst Mr. Longton, of Warrington, represented the complainant. Mr. Longton stated that on the day in question his client was given a warrant to arrest the defendant for non-payment of lls. 6d. He went to de- fendant's house and saw him working on a harry. He (the complainant) produced the warrant, and told the defendant to go with him. Defendant said his wife had paid the money that morning, but on his client asking for the receipt, it was not forthcoming. Complainant then attempted to get on the luny, but the defendant seized a pickel and made a lunge at him, grazing his cheek, and he also struck him across the shoulder with the pickel. The man was afterwards arrested with the assistance of another bailiff. This statement was borne out by the complainant and a bailiff named Thomas Fraime.—Mr. Knowles said that the warrant was not produced until after the assault was committed.—A man named Thomas Hogan corroborated this statement.— The Bench considered the case proved,, and fined the de- fendant 10s. and costs. or 14 days' hard labour. UNPROVOKED ASSAULI3.—A young woman named Mary Stokes was summoned for assaulting Susan Lee, at Sankey, on the 16th of June.—From the evidence it appeared that on the day in question, whilstcomplainant was in the street,. defendant came up, and without provocation struck her in the face and knocked his head against the wall. Defendant was fined 55. and costs, or in default seven days' imprisonment with hard labour. STRAYING HORSES.-A. farmer, named John Henley, was fined 2s. 6d. and costs for allowing horses belonging to him to stray on the highway at Rixton, on the sth of June.

UNAPPRECIATED VOCALISTS,—TWO men, named Joseph Stringer and William Knowles, were summoned for being drunk and disorderly on the 30th of May at Croft. Mr. Knowles, of Widnes, appeared for the defence. P.C. 1,025 said that on the night in question he saw the defendants come of a public-house drunk. They went down the lane shouting and singing the chorus of the song "The Farmer'S Boy." He told them several times to home quietly but they refused. Mr. Knowles called witnesses for the defence, but the Bench fined the defendants ss. and costs each.

TRESPASSING.—Four youths named James Elliman, Philip Davies, James Ford, and Henry Smith were tres- passing in the field of William Robinson, farmer, on the 13th June, at Poulton, doing damage to the meadow grass to the amount of ls.—They were each fined 2s. and costs and ordered to pay the damage.—Edward Bate was fined 2s. and costs for a similar offence in the same field on the 13th of June.

THEFT OF BEr-c-is..—Three lads named George Fogg, George James Hankinson, and Edward Bate, were sum- moned for stealing two ducks, value 55., the property of James Perrin, Orford, last Sunday. The prosecutor said that at four o'clock in the evening of the day in question he saw the ducks sate. He identified those produced as his property.—A farm labourer in the employ of the pro- secutor said he saw the defendants coming from Hough- ton Green on the Sunday in question. On observing him they decamped and threw the ducks into a pond.— Samuel Cowbarne said he saw the defendants running towards him. One of them said to him "Don't stop us mate. We've only been getting dandelions."—Mr. A. Browne, who appeared for the defence, said that the lads had always borne good characters.—The Bench imposed a fine of 10s. and costs on each or in default 14 days hard labour.

RUNCORN PETTY SESSIONS. MONDAT.—Before Mr. John Brundrit and Mr. Charles Reynolds. DRUNKENNESS.—Joseph Hancock. Joseph Martindale, and Jas. Duncan, were each fined 10s. and costs for being drunk and disorderly. BEGGING.—Edward Thornton, a young man, was charged with begging in Church-st., on Saturday night and he was sentenced to seven days hard labour. Does AT Lanoe.—A fine of Eid. and costs Bs. ed. was imposed upon Jas. Helsby, of Stone Hills, and Peter Darlington, of Westen, for permitting their dogs te be at large unmuzzled. WHEN DOGS BEGIN TO BARK AND BlTE.—Sanimel Barnes, a young man, was summoned for cruelly ill- treating a dog ; and Frederick Richardson was summoned for assaulting Barnes. It appeared that on the evening of the 9th inst., Barnes was passing Richardgon's stable in Stone Hills Lane, when his dog and a dog belonging to Richardson commenced to fight. Barnes kicked Richardson's dog three times and to prevent hina admin- istering a fourth kick Richardson knocked him down with his fist. A number of witnesses were called and Mr. Brundrit in ordering each person to pay the costs, said it was a very trumpery matter that ought never to have occupied the time of the court. MILK DEALERS BEWARE I—Thomas Finch, of Astmoor, was charged with furiously driving to the danger of foot- passengers. P.C. Woodrow deposed that about seven o'clock on the morning of the ninth, he saw the defend- ant driving a horse and cart containing milk cans along Church-st., in the direction of Runcorn Bridge. He was whipping the horse and causing the animal to gallop at its utmost speed. He followed on to the Bridge and the defendant said he had been driving fast on purpose to get the milk Across the river.—The'defendant said the horse had shied.—Mr. Superintendent Large said there would be more farmers summoned if they did not drive more carefully. In order to get their milk despatched they drove down Bridge-st. at a furious rate and it was a wonder no one had been hurt. M/SCELLANEOUS. Everything ^ conspired to make the 23rd annual sports of the Widnes'Athletic Club, on Friday and Saturday, an unqualified suctess. Good prizes attracted a largeentry, ' the N.C.A.A. favoured the meeting with two champion- ship contests, and the weather being highly favourable, f 7 ;the public attended in their thousands. The 'committee ,are thus amply compensated for the failure of last year's .venture, when the weather had a most prejudicial effect on the attendance, and an adverse balance was the un- pleasant result. The arrangements were on theusual complete and satisfactory scale, and the secretary, Mr. W. Davies, and all concerned, are to be congratulated on the admirable sport provided both on Friday and Saturday.

Irerhaps the most interesting feature of the festival' waa,the capital form, shown by Whittick in the scratch races. He cantered ima most easy manner for the mile charnpionship,and he alsovron the half-mile race with rid!. cutout; ease. A popular victory was that of Morgan, of Fairfiekl, in the 100 yards scratch, which he traversed+ in evea time, and just proved six inches better than that' well-known sprinter, Wilcdck. Of the local men, Kelly had the best reception when he secured the mile handicap from at large number of competitors. In the bicycle eventallailey, of St. Helens) secured the local mile and the open mile contests, in both of which he had good, starts, and was never overtaken.

CHEM Chess is an increasingly popular game in Lancashire and Cheshire. Seven years ago there were not more than three or four organised chess.clubs in Lancashire, now there are close on forty ; and in the same period the num- ber of matches played during the season has increased from about a dozen to over a hundred. Chess has also made great progress in Cheshire, which has now its County Association, with which a number of clubs are affiliated, and in connection with which there is an annual contest for a valuable/silver cup, now held by the BirkenheadClub.

With a view of giving a further impetus to the popu- P i arity of the game n the two counties a largely attended meeting of club delegates WU& held at the Manchester Chess Club en Saturday afternoon, under the presidency of Mr. E. Haslem. Warrington was amongst the clubs represented by its secretary, Mr., L. Chandler. The main object of the meeting was to arrange matches for next season, and at the outset a discussion arose as to the advisability of classifying the dubs into groups accord- ing to strength, with a view of establisbag combinations similar to football " leagues." This idea was at once taken'up by. the delegates, and a, resolution having been passed M favour of the Mrmation of leagues, a committee wact appointed to make the necessary classi&cation of the clubs.

The consultation of the committee ended in the follow- ing classification of. clubs :—First League; Manchester Club, 2nd, Liverpool North Etad4 'Liverpool Imperial, Bolton, and Burnley.—Second, League: Manchester Club 3rd, Clydesdale, Piccadilly, Rossendale, Crewe, Jewish, Bury„Rochdale, Warrington, Wigan Y.M.C.A., and Bolton 2nd.—Third Leag,nol: Manchester Club 4th, Manchester Y.M.C.A., Farnworth,, Exchange, Atherton, North Manchester Shaw, Chureh, Manchester Grammar School t Bredhury;Ardnick Co-operative, Clydesdale 2nd, and Pincadilly 2nd. —Fourth League :Randebottom,Hulme Libera; Blachley, Radcliffe, Higher Crompton St. John's' Institute, People's Institute, and St. Ch'risto- pher's.,

The-suggestlon was that elch club should play with every other in its cwn " league,7 but it was found that some of ,the delegates present were not empowered to make so many engagements, and others were desirous of consulting their committees otr the subject. In the end the arrangement of matches was-left to thediscretion of the representatives, who were urged,, however, to select opponcnts, as far as possible, from the groups in which their clubs were placed. The formal meeting then broke up and delegates began filling up their' match lists. In the course of an hour over seventy snatches for next season, nearly all in accordance with league lists, were arrangeeb

CRUXIM The Australian cricketers sustain their fourth defeat in the present tour on Saturday at Xottingham. After such a succession of disasters, the •Celonials must not be surprised if the question of "star " prices is raised by the puhlic, who are called upon to pay more to see he Australians than the Lancashire, Nottingham, or Surtey elevens Yorkshire added to their successes by defeating Middlesex :and Lancashire obtainedian easy victory over Warwickshire.

The general opinion with regardto thecolonials is that first impressions were right, and that they are not a for- midable lot. It was not, .perhaps, a matter of surprise that they should be beaten by an Eleven of England and by the Marylebone Club, .but the manner in which they have gone down before Yerkshire and Nottinghamshire serioualy lowers their preteasions to represent the full strength of Australia. They, may,, of course, hereafter inflict-defeats as severo a)0 they have received, but men who hive been beaten four times within the short com- pass ot falar weeks cannot be“regardecl as "champions."

A RAILWAY STATION ON FIRE. Arumlaming fire omurred on, Monday afternoon at the Caledonian Railway Station, Edinburgh. The fire origin- ated in or near the lamproom, and extended to the west end'of the station, a large number of carriages being ignited. The station, which, was. built of wood, was more than half destroyed. Most of the packages were got out of the left lvggage tae. Twenty carriages were defrayed and a dozen ninth, damaged. These lattea were drawn out oPthe flames. The refreshment-rooms were partially dectroyed by lite,, and a great deal of dam, age was done by water. The total loss is :stimated L,E),,000.

COMPENSATION. A LIVELY MEETING.

On Tuesday evening a public meeting, to protest a,gainst the compensation clauses of the Local Taxation Bill, was held in the Congregational Schoolroom, Lymm. Mr. Joseph Thorp presided. The room was well filled. Several members of the Warrington Licensed Victuallers' Association were kresent, as well as one or two Lymm publicans. he Chairman was supported on the platform by the chev• Win. Evans (Primitive Methodist), the Rev. -b",flB. Clay (Congregationalist), Lymm; and Messrs. Der ton. G. L. Welford, I. Mort. Thos. Ashton, and Theo lore Nash. „ Mr. Dutton said a letter had been received from the icev•John Gunnell (superintendent ot the Warrington esicyan Circuit), who had been announced as one of w sPeakers. It read as follows :—"4, Palmyra-square, arriogton. June 18, 1890. My dear sir,—l greatly re- gret that L shall be from home on Tuesday, and shall not oe able to attend the Protest meeting at Lymm.' Will _no do me the favour of saying how heartily I sympathise with the object of the meeting, and how disappointed I :111 that I am unable to further that object by my voice .117°te 7" Mr. Edwin Brown, of Lymm, wrote : •-iarrogate, June 16th, 1890. Dear Mr. Thorp,—lam ni extremely sorry I cannot be With you at the meeting to. . atiorrow• night, I should like to have raised my voice Clause entered my protest • against the Compensation ,•Ises of the Bill now before Parliament. I hope your 7a'ootion t will be as united as at the Band of Hope demons- tain and that the meeting will speak with no uncer n - s' frn,„ -tulo, and that from every Temperance Society, c(;•" every pulpit, and from every true patriot of his 60,11, trY, a voice should ,go forth from Lyn= which t'e-echo through the Halls of Westminster declaring ° Compensation.' " Mr. I. S. Leadam, the Liberal icea, for the division had forwarded the following ticlidate •ter M Mr. Dutton :—"'ll7, St. George's-square, S.W., tne I 17, 1890. My dear Mr. Dutton,—lt is with interest the tlizrido that the friends of temperance are holding protest against the compensation clauses of in ee„l4,_calTaxation Bill, now being forced through Parlia- viir oY the Government.• No one would wish to deal bat) the tenant of a well-conducted public-house in any ere a: considerate and equitable spirit. THE EXTENSION OF WARRINGTON.
OPPOSITION FROM STOCKTON HEATH.

On Tuesday evening a meeting of ratepayers in Stockton Heath and district was held at St. Thomas's Schoolroom, Stockton Heath, for the pur- pose of protesting against the inclusion of part of the township of Appleton-with-Hull in the pro- posed extension of the Warrington borough bound- ary. Mr. Thomr.s Hall presided, and was sup,3orted by Mr. J. Charlton Parr, C.C., and Mr. Robert Davies.—Amongst a fair attehdance were the Rev. J. C. Rolfe, Mr. ki.'Darbyshire, Mr. W. R. DePrez, Mr. D. Hooley, Mr. W. Weldby, Mr. Hallows, Mr. J. Derbyshire, Mr. W. Darlington, Mr. J. Pennington, Mr. J. Fryer, Mr. Seward, Mr. Vere Davies, and Mr. William ostock. The CHAIRMAN said that the proposal of the Warring- ton Corporation was to take from the township of Apple- ton something like £3,000 rateable value. Most of that sum being upon houses, made the matter all the more serious. The rateable value of the land proposed to be taken over was only £B5. The inhabitants of that dis- trict had already to contribute towards a sanitary rate for the sewers from which the farmers got no direct benefit. Three-fourths of that rate was levied upon property and the remaining fourth upon land, so that if £3,000 rate- able value were lost it would make the '\special sanitary rate a very heavy matter for the ratepayers who were eft in the township. He concluded by moving, "That this meeting objects strongly to the attempt made by the Corporation of Warrington in their Warrington Exten- sion Water and Improvement Bill to detach a portion of the township of Appleton-with-Hull from the rest of the township, and add it te the borough of Warrington, thereby depriving the township of the propemus part and okproperty of about £3,000 a year rateable value, and leaving the agricultural part and the village of Stockton Heath to bear the burden of the poor and the maintenance of the roads, which measure about 15 miles, after allowing far the length repaired •by the County Council. And, further, that this meeting calls upon the County Council to use its utmost efforts to pre- ven tso great an injustice being done as is proposed by he said Bill." (Applause.) Mr. WILLIA.3i DARLINGTON, sen., seconded the resolu- tion.

Mr. ROBERT DAVIES, speaking in support of the resolu- tion, said that in the 11th and l2th clauses of the Bill the ratepayers and inhabitants of the district proposed to be included were promised participation in the •• privileges, benefits, and advantages" enjoyed by the ratepayers and inhabitants of the borough, but nothing was said about the liabilities. It left that part to the imagination. (Laughter, and a Voice :" No concession at all.) The object'of the extension was to get not only the £3,000 ratable property which was included in the piece the Corporation proposed to take from Appleton, but also to get half of the Ship Canal; so that the rating which Appleton ought to get from the Ship Canal would be halved with Warrington. Looking at the question from the broad ground of the principles of justice, it was not fair that the mercantile portion of the township should be taken away, leaving what was to a great extent the agriculturtl part to struggle on by itself. At the present time, thanks to several liberal contributors, he man- gers of the Stockton Heath Schools had contrived to keep the schools out of debt. Supposing, however, a School Board were forced upon them, the children from the north side of the canal, being unable on account of the distance to go to Warrington, would have to attend their schools. Under all the circumstances, he eia not think that they were justified in losing any part of their rat- able area. (Hear, hear.) He cordially concurred in the desire of the Coui;ty Council to secure an expression of opinion from that neighbourhood. Without wishing the borough any harm, it must be remembered that justice was justice, and the inhabitants of that district were certainly justified in appearing at that meeting and asking the County Council to take up their case. (Ap- plause.) MT. J. CHARLTON PARR, C.C.,said he would like it to be clearly understood that he was present as an individual, and anything he might say was really not official. He dissociated himself, for the time being, from the County Council. He had that afternoon had the opportunity of meeting the Parliamentary Committee of the County Council, and he might tell that meeting that the Council would do what they considered the very best for that part of the county, and the county generally. (Hear, hear.) The injustice which had been pointed out was perfectly apparent to the Committee, and personally he entirely agreed with the resolution which had been pro- posed. There might possibly be ways and means of arranging the matter without coming to an open con- test. He had certain grounds for believing that, although that measure was contemplated, it wasnot contemplated entirely without compensation, and if compensation to the satisfaction of the district could be arranged, it might not be impossible to arrive at a modes vivendi with the Corporation. (Hear, hear.) If some arrangement could be made to meet the exigencies of the case it would be Preferable before actually declaring war against the Corporation. He would suggest that a deputation be appointed to wait upon the Corporation on the question of compensation. _ _
The esolution was submitted and carried unanimously, and it was decided, instead of appointing a deputation, to leave the matter in the hands of the County Council.

On the mntion of Mr. ROBERT Dena, seconded by Mr. WILLIAM BOSTOCK, it was agreed that the expenses of the meeting be paid out of the rates of the town- ship. Votes of thanks to the Chairman and overseers brought the meeting to a close.

div.head: ANOTHER PLOT AGAINST THE CZAR.
div.p: ANOTHER PLOT AGAINST THE CZAR.

A Berlin telegram says it is said that the St. Peters- burg police have discovered a widespread conspiracy' against the Czar's life. The Imperial palace at Gatschina is said to have, been undermined, as was the Winter Palace years ago. The Czar is said to be very depressed in consequence of the discovery of the plot. The police force in the capital has been reinforced, and the guards at the Imperial Palace have been doubled. Numerous arrests have been made.
