div.head: Ztttero to tbe Obitor.
div.p: Ztttero to tbe Obitor.
"DISEASE AND STENCH FROM THE WAR- RINGTON DRAINS,"

Sir,—l was very much pleased to see a letter in yoar last issue on this subject, over the signature of Thomas Fletcher. In common with my fellow ratepayers, I have felt and suffered from the nuisance, but being of humble circumstances I have not liked to complain of the municipal management of what are called my betters. I have, however, a ncse with which to smell, and in Warrington it is kept occupied in a very unplea- sant manner sometimes. lam very glad that Mr. Fletcher has spoken out on the matter, which so nearly concerns the health as well as the comfort of the commu- nity, and it is to be hoped other persons of influence will follow suit.—Yours truly, •A HUMBLE RATEPAYER. Warrington, June 19, 1890,

INTOXICANTS IN WARRINGTON WORKHOUSE. Sir,—An opinion appears to be held by many people in Warrington that a large amount of money is spent unnecessarily, on liquors for the inmates of the Union Workhouse. The subject was explained by Mr. Gill some time ago but as he onh dealt with the amount for two weeks many people still express dissatisfaction. I append a statement ot all sums expended on liquors during the year ending March 2nd, 1890, which, I think, shows that the amount is not very large, especially when it is known that that the whole amount, except a pint of beer to each inmate on Christmas Day, was ordered medicinally by the Union doctor. Cost of ale, wine, and spirits for 12 months at the Wurrington Union Workhouse, 1890. Ale £5 Us. 2d., brandy Bs. 9d„ wine £lO 9s. 2d., whiskey, £l9 3s. 9d., total £35 12s. 10d., averaging 13s. 84d. or id. per head per week.—Yours truly, JOSEPH DOBSON. Lumb Brook, June 20th, 1890.

div.head: SHOP ASSISTANTS' HALF-HOLIDAY.
div.p: SHOP ASSISTANTS' HALF-HOLIDAY.

Sir,—Thereis an old proverb known to everyone, "If at first you don't succeed try, try, try again." Well, sir, I have tried, tried again, and with your permission I would like to try a third time. They say a third time pays for all. I hope it does for lam trying for a good cause, viz., "The assistants' half-holiday movement." I sup- pose Warrington will be behind hand in this as well as in other respect's. But it has been behind hand long enough, and I think it is quite time for a stiito be made. Already some shops are having a half-holiday, but then the" some "are not all, and I would like to see all the shops closed one half-day in the week. The summer time is now with us, and I hope before the summer has passed to see an assistants' cricket club formed. Eh, wouldn't it be grand to fancy that we could have a half-day to oursilives ! There:are in other towns cricket, football, tennis, rambling, sketching and other clubs for the assistants' recreation. " Why not in War- rington ?" Other towns can afford to give their assist- ants a few hours more. "Why not Warrington ? " The Stores, the hair dressers, several boot shops can see their way clear to benefit their assistants in this respect. Why not the other trades ? Is there not one trades- man who will support this letter and do good to his fellow creatures, who, poor mortals, have to work,work, work, from Monday morning until Saturday night with a paltry hour or two at night. Work and sleep is the assistant's life, the old proverb "all work and no play. , etc.," being put to one side, and," We don't pay you to have half-holidays" is put up instead. I should like some meetings to be held. Now that the summer nights are on we should have open-air meetings. There are many places for these, and they would do just as good, and cost nothing, and then if we could get some influential gentleman to support us, I think we could secure half-a-dayto ourselves. You young men or young women, who read this, please join with me in agitating. If you think you would not like your employer to know of you writing, you can do as lam doing—sign with a nom de plume. The editor has my address, for I myself do not know how my employer thinks on this subject. I hope sincerely something further will be done, for I am looking forward to the first afternoon when the shops shall with one consent close.—l remain yours respectfully, GROCER. Warrington, June 16th, 1890.

HOW PUBLIC MONEY IS SOMETIMES SPENT. Sir,—A couple of paragraphs that I have read in a re- cent issue of " Truth " afford considerable material for thought, and involve a question that is of no little im- portance to the rate-paying public at large—the question of how the money contributed in rates is sometimes frit- tered away. The first paragraph lefers to a remarkable piece of expenditure at Blackpool, and the second to the cost incurred by a Bolton deputation, at the expense of the ratepayers. At a meeting of the Council of the sea- side borough, we are told, an "audacious member," who greatly shocked many of his colleagues by declaring that "he objected to extravagance, especially in refresh- ments," called attention to a little bill in the accounts of the Licensing Committee. On May Bth five gentlemen belonging to the committee, and three officials, were en- gaged in granting licenses (presumably for cabs, con- veyances, &c., for hire), and the charges for refresh- ments were as follows :—Dinners, ; wine, £3 135.; suppers, Ll is. ; drinks and cigars, 10s. 6d. ; and other drinks, £2 as. 9d. ; total £9 7s. 2d. In regard to the Bolton instance, " Truth " says "Bolton is another town where service in the Town Council is not without its compensating pleasures. Last week a protest was very properly made in the Council— though without effect, of course—against the appoint- ment of Alderman Miles, the chairman of the Gas Com- mittee, and the gas engineer to attend, at the cost of the borough funds, the annual meeting of the Gas Institute, which is to be held at Byde. The meeting lasts three 11 days, and the business,' the Bolton Town Council was informed, • includes smoking concerts, rose shows, musical soirees, water excursions, and promenade con- certs.' A visit to the Isle of Wight with such a pro- gramme in view, will naturally be attractive to Alder- man Miles and the gas engineer, but the Bolton rate- payers must be unusually generous people jf they are con- tent to pay for holiday excursions of this kind." Such examples as these are so glaring as to require little or no comment; they are what one might call such very palpable frauds; but all the same they naturally lead to the suggestion that what is taking place in one borough may te a greater or lesser extent be taking place in others. There has at different times past grumbling been heard in Warrington as to the cost of deputa- tions, and, as a great principle is involved, it would be well if ratepayers would be on the alert in regard to such matters. It is true we are rather inclined to be sleepy municipally, but, if we must needs sleep, let us do so with one eye open, so to speak. I am not alleging anything against the local Corporation, but we do occasionally read a very terse entry in the minutes to the effect that Messrs. So and Ss had attended such and such a place as a deputation. If a deputation is a necessity let it " deputate, but are not the public entitled to a detailed statement of the expense incurred, and how it has been incurred ? I believe it is the custom for Corporation officials and members of Committees to attend the Municipal Corporations, and other Association meetings at the expense of the rates, and surely this in itself is a waste of money. If anyone wishes to attend these meetings, why shouldn't he do it at his own expense P Such cases, separately considered, may not seem of much importance, but collectively they may represent a good round sum in the course ot the year. Anyway, whether the amount is little or big, the principle of the thing remains, and ratepayers should constantly be ON THE LOOK OUT. Warrington, June, 1890.

div.head: COMPENSATION.
div.p: COMPENSATION.

"WE DON'T OWE, AND WE WON'T PAY." We do not owe, and will not pay, The Brewers any compensation! Answer the Bill with a clear nay— Its shame alike and condemnation. Loud the national storm now rages— Hurls them on the rovks of reason ; Doomed to wreck are Goschen's wages, His bill's a glaring fraud and treason.

For all our Laws, and all our Judges, Denounce such unjust compensation, And our loved nation owes its gru.dges, To the trade of drink and ruination. Lo !the Brewers' numerous victims Loudly call for retribution! May their wailings work convictions Deep in each heart in our nation. Rise! ye humane souls ! The battle Is now raging on each hand; "Be not like dumb driven cattle !" But weild your arms and firmly stand. Boldly face the nation's foes— The greedy Brewers and their friends; Strike, stoutly strike your moral blows Till God the rightful victory sends

Surely, brewers and publicans are making wealth nnemnh T ...40_1c; for instance, at the brewers in our midst who have made thousands and tens of thousands in a very short period. Meantime their traffic has ruined many thousands, among whom have doubtless been some of the reader's own flesh and blood—victims who loved you dearly, and whom you dearly loved in return. But, alas ! what has the brewer's cursed traffic dene? Ruined homes, health, business, character, and the fair fame of our helpless, fallen sisters. Shall we tnen rest satisfied with this sad state of things, and allow the brewers to put their greedy hands still deeper into the public purse? No, never! ..

Oh ! ye humane Englishmen—sons of nob.e sires, whose love and courage led your brave fathers to break the chains which bound the slaves—haste ye, nor rest till you have freed your brother slaves at home !

Your country is already groaning under the gall- ing yoke of brewers and publicans; and should the principki of the "Public-house Endowment Bill "be acceeded to, woe to the social and moral improve- ment of our dear old England. Up, now! and do your duty in the interest of your wives, your children, yourselves, your homes, and your country; for man and God, for time and for eternity. Having right and God on your side, march fearlessly on in His mighty strength until our be- loved country shall be free from the thraldom under which it now groans, and old England is won for humanity and its Christ!
Pray y-e him to hasten the happy day !—Yours sincerely,
A WORKING-M AN.
Warrington, Jane 19th, 1890.

div.head: TTTE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JUNE 21, 1890.
div.p: TTTE EXAMINER. SATURDAY, JUNE 21, 1890.
THE SHIP CANAL.

ILLICIT DRINK TRAFFIC: HEAVY PENALTIES. At the Chester County Petty Sessions, held at Chester Castle, on Saturday afternoon, before the Rev. E. A. P. Cambpell, the Hon. C. T. Parker, and Mr. B. C. Roberts, a woman named Jane Mortimore, who did not appear, was summoned for selling beer on the Ship Canal, with- out having previously obtained a license, on the 11th May. Constable Leah, of Liscard, deposed that whilst in plain clothes Le, together with other officers, entered defendant's hut on the Ship Canal at Ellesmere Port. He sat down. and a man who was with him called for a quart of beer, which was served and he paid for it. At that time there were seventeen men sitting with jugs and glasses of beer before them on the premises. Three more quarts of beer were called for and paid for. Wit- ness discovered concealed in 3, corner an eighteen-gallon barrel containing beer, and two quart bottles and one pint bottle full of beer. He also found in the scullery an empty eighteen-gallon barrel, the tap of which had not been taken out. He informed defendant that she would be summoned, and she said" All right." A few days after the search was made defendant absconded. In 1888, when defendant and her husband were living at Ellesmere Port, the latter was summoned for selling drink without a license at the same hut, and fined £lo.—The magistrates considered the case to be a very serious one, and inflicted a fine of £25 and costs, or in default of distress three months' imprisonment.

div.head: ANOTHER CASE.
div.p: ANOTHER CASE.

_ George Diamond, who also did not put in an appear- ance, was summoned for a similar offence. Constable Leah, of Liscard, stated that about ten o'clock on the morning of the 11th ult, he visited defendant's hut at Ellesmere Port, and found twelve men sitting around a table, on which were jugs and glasses partly fullof beer. When he approached the hut at the back someone called out to him, "We have no beer here for anyone."—lnspec- tor Brittain deposed to searching defendant's hut on the 23rd ult, when the defendant was absent, but while his wife was there. He found an eighteen-gallon barrel of beer on stillage (from which he took a sample), an empty beer barrel,and under a bed a half-gallon whisky jar. He told defendant's wife that her husband would be sum- moned, and she answered, " All right."—The Bench did not consider this so serious a case as the previous one, but as there had been a former conviction, they would impose a fine of £l2 10s. and costs, or in default two months' imprisonment. SIR JOSEPH LEE ON THE SHIP CANAL.

What is popularly known as the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board excursion took place on Saturday, and was favoured with glorious weather. The ostensible object of the outing is to afford the members of the board and a select company of invited guests an opportunity of inspecting the lightships, buoys, &c., which mark the channels at the mouth of the river, but it is in reality a marine picnic on an extended scale, and is therefore looked forward to by those who are the fortunate re- cipients of invitations to be present with a considerable amount of pleasurable anticipation. Last year the excur- sion was not held in consequence of the illness and death of Mr. T. D. Hornby, the chairman of the Dock Board. The splendid Isle of Man steamer Mona's Queen, with Captain Hill in command, was chartered for the excur- sion, and there was a large number of guests. Shortly before six, the company assembled in the saloon for dinner, the chairman of the Dock Board pre- siding, and being supported on the right by the Mayor of Liverpool and Sir Joseph Lee, and on tile left by the Mayors of Birkenhead and Bootle. After dinner, the loyal toasts were honoured, and the chairman then gave " Prosperity to the Corporations of Liverpool, Birken- head, and Bootle:
Tie Mayor of Liverpool, in responding, referred to the efforts now being made by the Dock Board to deepen the water on the Mersey Bar, and to improve the Canada Dock entrance.

The Chairman next proposed the toast of "The Visit- ors," coupling with it the name of Sir Joseph Lee, the deputy-chairman of the Manchester Ship Canal Com- pany. After referring to the negotiations which had led up to the final passing of the Ship Canal Bill in Parlia- ment and to the success with which the monetary diffi- culty had bcen overcome, he said he was not going to make any remarks as to the wishes or fears they might have regarding the canal. There had been dividedin- terests, as was well known, and it would be mere insin- cerity on his part to hide that. The Dock Board had opposed the Canal Company in the past, and they might find cause to do so again, but there was no reason what- ever why any contention they might have to the scheme should be extended to the persons connected with it (hear, hear). He wished with the relationships which must take place between the Dock Board and the com- munity of Liverpool on the one hand, and the directors of the Manchester Ship Canal-on the other, that person- al amity and good friendship, and all those attributes which contribute to smoothness of action in their rela- tions, might exist (applause). With that view he asked them, in drinking to the toast, to bear in mind Sir Joseph Lee and the directors of the Ship Canal Company (applause). The toasts was very heartily received. .

Sir Joseph Lee, in responding, said he felt highly honoured in being selected by the chairman to give expression to the thanks of the guests who were present on that occasion. The chairman had referred to the company and the enterprise to which he had the honour to belong. The Manchester Ship Canal was the effort of a number of merchants of Manchester. He was quite aware that in Liverpool they had been looked upon as a sort of hat Their, but he assured them they were in their own estimation—and he trusted they would be in theirs also before long—veritable lambs (laughter). As to the enterprise and those connected with Liverpool. and more particularly the Dock Board, he was one of those who earnestly and seriously believed that it would be of the greatest advantage to the port of Liverpool. He was quite aware that that was not the popular opinion, but at the same time he fearlessly expressed it, and he thought he had given a considerable amount of thought and attention and interest to that question before he in- duced all his friends to put so much capital into the enterprise. They might rest assured that the people of Manchester had not the slighest feeling of enmity against these who were in Liverpool, but they had every des're to work in the most cordial manner, not only with Liverpool merchants, but more particularly with the Mersey Docks and Harbour Board. (Applause.) They had one interest to serve, and that was the interest of the Lancashire industry. They had within a radius of forty-eight miles of Manchester a population of 7,250,000 people, and bethought there was room enough within that population to supply all their needs, and he thought I they had reason for wishing to create Manchester a port by having that great population around it. He could only say, on behalf of his colleagues, that any overtures that came from Liverpool should be most seriously con- sidered, and that Liverpool should have from them—to use a diplomatic phrase—the "most favoured nation" treatment, and ho trusted they might receive the same treatment in return. He felt that this enterprise, if properly worked, would be of advantage both to the city of Liverpool, and to the city of Manchester, and he trusted they might rely upon the Mersey Dock Board endeavouring to show that kindliness—he could not say that enthusiasm—but that favoured treatment towards their enterprise to which he thought they were entitled. (Applause.)
Sir Joseph C. Lee, deputy-chairman of the Manches- ter ship Canal Company, expects that the canal will be opened in about eighteen months, most probably early in 1892.

div.head: ST. HELENS TOWN CLERKSHIP.
div.p: THE ST. HELENS TOWN CLERKSHIP.

Mr. Thomas Bre'wit., who has been Town-clerk of St. Helens for seventeen years, tendered his resigna- viva to tha Parliamentary and Official Staffs Com- mittee of the Corporation on Wednesday, his reason being that he is not prepared to give up his private practice. Mr. Brewis, in addition to the town-clerk- ship; is clerk to the borough justices, clerk to the Burial-B6ard, clerk to the Governors of Cowley Charity, and has a large practice in the town. The Town Council' at their last meeting -adopted a resolution to the effect that the time had arrived when.they should have a Town- clerk to devote the whole of his time to the duties of the office and it was expected that Mr. Brewis would require a strong inducement to give up such lucrative appoint- ments as those stated. The Council will probably fix £7OO or £750 as ths sum to be. paid to the new Town- clerk, who may have to commence his duties in January, 1891. Among the probable candidates are Mr. Jeeves, deputy Town-clerk, Mr. Robert VV. H. Thomas, solicitor, Mr. Davidson. deputy magistrates' clerk, all of St. Helens, and Mr. J. H. Craik, Town-clerk of Batley, and lex-deputy clerk of St. Helens. ,

div.head: SINGULAR CONTEST AT WIDNES.
div.p: SINGULAR CONTEST AT WIDNES.

For some time past Tommy Burns, the hero of Runcorn Bridge, has been open to throw down a challenge for £lOO to dive from Runcorn Bridge into the Mersey, swim ashore, and thpn run ten miles, but no one ven- tured to oppose him until Carlisle D. Graham, of America, who has twice navigated the Niagara Rapids in a barrel and has jumped off several high structures in the States, arrived on these shores. A match was made for £25 a side, and the event came off on Thursday at one o'clock. Graham, who was disguised as a working mechanic, dropped into the water from the end of a short rope, while Burns attired in women's garments took a header from the ledge outside the footwalk. In the swim to the shore, a distance of about 350 yards, Burns, although he did not dive, until his opponent had touched the water, arrived on shore fully two minutes in advance. After a "rub down" in the Mersey Hotel, the competitors appeared on the Bowling Green where a track had been marked out, and commenced the ten mile race. Graham led the way at a slow speed,and Burns was content to trot behind him for several miles, when he went a lap ahead, and eventually won easily by 4 laps and 10 yards, in the time of one hour and a quar- ter. The quickest time fora mite was seven minutes and a half, and it was palpable that Burns, who is a noted runner, could have given his opponent a few miles start, and "lost him." Mr. W. H. Wright, of the Zoological Vaults, was the referee.

div.head: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
div.p: THINGS HEARD AND SEEN

That the election of Mr. Samuel Taylor to the position of chairman of Runcorn Board of Commis- sioners will be hailed with satisfaction by all sec- tions of the ratepayers. That he might have occupied the chair several years ago, but he resolutely declined the honour to which he was entitled by length of service, business ability and integrity of character. That Mr. Lightburn retired after a very successful years" work, and each member present at the meet- ing, on Wednesday, added his tribute to the good qualities he had displayed in managing the town's business during his year of office. That the effort which is being made provide a horse ambulance for the hospitals of Widnes is meeting with considerable success, and the promo- ters have no doubt as to being able to obtain the £lOO which is required. That the strike of salt cake men at Widnes Alkali Company's Works has ended in a victory of the men, who have been conceded the 2d. per ton advance and 6d. extra for Sunday labour. Mr. P. J. King the organiser of the Chemical Labourer Union has taken a prominent part in the struggle. That about 6,000 people assembled on the shores of the Mersey, on Thursday, to witness Graham and Burns dive 80 feet into the Mersey. The English- man won the contest with ridiculous ease.

That pieces of timber, of all sorts and sizes, are continually floating up and down the river, some- times about a foot beneath the surface, and some time the hero of these daring feats will be alighting on one of these pieces of " wreckage "and, probably, have to be fished out with a boathook. •

That the several hundreds of persons who pay for admission to Runcoin Bridge on these occasions, is a nice addition to the revenue of the Railway Com- pany, and, perhaps,were it not for this, the company would put a stop to these dangerous acquatic dis- plays from the lofty structure.
THE OUTBREAK OF PLEURO- PNEUMONIA. ANOTHER OUTBREAK IN WARRINGTON.

A further outbreak of pleuro-pneumonia has taken place in Warrington among cows belonging to Mr. John Wainwrignt, of Buttermarket-et. One animal which was suffering from the disease was destroyed yesterday morning, and other four, which had been in contact with the infected cow, were slaughtered in the afternoon. The fact that two cows at Arpley had been in contact with those above mentioned has been reported to the county authoritie‘, Wand the animals will be dealt with by them. THE COMPENSATION: A HEAVY BILL.

At their meeting on Wednesday, the Warrington Sanitary Committee passed accounts for £347, as compensation to persons within the borough whose cattle have been slaughtered in consequence of the outbreak of pleuro-pneumonia.

div.head: TIIE OUTBREAK AT APPLETON.
div.p: TIIE OUTBREAK AT APPLETON.

Nine cows and heifers have during the week been slaughtered on the farm of Mr. Peter Simpson, ot Appleton, two of these animals having been suffer- ing from the disease. As the infected cattle had been in connection with a herd of seventeen belong- ing to Mr. Joseph Knowles, the whole of this lot has also been slaughtered by order of the county author- ities, although only. one of I hem was found to have the disease upon it.

div.head: OUTBREAK AT PADGATE.
div.p: OUTBREAK AT PADGATE.

An outbreak of pleuro-pneumonia occurred at Tidy-lane Farm, Padgate, in the occupation of Mr. William Bennett. The disease manifested itself in one fat cow, which was immediately slaughtered. Subsequently it was found necessary to slaughter 22 head of cattle which had been in contact with the former beast.

div.head: TILE_ DISEASE AT CROFT.
div.p: TILE_ DISEASE AT CROFT.

An outbreak of pleuro-pneumonia was discovered amongst some cattle on Miss Brideoake's farm, at Little Town. Croft. It appears that a cow took ill, and was attended by Mr. Bennett, VS., of Leigh. On Monday it was found necessary to destroy it, as it was supposed to be suffering from the above com- plaint. Superintendent Weir and Mr. Darwell, V.S., of Leigh, examined the animal, and it is under- stood the remainder of the stock, consisting of two COWS, two stirks, and four calves have since been killed.

MR. CHAPLIN ON TIIE OUTBREAK. In the House of Coinmons, on Friday, Colonel Blundell asked the President of the Board of Agri- culture whether the Agricultural Department was aware that pleuro-pneumonia had broken out in the districts of Wigan. Pemberton, and Newton, Lanca- shire; whether in the four cases which had occurred the cattle had been bougnt from the same firm of cattle dealers; and whether the inspector was taken to only one of several farms belonging to the firm of eattle dealers in question.—Mr. Chaplin : Yes, sir. I am aware that there have unfortunately been out- breaks of pleuro-pneumonia in the districts of Wigan and Newton, but we have received no returns from Pemberton. In the case of five recent out- breaks in the neighbourhood of Wigan and Warring- ton, it has been ascertained by the inspector of the Board that the diseased animals were bought of a local dealer at Padgate, who has professed his in- ability to give any information as to the origin of the cattle. I have no information as to whether the inspector was taken to only one of the several farms belonging to the firm referred to in the ques- tion.
FRODSIIAM.

ANNIVERSARY SERVICES AT HELSBY.--011 Sunday two sermons were preached in the Wesleyan Chapel, by the Rev. E. H. Jackson, of Warrington. The collections amounted to £l47s. 6d. PAROCHIAL COMMITTEES.—At the monthly meeting of these Committees, held at the Town Hall, Frodsham, on Friday evening. Colonel Ashton presiding, a letter was read from the Rev. H. R. Blogg, vicar of Vrodsham, call- ing the Committees' attention to the great want of a public water supply, and stating that unless steps are taken to procure such a supply the attention of the Local Government Board will be directed thereto. After some discussion, it was decided to defer the consideration of the letter to the next meeting, when the position of the Committees as regards the Frodsham Gas and Water Company's Act wilrhavebeen ascertained.—The Inspector of Nuisances reported that he had received complaints with respect to the landing of bones, &c., at the Frodshans Railway Station,andthatbhe had been in communication with the railway authorities, and they had promised to attend to the matter complained of.—An application was made on behalf of Mr. T. Davies for certificates of occu- pation of seven new cottages erected by him, situate at Marsh Greens, when it was resolved that the Authority be recommended to grant such certificates.

div.head: TILE MUSEUMS ASSOCIATION.
div.p: TILE MUSEUMS ASSOCIATION.

The first annual meeting of the Museums Asso- ciation has been held at the Free Public 31useum, Liverpool, this week, under the presidency of the dev, H. H. Higgins, M.A., the chairman of the Museum Sub-Committee of that institution. Dele- gates were present from twenty museums in various parts of the country, the representatives of the Warrington Museum being Mr. Councillor H. Roberts, vice-chairman; Mr. Greening, chairman of the bluseum Sub-Committee; and Mr. MadeleY, curator In his inaugural ad. iress delivered on Tues- day evening, the president, after giving an account of Conrad Gesner, the "father of museums," des- cribed some of the novel appliances used in the ILiverpool Museum, and concluded with claiming that the highest work of the museum is to kindle in the hearts of its visitors that wonder and sympathy which are really the "Now Knowledge" to be gained by the study of the works of nature. The papers read were all of a very practical charac- ter. Professor Boyd Dawkins, F.R S., discoursed with his usual lucidity upon "Museum Organ- ization and Arrangement," as exhibited by the Manchester Museum at Owens College. Mr. Rudler, of the Geological Survey, in making "Suggestions for aid inthe &termination of Natural History Specimens," accurately des- cribed the difficulties under which museums' especially the smaller ones, labour in dealing with specimens in so many different branches of science, each of which requires the aid of a specially quali- fied expert. The plan of co-operative action which he sketched is one which, if carried out, will remove many of these difficulties. Mr. Chard, assistant in the Liverpool Museum, read a capital paper des- cribing the system of circulating cabinets of speci- mens amongst the elementary schools in Liverpool, which has been carried on with such gratifying success, diiring the last six years. The ,cabinets themselves were exhibited in the Museum, and attracted very great interest amongst the members. 'Mr. Cameron, J.P. (Sunderland;, read a very sug- gestive paper on "The best means of , making museums attractive to the public "—a subject which cropped up on several occasions during the discussions. Lamenting the ignorance, in regard to science, of the great mass of museum visitors, which the present system of populareducation does little to remove, he advocated amongst other aids the use of English, rather than Latin names; the arrangement of the cases and rooms so as to make prominent the classification of the specimens; and the avoiding of crowded cases. The Museum should be made the head-quarters of the scientific institutions of the district. During a long discus- cussion,a curious difference appeared in the experi-' ence of different places in regard to the popularity of evening opening. "Museum Cases and Visitors' by Mr. Howarth (Sheffield), and "Winter evening lectures " by Mr. Paden (Li v erpool), dealt with other views of the same subject, and contained useful information based on experience. The social arrange- ments made by the local committee were very elaborate, and were carried out with entire success. Luncheon was provided each day, the visitors being entertained by the Mayor, on Wednesday, whilst the reception in the museum by the Museum, Library, and Arts Committee, on Tuesday evening, was fol- lowed by excursions to Chester, and on the Mersey the following days; and on Thursday evening Mr. J. L. Bowes. the Japanese consul, gave a conver- sazione to the members at which the Museum, which he has built to contain his magnificent collection of Japanese art .work, was opened by the Mayor of Liverpool. The entertainment was of the most elaborate character, and was attended by some 600 persons. It was announced that the next meeting of the Association would be held at Cambridge.

Sr. MARY'S CRllRCH.—Special sermons were preached at St. Mary's Church, on Sunday, .1?y the Rev. J. A. Hayden, M.A., organising secretary on behalf of Church education throughout England and Wales: There were good'congregations and the amount received in collec- tions was £8 4s. 9d.

POLICE COURT.-At this court on Monday, before Mr. G. B. DewhuAt and Dr. Brabazon, Frank Massey and Frederick Gilberts were charged with being drunk and disorderly in the village on Saturday night.—P.C. Griffiths proved the case. He • stated that Massey was very troublesome on the way to the Police Station.— Massej was fined ss. and costs (12s. 4d.) and' Gilbert ss. including costs.

BAPTIST CHAPEL.—The anniversary services which were conducted in the above chapel isn Sunday were very successful. The preacher, aftern6on and evening, , was Mr. H. E. Greenwood, of Halifax. and the congrega- tions were very large, especially at the evening service, when the little chapel was crowded, many being unable to gain admittance. The collections for the clay realised £2O. Mn. BRUNNER, M.P. THE PLEURO PNEUMONIA OTJTERBAKS,--JOIMI Marsh, farmer, Rostherne, was summoned for causing a cow to be removed without a licence into an infected area, in contravention of the Contagious Diseases, (Animals) Act, 1888. Warren, farmer, Bol- lington, was summoned for removing two cows into an I infected area without a licence, on the 4th June. A fine of is and 15s. 6d. costs was imposed.—Robert Oldfield , farmer, Lymm, was summoned for causing nine cows to be removed in a pleuro pneumonia infected area, with- out a licence, on the 6th June.—Edward Boyle was sum- moned for removing the above cows. P.C. Ennion proved the case, and defendants were each fined is. and costs.

ASSAIILT.—Esther Sutton, a widow,, was summoned for assaulting Ellen Dixon, an old woman, at Lynam, on the 31st May, and was bound cver in the sum of LS to keep the peace for six months. MAINTENANCE ORDERB.—Joseph Asprey, and William Asprey, Lymm, were ordered to contribute is. per week to the maintainance of their father who had become chargeable to the Altrincham Union.—John Darlington, milk seller, Manchester, was ordered to contribute is. 6d. per week towards the naaintainance of his mother. DAMAGING SUEDES AT THELNALL. —William Pearson,, a youth employed on the Ship Canal, was summoned for damaging the shrubs of Admiral Parry, on the Ist. June,, and doing damage to the amount of Is.—Defendant was discharged with a caution. ALLEGED SUNDAY DRINKING AP LYMM.—Jane Macree,, of the Church Inn, Lymm, was summoned for permitt- ing drunkenness on her licensed premises and William OkMeld, Ashton-under-Lyne, was summoned, for being drunk on the premises,. at 4.150 n the 18th May.—Mr. Fletcher, solicitor, Northwich, appeared for the police and asked the magistrates to assist the police in putting down the drunkenness which prevailed in Lymm on Sunday through excursions parties coming inte the town and being served at the public-houses.—Mr. flockin, solicitor, Manchester, appeared for the defence,, and; it was contended that Oldfieki did net dine at her house, and had no think there whatever. He must have come in the house with the others and fell asleep. Aftes: several witnesses had been examined the charge against Mrs. Macree was dismissed, and Oldfield -was also dis- missed —Peter Howard, landlord of the Stamford Arms, Bollingtan„ was summoned for keeping hhouse open on Sunday the ;25th May, during prohil.ited hours., and Thomas Brannon, Patrick Merry, John Kelly, of Altrin- cham, were summoned for being drank on licensed premises—Mr. Fletcher, Northwich, appeared for the prosecution, and Mr. Hockin, Manchester, represented the defendants.—For the defence Mr. Hockin said that his clients' predecessor had served persons from Altrincham on Sundays for 45 years, and his action had not been challenged. After hearing evideace the magistrates said the cases would be dismissed. They, however, thought it was a dangerous thing to supply drink to anyone com- ing from Altrineham.

Miss Victoria Sackville West, eldest daughter of Lord Sackville, late British Minister at Washington, was married on Tuesday afternoon to her cousin, Mr, Lionel Sackville West, prospective heir to the title and to the estates of Knole, and eldest son of Colonel Sackville West, of Bangor,

div.head: LATEST NEWS.
div.p: LATEST NEWS.

THREE MEN DROWNED. Six men, in the employ of a florist in King's-rd., Chelsea, went for a row on the Thames when by some means the boat was capsized and the occupants all thrown into the water. Three of them were rescued, but the other three were drowned. SUSPECTED MURDER OF A COOK. The body of a young woman named Elizabeth Wyatt, who belonged to Exeter, and had been in the employ of a draper in Porchester-road, Royal Oak, as cook, has been found in Regent's Canal, bearing 5u..11 marks of violence, that the police think she has laet with foul play.

A BIG PURCHASE. Mr. S. C. Lister, of Bradford, chai I man of Lister and Co., silk manufacturers, Bradford, has purchased the Acton Manor Estate and Coal Mines between Normanton and Pontefract. The price to be paid is £lBO,OOO. There are 1,100 acres of land with coal beds, including the well-known Stanley Main and Haigh Moor seams. The Lister Mills use about 200 tons of coal per day.

div.head: YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.-FRIDAY.
div.p: YESTERDAY'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS.-FRIDAY.

MISCELLANEOUS.—The Metropolitan Police Provisional Order Bill was read a third time.--Lord NORTON moved for a return of all money voted by Parliament for ele- mentary and technical education in the United Kingdom, and concluded by moving that elementary education should be more distinctly defined in the code and the cost of public instructions above such limits should be met by fees or exhibitions.—Earl Cranbrook agreed to the return but declined to discuss questions of elementary and technical education as defined by the Education Act. —The motion was withdrawn. A Select Committee on the motion of the Bishop of Peterborough was appointed to inquire into children's life insurances.—The Municipal Elections Scotland Bill was read a third time. The House then adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS—FRIDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at three o'clock. QumTwigs, &C.—Mr. BALFOUR replying to Mr. John Morley, said the funds at the disposal of the Commission under /rish Land Purchase Acts would, he expected, be exhausted in about 14 months.—Lord GEO. HAMILTON informed Sir Thomas Esmonde, that an inquiry had been ordered into the circumstances of the mutiny on H.M.S. Egeria.—Sir. J. FERGUSSON replying to Sir T. Esmond, said the necessary steps had been taken to put the Samoan Convention into force, bat time was required to make local arrangements.

THE NEW POLICE COMMISSIONER.-10. MArrnews an- nounced the appointment of Sir Edward Bradford as Commissioner of the Metropolitan Police, in succession to Mr. Munro. He had, he said, rendered distinguished service in India. (Cheers and laughter.) THE LONDCrN POLICE.—The House then went into com- mittee on the police vote. Sir W. HARCOURT condemned the way in which the Home Secretary had managed the metropolitan police. He viewed the conflict between the Home Office and Scotland Yard with regret and sur- prise, because the result was dissatisfaction, and discon- tent, results that had attended the four years' adminis- tration of the present Home Secretary. He censured the attempt to appoint Mr. Ruggles Brise as successor to Colonel Pearson, and he said Mr. Munro had grounds for hisretirement,. and as regarded the Police Bill. the Home Secretary had allowed the Chief Commissioner-to resign, and gather round him as their champion the police force of the metropolis, and the consequence was that the pensions could not be settled on the old terms—the rate- payers would have to suffer in increased demands owing to the mismanagement of the Home Secretary.—The Home Secretary defended his action in the matter. He had discussed the appointment of Mr. Ruggles Brise with the Chief Commissioner but the moment he found it would be unpopular he gave the matter up, and no one could be more surprised than he was at the Chief Com- missioners resignation. As to the pensions bills, he had framed the scheme as far as his financial conscience would allow.

Some Italian journalists have interviewed Kos- suth, at Superga. He is afflicted with slowly pro- gressing cataract, but he himself believes that death will arrive sooner than blindness. He lives in retirement. He declines to see visitors, saying that having retired from the world, the world ought to forget him. But he still writes, working regu- larly till near midnight. He walks on the hills in the morning, and dines alone at noon. He intends, if possible, to live in future at Naples, where he expects to be next autumn. "The tallest school-girl in the world," a German contemporary assures us, lives at Rieduaun, near Sterzing. She is in hereleventh year, and is about six feet in height. She is taller than any woman in that community. A showman from Vienna has paid a visit to her parents, and offered them a good round sum to allow him to exhibit to the world so much feminine beauty. Bat the parents have no desire, they say, to part with their" Maderl " (little girl) for any amount of money, though they have no objection to an occasional "At Borne."

FATAL COLLISION. The Maryport steamship West Cumberland has been lost in collision while on a Voyage from Carthagena to Mostyn. With the exception of Mr. Thornber, the second engineer, the crew were saved. Mr. Thornber's wedding was fixed for Wednesday, and in the midst of the preparations for the marriage a telegam was received at Whitehaven stating that he had been drowned. It is supposed that he was below at the time of the collision and went down with the ship, 410, IMPORTANT CAUTION.
